Chapter 9 described a system with a single number: one coordinate, one equation and one frequency. Such a model is enough for a weight on a cantilever or for a machine on mounts that moves only vertically. Real systems, however, have several parts that move at the same time. A structure with two floors (stropa) has two horizontal displacements, one for each floor. A pin in which two bars meet can move in two directions. A machine on mounts also tilts, besides bouncing. A bar cut into sixteen finite elements from chapter 7 has sixteen nodes and each has its own displacement. How many numbers describe the motion of such a system? How do these numbers move if we displace the system once and release it? And how do we compute the motion caused by a force of arbitrary shape?

The answer rests on an idea we already know from section 8.13.3. Among all motions some are simple: all coordinates move in step, with the same frequency, and reach zero together. Such motions are modes of vibration (definition 8.122). The chapter will show that a system with \(n\) degrees of freedom has \(n\) such modes, that every free motion is their sum, and that a motion driven by a force also splits into motions along the modes. Each mode obeys the equation with one degree of freedom from chapter 9, so all we know about one degree of freedom is used once for each mode.

What is new here? Chapter 8 found the modes of order two with a \(2 \times 2\) determinant. For order \(n\) the book has no determinants (it treats them only for orders two and three), and we do not need them: we shall prove the theorem on modes by finding a smallest value, as in chapter 2 we proved the theorem on the principal directions of a symmetric matrix (theorem 2.61). Chapter 9 added damping and force for one coordinate, here we get them for \(n\) coordinates. It is also new that we must be able to assemble the mass matrix, not only the stiffness matrix, and that the orders \(n\) of computer models reach into the tens and hundreds.

The route is this. In the first section (10.1) we write the equation of motion for \(n\) coordinates and show where the matrices in it come from. In the second (10.2) we ask at which frequencies and in which shapes the system can vibrate so that all coordinates move in step. For an order larger than two the answer needs a theorem, which we prove in the third section (10.3). In the fourth (10.4) we use it to split the free motion, in the fifth (10.5) we treat systems that can move as a rigid body. The sixth section (10.6) shows how to estimate a frequency from an approximate shape without solving the whole problem. The seventh (10.7) shows how the mass of a bar is shared among its nodes, the eighth (10.8) uses the estimates for approximate computations. In the ninth section (10.9) we add damping and a force of arbitrary shape, in the tenth (10.10) a harmonic force, in the eleventh (10.11) we show how an additional mass on a spring calms the vibration of a cantilever, and in the last (10.12) how to compute the motion step by step in time when splitting into modes is not enough.

Four models of ours will accompany us, and we fix their numbers when we use them: a frame with two floors, the cantilever of two bars from chapter 4 with a mass at the joint, a steel bar of finite elements, and a machine on mounts that also rocks besides bouncing. The first section introduces the first, the second and the last.

10.1 Equations of motion of a system with several degrees of freedom (gibalne enačbe sistema z več prostostnimi stopnjami)

What equation describes small motions of a system with several coordinates about equilibrium, and where do the matrices in it come from? Chapter 9 showed this for one coordinate (theorem 9.3) and chapter 8 for \(n\) coordinates without damping and without an external force (theorem 8.118). Here we combine the two. First we look at a simple system with two coordinates, on which we shall test everything as we go.

10.1.1 The frame with two floors (okvir z dvema stropoma)

Frame A is our laboratory model (figure 10.1). Two rigid floors (strop) have a mass \(m = 500\) kg each. The lower floor stands on the ground on two steel columns (stebri), the upper one on the lower one, again on two columns. All columns are \(h = 1\) m long and have the \(20\ \text{mm} \times 40\ \text{mm}\) cross section from chapter 5. The section is mounted so that the column bends in the direction of the 40 mm side, so \(I = 1{,}0667\cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^4\) and \(EI = 20\,906{,}7\ \text{N m}^2\), as for the cantilever in section 5.9.2. Each column is clamped at both ends: at the bottom into the ground or into the lower floor, at the top into the upper floor, and it cannot rotate in the clamp. The floors move only horizontally. The displacement of the lower floor from equilibrium is denoted \(q_1\), that of the upper floor \(q_2\), both positive to the right.

Our model has two idealizations: the columns have no mass and the floors do not rotate. Real columns have the mass \(\rho A h = 7800 \cdot 8\cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 1\ \text{kg} = 6{,}24\) kg, two columns below a floor together 12,48 kg, which is 2,5 % of the mass of a floor. A real floor has beams that bend a little and soften the clamp of the column somewhat, so the real stiffness is somewhat smaller than ours. We do not count the shortening of the columns along the axis, which is of second order for small displacements.

How much force does a floor need to move by \(q\)? A column that cannot move or rotate at the lower clamp, and moves at the upper clamp without rotating, is the cantilever from section 5.9.5, loaded at the free end with a force \(F_{\mathrm{y}}\) and with a couple \(M_0\) that prevents the rotation. By equation (5.59) the displacement and the slope of the end are

\[v(h) = \frac{F_{\mathrm{y}}\,h^3}{3EI} + \frac{M_0\,h^2}{2EI} , \qquad v'(h) = \frac{F_{\mathrm{y}}\,h^2}{2EI} + \frac{M_0\,h}{EI} .\]

The end does not rotate, \(v'(h) = 0\), so \(M_0 = -F_{\mathrm{y}} h/2\) and

\[v(h) = \frac{F_{\mathrm{y}}\,h^3}{3EI} - \frac{F_{\mathrm{y}}\,h^3}{4EI} = \frac{F_{\mathrm{y}}\,h^3}{12EI} .\]

The force that moves the end of the column by \(v\) is therefore \(F_{\mathrm{y}} = (12EI/h^3)\,v\), which is the force of a spring with the stiffness

\[k_{\mathrm{s}} = \frac{12EI}{h^3} = 250\,880\ \text{N/m} .\]

This is four times the stiffness of a cantilever with a free end, \(3EI/h^3 = 62\,720\) N/m (the force \(F_{\mathrm{y}} h^3/(3EI)\) from the equation for \(v(h)\) without the couple). The reason is the couple \(F_{\mathrm{y}} h/2\), which keeps the end parallel to the initial position: its part of the displacement is opposite to the displacement due to the force and reduces it from \(F_{\mathrm{y}} h^3/(3EI)\) to \(F_{\mathrm{y}} h^3/(12EI)\) (figure 10.2). The two columns between the ground and the lower floor, or between the lower and the upper floor, together we call a storey (etaža). Their forces add, so the stiffness of a storey (storey stiffness, togost etaže) is

\[k = 2k_{\mathrm{s}} = 501\,760\ \text{N/m} .\]

The same holds for the upper storey: both ends of its columns move but do not rotate, and the force depends only on the difference of the displacements, since a rigid displacement of the columns causes no force.

Why does the axis have the shape of an S? There is no load along the column, so the shear force is constant, \(V = F_{\mathrm{y}}\), and by the differential relations (corollary 5.11) the moment satisfies \(M' = -V = -F_{\mathrm{y}}\). At the end \(M(h) = M_0 = -F_{\mathrm{y}} h/2\), so \(M(x) = F_{\mathrm{y}}\,(h/2 - x)\). The moment is zero at \(x = h/2\) and has opposite signs on the two sides of this point. The curvature is proportional to the moment, \(v'' = M/(EI)\) (theorem 5.35), so the lower half of the column curves to one side, the upper half to the other.

Now we can write the equations of motion of the frame. First with Newton, then with Lagrange.

Example 10.1 Equation of motion of the frame with two floors (gibalna enačba okvira z dvema stropoma)

Frame A as above, on floor \(i\) let a horizontal external force \(Q_{\mathrm{i}}(t)\) act, positive to the right. We look for the equations for \(q_1(t)\) and \(q_2(t)\).

First way, forces on the floors.

  1. A floor is a rigid body that moves horizontally, so by theorem 8.72 the mass times the acceleration equals the sum of the horizontal forces: \(m\ddot{q}_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum F_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  2. The ends of the lower pair of columns are displaced relative to each other by \(q_1\) (the lower end is in the ground). The pair acts on the lower floor with the force \(-k\,q_1\), since the force on the end of a column equals the stiffness times the relative displacement of the ends and points towards equilibrium.
  3. The ends of the upper pair of columns are displaced relative to each other by \(q_2 - q_1\). It acts on the upper floor with the force \(-k\,(q_2 - q_1)\) and on the lower floor with the opposite force \(+k\,(q_2 - q_1)\) by the law of action and reaction (section 2.1).
  4. The equation of the lower floor is \(m\ddot{q}_1 = -k q_1 + k (q_2 - q_1) + Q_1\), of the upper one \(m\ddot{q}_2 = -k (q_2 - q_1) + Q_2\). We move the terms with \(q\) to the left:
    \[\begin{aligned} m\ddot{q}_1 + 2k\,q_1 - k\,q_2 &= Q_1 , \\ m\ddot{q}_2 - k\,q_1 + k\,q_2 &= Q_2 . \end{aligned}\]

Second way, Lagrange's equations.

  1. The kinetic energy is \(T = \tfrac12 m\dot{q}_1^2 + \tfrac12 m\dot{q}_2^2\) (theorem 8.84).
  2. Each pair of columns behaves as a spring with the stiffness \(k\) with respect to the relative displacement of its ends. If the relative displacement is \(\delta\), the force grows from zero to \(k\delta\), its work is \(\int_0^\delta k s\,\mathrm{d}s = \tfrac12 k\delta^2\) (section 4.1) and this work is stored as potential energy. The relative displacement of the lower pair is \(q_1\), of the upper \(q_2 - q_1\), so \(V = \tfrac12 k q_1^2 + \tfrac12 k (q_2 - q_1)^2\).
  3. The derivatives are \(\partial V/\partial q_1 = k q_1 - k(q_2 - q_1) = 2k q_1 - k q_2\) and \(\partial V/\partial q_2 = k(q_2 - q_1)\). The external force on floor \(i\) has the generalized force \(Q_{\mathrm{i}}\), because its point of application moves by \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) (definition 8.50).
  4. The kinetic energy does not contain the coordinates, so \(\partial T/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} = 0\) and \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\dfrac{\partial T}{\partial\dot{q}_{\mathrm{s}}} = m\ddot{q}_{\mathrm{s}}\). By theorem 8.88 therefore \(m\ddot{q}_{\mathrm{s}} + \partial V/\partial q_{\mathrm{s}} = Q_{\mathrm{s}}\), which equals the equations of step 4.

In matrix form

\[\begin{aligned} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} m & 0 \\ 0 & m \end{bmatrix}}_{\mat{M}}\begin{bmatrix} \ddot{q}_1 \\ \ddot{q}_2 \end{bmatrix} \\ &\quad + \underbrace{k\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mat{K}}\begin{bmatrix} q_1 \\ q_2 \end{bmatrix} \\ &= \begin{bmatrix} Q_1 \\ Q_2 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad k = 501\,760\ \text{N/m} , \ m = 500\ \text{kg} . \end{aligned} \tag{10.1}\]

The matrix \(\mat K\) is the Hessian matrix of the potential \(V\) (definition 8.59): \(\partial^2 V/\partial q_1^2 = 2k\), \(\partial^2 V/\partial q_1\partial q_2 = -k\), \(\partial^2 V/\partial q_2^2 = k\) (SymPy). The equation is exactly linear, because \(V\) is a quadratic function and \(\mat M\) is constant, so the remainder from theorem 8.118 is zero.

Source: CK section 8.1 and Example 8.1 (PDF p. 230): Newton's laws for a system of springs and masses, among the models a building with three floors, and the matrix form (8.1) (PDF p. 229). We did not find a frame with two floors in the sources. The model, the storey stiffness from section 5.9.5 and the numbers are ours.

Why does \(\mat K\) have this form? The element \(K_{22} = k\) is the stiffness of one storey, because the upper floor is held only by the upper pair of columns. The element \(K_{11} = 2k\) is the sum of both stiffnesses, because a displacement of the lower floor shifts the ends of both pairs of columns. The off-diagonal element \(K_{21} = -k\) says that when we move the lower floor to the right, the upper pair pulls the upper floor after the lower one with the force \(k\), so we must hold it with the force \(-k\).

10.1.2 The equation of motion for \(n\) coordinates (gibalna enačba za \(n\) koordinat)

The frame is a special case. What equation holds for a system with \(n\) coordinates that also has dampers? Damper \(k\) (definition 9.1) has a coefficient \(c_{\mathrm{k}} \ge 0\) and joins the points \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(B_{\mathrm{k}}\) of the system at the distance \(\ell_{\mathrm{k}}(\vek q) = |\vek x_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}} - \vek x_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}}|\). This distance is a function of all coordinates, so the rate of its change \(\dot\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\) is a sum of contributions of all velocities \(\dot{q}_{\mathrm{j}}\), each with its own coefficient \(\partial\ell_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}\). The force of a damper is proportional to \(\dot\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\), so we expect the generalized force of the dampers to be a linear function of the velocities, with a square table of coefficients. We announce its elements in advance:

\[C_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek q) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} c_{\mathrm{k}}\,\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}}\,\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}} , \qquad s, j = 1, \dots, n . \tag{10.2}\]

The matrix \(\mat C\) with these elements is symmetric, since \(C_{\mathrm{sj}}\) does not change if we swap \(s\) and \(j\). The theorem will show that indeed \(Q^{\mathrm d}_{\mathrm{s}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{j}} C_{\mathrm{sj}}\dot{q}_{\mathrm{j}}\). The proof derives this from the definition of a damper, from the generalized force (definition 8.50) and from the chain rule.

Theorem 10.2 Equation of motion of a system with several degrees of freedom (gibalna enačba sistema z več prostostnimi stopnjami)

Let a system have \(n\) degrees of freedom with generalized coordinates \(\vek q\) on an open set \(U \subset \mathbb R^n\) (definition 8.45), ideal holonomic scleronomic constraints and kinetic energy \(T = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M(\vek q)\,\dot{\vek q}\) by theorem 8.84 with continuously differentiable \(\mat M\). Let the applied forces be conservative with a three times continuously differentiable potential \(V(\vek q)\). Let the viscous dampers (definition 9.1) have coefficients \(c_{\mathrm{k}} \ge 0\) and join points with twice continuously differentiable positions \(\vek x_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}}(\vek q)\) and \(\vek x_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}}(\vek q)\), whose distance \(\ell_{\mathrm{k}}(\vek q) = |\vek x_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}} - \vek x_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}}|\) is positive everywhere on \(U\). Let the external forces have the generalized force \(\vek Q(t)\), a continuous function of time. Let \(\mat C(\vek q)\) be the matrix with the elements (10.2). Then:

  1. The matrix \(\mat C(\vek q)\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite (definition 7.15), continuously differentiable, the generalized force of all dampers on the coordinate \(q_{\mathrm{s}}\) is \(Q^{\mathrm d}_{\mathrm{s}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{j}} C_{\mathrm{sj}}\,\dot{q}_{\mathrm{j}}\) and equals \(-\partial\mathcal D/\partial\dot{q}_{\mathrm{s}}\) with the dissipation function \(\mathcal D = \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{k}} c_{\mathrm{k}}\dot\ell_{\mathrm{k}}^2 = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat C\,\dot{\vek q}\).
  2. A twice continuously differentiable motion \(\vek q(t)\) is a motion of the system if and only if for \(s = 1, \dots, n\)
    \[\begin{aligned} &\sum_{\mathrm{j}} M_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek q)\,\ddot{q}_{\mathrm{j}} + g_{\mathrm{s}} \\ &\quad + \frac{\partial V}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} C_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek q)\,\dot{q}_{\mathrm{j}} \\ &= Q_{\mathrm{s}}(t) , \\ &g_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j},\mathrm{k}}\Big(\frac{\partial M_{\mathrm{sj}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{k}}} \\ &\quad - \frac12\,\frac{\partial M_{\mathrm{jk}}}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}}\Big)\dot{q}_{\mathrm{j}}\dot{q}_{\mathrm{k}} . \end{aligned} \tag{10.3}\]
  3. Along the motion \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(T + V) = \vek Q\cdot\dot{\vek q} - \dot{\vek q}^\T\mat C\,\dot{\vek q} \le \vek Q\cdot\dot{\vek q}\).
  4. Let \(\vek q_0 \in U\) be an equilibrium, \(\nabla V(\vek q_0) = \vek 0\), and let \(\mat M_0 = \mat M(\vek q_0)\), \(\mat C_0 = \mat C(\vek q_0)\) and \(\mat K\) the matrix of second derivatives of \(V\) at \(\vek q_0\). Then \(\mat M_0\) is symmetric and positive definite, \(\mat K\) is symmetric and \(\mat C_0\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite. For the displacement \(\vek x = \vek q - \vek q_0\) there exist numbers \(\rho > 0\) and \(c\) such that for every time at which \(|\vek x| \le \rho\)
    \[\begin{aligned} &\mat M_0\,\ddot{\vek x} + \mat C_0\,\dot{\vek x} \\ &\quad + \mat K\,\vek x = \vek Q(t) + \vek R , \\ &|R_{\mathrm{s}}| \le c\,\big(|\vek x|^2 + |\dot{\vek x}|^2 \\ &\quad + |\vek x|\,|\dot{\vek x}| + |\vek x|\,|\ddot{\vek x}|\big) . \end{aligned} \tag{10.4}\]
Proof

We must show that the dampers contribute the generalized force \(-\mat C\dot{\vek q}\), that Lagrange's equations with it give (10.3), and then bound the terms that are not linear in the displacement and its derivatives by the remainder \(\vek R\). Let \(\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\) be the derivative with respect to \(q_{\mathrm{s}}\).

  1. Let \(\vek e_{\mathrm{k}} = (\vek x_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}} - \vek x_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}})/\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the unit vector from \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\) towards \(B_{\mathrm{k}}\). From \(\ell_{\mathrm{k}}^2 = (\vek x_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}} - \vek x_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}})\cdot(\vek x_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}} - \vek x_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}})\) and the product rule (lemma 1.81) follows \(2\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}} = 2\,(\vek x_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}} - \vek x_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}})\cdot(\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}} - \partial_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}})\), so \(\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot(\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}} - \partial_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}})\). The function \(\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\) is twice continuously differentiable, because it is the root of a positive twice continuously differentiable function.
  2. By the chain rule (lemma 8.29, point 1) for the function \(t \mapsto \ell_{\mathrm{k}}(\vek q(t))\) we have \(\dot\ell_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \partial_{\mathrm{j}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,\dot{q}_{\mathrm{j}}\). By definition 9.1 the force on \(B_{\mathrm{k}}\) is \(\vek F_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}} = -c_{\mathrm{k}}\,\dot\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\) and on \(A_{\mathrm{k}}\) it is \(\vek F_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}} = c_{\mathrm{k}}\,\dot\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  3. By definition 8.50 the generalized force of damper \(k\) on the coordinate \(q_{\mathrm{s}}\) is \(\vek F_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}}\cdot\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}} + \vek F_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}}\cdot\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}} = -c_{\mathrm{k}}\,\dot\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot(\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{B}_\mathrm{k}} - \partial_{\mathrm{s}}\vek x_{\mathrm{A}_\mathrm{k}}) = -c_{\mathrm{k}}\,\dot\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\) by step 1. By step 2 this is \(-\sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial_{\mathrm{j}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,\dot{q}_{\mathrm{j}}\), and the sum over all dampers is \(Q^{\mathrm d}_{\mathrm{s}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{j}} C_{\mathrm{sj}}\,\dot{q}_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  4. Since \(\dot\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\) is a linear function of the velocities by step 2, \(\partial\dot\ell_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial\dot{q}_{\mathrm{s}} = \partial_{\mathrm{s}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\partial\mathcal D/\partial\dot{q}_{\mathrm{s}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} c_{\mathrm{k}}\,\dot\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}} = -Q^{\mathrm d}_{\mathrm{s}}\) by step 3. From step 2 we also have \(\mathcal D = \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{k}} c_{\mathrm{k}}\sum_{\mathrm{s},\mathrm{j}}\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial_{\mathrm{j}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,\dot{q}_{\mathrm{s}}\dot{q}_{\mathrm{j}} = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat C\,\dot{\vek q}\).
  5. The matrix \(\mat C\) is symmetric, because the product \(\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial_{\mathrm{j}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\) is symmetric in \(s\) and \(j\). For every column \(\vek z\) we have \(\vek z^\T\mat C\vek z = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} c_{\mathrm{k}}\,\big(\sum_{\mathrm{s}} \partial_{\mathrm{s}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\,z_{\mathrm{s}}\big)^2 \ge 0\), so \(\mat C\) is positive semidefinite. The elements \(C_{\mathrm{sj}}\) are continuously differentiable, because the \(\partial_{\mathrm{s}}\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\) are continuously differentiable. This is point 1. The generalized force of the forces that are not in the potential is \(Q^{\mathrm{nc}}_{\mathrm{s}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{j}} C_{\mathrm{sj}}\dot{q}_{\mathrm{j}} + Q_{\mathrm{s}}(t)\).
  6. By theorem 8.88 the motion is a motion of the system if and only if for \(\mathcal L = T - V\) we have \(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\dfrac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\dot{q}_{\mathrm{s}}} - \dfrac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial q_{\mathrm{s}}} = Q^{\mathrm{nc}}_{\mathrm{s}}\). The left side depends only on \(T\) and \(V\), so steps 1 to 4 of the proof of theorem 8.118 stay the same (they do not contain the right side) and give \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} M_{\mathrm{sj}}\ddot{q}_{\mathrm{j}} + g_{\mathrm{s}} + \partial_{\mathrm{s}} V = Q^{\mathrm{nc}}_{\mathrm{s}}\). When we move the term with \(\mat C\) to the left, we get (10.3). All steps are equivalences, so the converse holds too. This is point 2.
  7. Theorem 8.104 with \(Q^{\mathrm{nc}}\) from step 5 gives \(\mathrm{d}(T + V)/\mathrm{d}t = \vek Q\cdot\dot{\vek q} - \dot{\vek q}^\T\mat C\dot{\vek q}\). The term with \(\mat C\) is not positive by step 5. This is point 3.
  8. The displacement \(\vek x = \vek q - \vek q_0\) shifts the coordinates by a constant, so \(\dot{\vek x} = \dot{\vek q}\), \(\ddot{\vek x} = \ddot{\vek q}\). The functions \(\tilde V(\vek x) = V(\vek q_0 + \vek x)\), \(\tilde M_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek x) = M_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek q_0 + \vek x)\) and \(\tilde C_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek x) = C_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek q_0 + \vek x)\) have the same derivatives as \(V\), \(M_{\mathrm{sj}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{sj}}\), and \(\vek x = \vek 0\) is an equilibrium. Let \(\rho\) be so small that the closed ball \(|\vek x| \le \rho\) lies in \(\{\vek x : \vek q_0 + \vek x \in U\}\). The estimates from steps 5 to 7 of the proof of theorem 8.118 do not contain the right side of the equation and hold unchanged for \(\tilde V\) and \(\tilde M_{\mathrm{sj}}\): \(\partial_{\mathrm{s}} V = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} K_{\mathrm{sj}}x_{\mathrm{j}} + r_{\mathrm{s}}\) with \(|r_{\mathrm{s}}| \le \tfrac12 n^2 c_{\mathrm{V}}|\vek x|^2\), \(\big|\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (M_{\mathrm{sj}} - M_{0,\mathrm{sj}})\,\ddot{x}_{\mathrm{j}}\big| \le n^2 c_{\mathrm{M}}|\vek x|\,|\ddot{\vek x}|\) and \(|g_{\mathrm{s}}| \le \tfrac32 n^2 c_{\mathrm{M}}|\dot{\vek x}|^2\), where \(c_{\mathrm{V}}\) and \(c_{\mathrm{M}}\) are the largest absolute values of the third derivatives of \(V\) and of the first derivatives of \(M_{\mathrm{sj}}\) on the ball.
  9. We estimate the difference \(C_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek q) - C_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek q_0)\) like the difference of \(M_{\mathrm{sj}}\) in step 6 of the same proof: by the mean value theorem 1.84 on the function \(\tau \mapsto \tilde C_{\mathrm{sj}}(\tau\,\vek x)\) and lemma 8.28. Let \(c_{\mathrm{C}}\) be the largest absolute value of the derivatives \(\partial_{\mathrm{k}} C_{\mathrm{sj}}\) on the ball (theorem 8.26, the derivatives are continuous by step 5). Then \(|C_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek q) - C_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek q_0)| \le n\,c_{\mathrm{C}}\,|\vek x|\) and \(\big|\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (C_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek q) - C_{\mathrm{sj}}(\vek q_0))\,\dot{x}_{\mathrm{j}}\big| \le n^2 c_{\mathrm{C}}\,|\vek x|\,|\dot{\vek x}|\).
  10. In (10.3) we insert \(M_{\mathrm{sj}} = M_{0,\mathrm{sj}} + (M_{\mathrm{sj}} - M_{0,\mathrm{sj}})\), the same for \(C_{\mathrm{sj}}\), and step 8. We get (10.4) with \(R_{\mathrm{s}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (M_{\mathrm{sj}} - M_{0,\mathrm{sj}})\ddot{x}_{\mathrm{j}} - g_{\mathrm{s}} - r_{\mathrm{s}} - \sum_{\mathrm{j}} (C_{\mathrm{sj}} - C_{0,\mathrm{sj}})\dot{x}_{\mathrm{j}}\). By steps 8 and 9 the inequality for \(R_{\mathrm{s}}\) holds with \(c = n^2\max\big(\tfrac12 c_{\mathrm{V}},\ \tfrac32 c_{\mathrm{M}},\ c_{\mathrm{C}}\big)\), since \(n^2 c_{\mathrm{M}} \le \tfrac32 n^2 c_{\mathrm{M}}\).
  11. The matrix \(\mat M_0\) is symmetric and positive definite by theorem 8.84, \(\mat K\) is symmetric because mixed derivatives commute (theorem 8.30). The matrix \(\mat C_0\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite by step 5. This is point 4.

Source: CK (8.1) (PDF p. 229) and (8.9) (PDF p. 241): \(\mat M\ddot{\vek u} + \mat C\dot{\vek u} + \mat K\vek u = \vek p\) and Lagrange's equations. GR section 2.1 (PDF p. 77-79): linear vibrations about equilibrium. GR (1.53) and (1.54) (PDF p. 53): the dissipation function and the generalized force of dampers. The damping matrix from the distances \(\ell_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the bound on the remainder are not from a source.

The matrix \(\mat C\) is not necessarily positive definite. In frame A a horizontal damper between the ground and the lower floor has the distance \(\ell = \ell_0 + q_1\), so \(\mat C = \begin{bmatrix} c_{\mathrm{d}} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\vek z^\T\mat C\vek z = 0\) for \(\vek z = (0, 1)^\T\): the damper does not resist a motion of the upper floor while the lower one is at rest.

The theorem says what the model is. The exact equation (10.3) is nonlinear, because the mass matrix depends on the coordinates, and this shows in the quadratic form of the velocities \(g_{\mathrm{s}}\). When the displacement is small, a linear equation remains in the unknown \(\vek x\) with a remainder of second order, as for one coordinate. Chapter 8 already warned that the theorem does not bound the error of the solution in time, but the difference between the equations at each moment, and so we take the linear equation as a model whose validity we check with numbers. The displacement from equilibrium we from now on again write \(\vek q\), as in chapter 9, and the equation

\[\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek Q(t) \tag{10.5}\]

we call the equation of motion of a system with several degrees of freedom. The matrix \(\mat M\) is the mass matrix (masna matrika), \(\mat K\) the stiffness matrix (togostna matrika) and \(\mat C\) the damping matrix (dušilna matrika), all with \(n \times n\) elements. For \(n = 1\) this is equation (9.8) from chapter 9: the matrices correspond to the numbers \(m\), \(c\) and \(k\).

The matrices have \(n \times n\) elements. For coordinates with different units, such as a length and an angle, different elements have different units, as we saw for the bar on springs (section 8.13.3). The quadratic form \(\vek q^\T\mat K\vek q\) always has the unit J, the same as energy, and the quadratic form \(\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat C\dot{\vek q}\) the unit W, the same as power.

10.1.3 Stiffness and flexibility coefficients (togostni in podajnostni koeficienti)

In the theorem the matrix \(\mat K\) is the Hessian matrix of the potential. For a structure of linearly elastic material we do not need to compute the potential and differentiate it twice. Chapter 7 defined the matrix as the matrix of forces that hold the state (definition 7.4): the element \(K_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the force in the direction of unknown \(i\) that we need so that \(q_{\mathrm{j}} = 1\) and all other displacements are zero. The two descriptions are the same matrix. The state \(\vek q\) is an equilibrium state under the forces \(\vek F = \mat K\vek q\), so by Castigliano's first theorem (theorem 4.92) the force in the direction of \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) that holds this state is \(F_{\mathrm{i}} = \partial U/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}\), where \(U(\vek q)\) is the strain energy of the structure. The potential of the structure differs from \(U\) by a term that is linear in \(\vek q\) (the work of constant loads) and does not change the second derivatives. Therefore \(\partial^2 V/\partial q_{\mathrm{i}}\partial q_{\mathrm{j}} = \partial F_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{j}}\), and since \(\vek F = \mat K\vek q\) is a linear function by definition 7.4, the derivative is \(\partial F_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial q_{\mathrm{j}} = K_{\mathrm{ij}}\). The elements \(K_{\mathrm{ij}}\) are called stiffness coefficients (togostni koeficienti), as CK (8.16) (PDF p. 248) calls them, in the spirit of the flexibility coefficients of chapter 4. Their columns we get by the column rule.

In frame A the first column is the force we need to move the lower floor by 1 m while the upper one stays. The relative displacement of the lower pair is \(1\) m, of the upper one \(-1\) m. The columns act on the lower floor with the force \(-k\cdot 1 + k\cdot(-1) = -2k\) and on the upper one with the force \(-k\cdot(-1) = k\), so the floors must be held by the forces \(2k\) and \(-k\). The column \((2k, -k)\) is indeed the first column of the matrix from (10.1). The second column (upper floor 1 m, lower one at rest) is \((-k, k)\) (figure 10.3, top).

The converse question is: how much does a point move if a unit force acts on it? Chapter 4 introduced the flexibility matrix \(\mat D\) for it (definition 4.138), whose columns are the displacements due to unit forces. In frame A we get \(\mat D\) without computing with matrices. A force \(F\) on the upper floor runs through both pairs of columns, because the upper pair holds the upper floor and the lower pair holds both. The lower floor therefore moves by \(F/k\) and the upper one by \(F/k + F/k = 2F/k\). A force \(F\) on the lower floor loads only the lower pair, so both floors move by \(F/k\). The first column is \((1, 1)/k\) and the second \((1, 2)/k\), so

\[\mat D = \frac1k\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} . \tag{10.6}\]

The two matrices are inverse to each other, which we shall use in computations.

Lemma 10.3 Stiffness and flexibility matrix (togostna in podajnostna matrika)

Let a structure be of linearly elastic material as in definition 4.138 (for a truss the point is a joint), and let its state be determined by a column \(\vek q\) of displacements of \(n\) chosen points in chosen directions, so that every column \(\vek q\) gives a state that respects the supports. Let the supports prevent every small rigid motion of the structure. Let \(\mat K\) be the stiffness matrix (definition 7.4) and \(\mat D\) the flexibility matrix (definition 4.138) for these displacements and forces at the same points and in the same directions. Then \(\mat K\mat D = \mat D\mat K = \mat I\), so \(\mat D = \mat K^{-1}\), and \(\mat D\) is symmetric.

Proof

We must show that the displacement due to forces \(\vek F\) is exactly \(\mat K^{-1}\vek F\). We use the uniqueness of the solution for given forces.

  1. Let \(\vek F\) be an arbitrary column of sufficiently small forces at the chosen points and in the chosen directions. By definition 4.138 there is a solution with small deformations for each single force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\), and by the principle of superposition (lemma 4.134) the sum of these solutions is a solution for all forces at once. Its displacements of the chosen points are \(\vek q = \mat D\vek F\), since column \(j\) of \(\mat D\) is the displacement due to the force \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\), divided by \(F_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  2. In this state exactly the forces \(\vek F\) act at the chosen points, there are no other loads. By definition 7.4 therefore \(\vek F = \mat K\vek q = \mat K\mat D\vek F\).
  3. Since \(\vek F\) is arbitrary, we take \(\vek F = \varepsilon\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) with a small \(\varepsilon > 0\) for each \(j\). From step 2 follows \(\varepsilon\,\mat K\mat D\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}} = \varepsilon\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), so column \(j\) of \(\mat K\mat D\) equals \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) for each \(j\) and \(\mat K\mat D = \mat I\).
  4. Let \(\vek q\) be an arbitrary column of sufficiently small displacements. By assumption a state with these displacements exists, and the forces that hold it are \(\vek F = \mat K\vek q\) (definition 7.4). This state is a solution for these forces. The supports prevent every small rigid motion, so the solution for given forces is unique (lemma 4.133), and it equals the solution from step 1. So \(\vek q = \mat D\vek F = \mat D\mat K\vek q\). Since \(\vek q\) is arbitrary, \(\mat D\mat K = \mat I\).
  5. Steps 3 and 4 show \(\mat D = \mat K^{-1}\) by definition 1.107. The matrix \(\mat D\) is symmetric by Maxwell's theorem (theorem 4.140).

Source: Not from a source. CK (11.49) and footnote 4 (PDF p. 367) use \(\mat K^{-1}\) as the flexibility matrix and remark that it does not exist for systems with rigid modes. Check on a truss of two bars: chapter 4, verified with SymPy.

The lemma says when the flexibility matrix exists: when the supports prevent every rigid motion. For a system without supports, such as an aeroplane or a machine in space, the matrix \(\mat K\) has no inverse and the lemma does not hold. The chapter will treat such systems separately in section 10.5.

For frame A \(\mat K\mat D = \mat I\) is a computational check: \(k\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\cdot\dfrac1k\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 - 1 & 2 - 2 \\ -1 + 1 & -1 + 2 \end{bmatrix} = \mat I\). The same holds for the truss from chapter 4, where the product of the matrices was checked with SymPy.

The flexibility matrix gives the equation of motion a second form.

Corollary 10.4 Flexibility form of the equation of motion (podajnostna oblika gibalne enačbe)

Let \(\mat M\), \(\mat C\), \(\mat K\) and \(\vek Q\) be as in equation (10.5) and let \(\mat K\) be invertible with the inverse matrix \(\mat D = \mat K^{-1}\). Then \(\vek q(t)\) is a solution of equation (10.5) if and only if

\[\mat D\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat D\mat C\,\dot{\vek q} + \vek q = \mat D\vek Q(t) . \tag{10.7}\]
Proof

We must show that one equation follows from the other by multiplication with an invertible matrix.

  1. If (10.5) holds, we multiply it from the left by \(\mat D\). Since \(\mat D\mat K = \mat I\) by the definition of the inverse matrix (definition 1.107), we get (10.7).
  2. If (10.7) holds, we multiply it from the left by \(\mat K\). Since \(\mat K\mat D = \mat I\), we get (10.5).

Source: CK (11.49) (PDF p. 367) for the flexibility matrix. The proof is not from a source.

What is the second form good for? When it is easier to compute the displacements due to unit forces than the forces for unit displacements, we do not need the matrix \(\mat K\) at all. In frame A we read \(\mat D\) directly from (10.6). The matrix \(\mat D\mat M\) is not necessarily symmetric, even if \(\mat D\) and \(\mat M\) are symmetric. Its transpose is \(\mat M\mat D\) by lemma 1.101, which equals \(\mat D\mat M\) only if the matrices commute. In frame A \(\mat M = m\mat I\) and \(\mat D\mat M = (m/k)\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) is symmetric, but for the machine with coordinates of different units below it is not. The motion in which all coordinates move in step, \(\vek q = \vek\varphi\cos\omega t\), which we shall look for in the next section, we insert into equation (10.7) without damping and force and get \(-\omega^2\,\mat D\mat M\vek\varphi + \vek\varphi = \vek 0\). We keep the search for motions in step in the symmetric form with the matrices \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\), and the flexibility form says the same.

10.1.4 The bracket and the machine (konzola in stroj)

We test the theorem on two more systems that are not a frame of floors.

Bracket B. The truss of two bars from chapter 4 (figure 10.4): bar \(AC\), horizontal and 4 m long, bar \(BC\), 5 m long, pins \(A\) and \(B\) fixed to the wall, as in section 4.8.1. Both bars have \(EA = 19{,}6\) MN. At the joint \(C\) let there be a point mass \(m = 1000\) kg, which is our model: its weight 9,81 kN is close to the load 10 kN of chapter 4. The bars have no mass. Together they have 7,02 kg, which is 0,7 % of the mass \(m\). The coordinates are the displacements of the joint \(C\), \(\vek q = (u, v)\), \(u\) to the right and \(v\) upwards, as in chapter 4.

Example 10.5 Equation of motion of the bracket with a mass at the joint (gibalna enačba konzole z maso v vozlišču)

Bracket B as above. We look for \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) for the coordinates \((u, v)\) and check \(\mat K\mat D = \mat I\).

  1. Bar \(k\) with the unit vector \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\) from the wall towards \(C\) and length \(L_{\mathrm{k}}\) elongates by \(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek q\) at the joint displacement \(\vek q\) (chapter 4, section 4.8.1, step 4). The axial force is \((EA/L_{\mathrm{k}})\,\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek q\), and the bar acts on the joint with the force \(-(EA/L_{\mathrm{k}})(\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\cdot\vek q)\,\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\).
  2. The force that holds the joint in the state \(\vek q\) is opposite to the sum of these forces, \(\vek F = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} (EA/L_{\mathrm{k}})\,\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\,\vek q\). By the column rule (definition 7.4) therefore \(\mat K = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} (EA/L_{\mathrm{k}})\,\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}\vek n_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\).
  3. For bar \(AC\) we have \(\vek n = (1, 0)\) and \(EA/L = 4{,}9\cdot 10^6\) N/m, for bar \(BC\) \(\vek n = (4, -3)/5\) and \(EA/L = 3{,}92\cdot 10^6\) N/m. The first gives \(4{,}9\cdot 10^6\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), the second \(3{,}92\cdot 10^6\cdot\frac1{25}\begin{bmatrix} 16 & -12 \\ -12 & 9 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2{,}5088 & -1{,}8816 \\ -1{,}8816 & 1{,}4112 \end{bmatrix}10^6\), and the sum is
    \[\mat K = \begin{bmatrix} 7{,}4088 & -1{,}8816 \\ -1{,}8816 & 1{,}4112 \end{bmatrix}10^6\ \frac{\text{N}}{\text{m}} .\]
  4. The flexibility matrix of chapter 4 (equation (4.82)) is \(\mat D = \dfrac{1\ \text{m}}{EA}\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 16/3 \\ 16/3 & 21 \end{bmatrix}\), and \(\mat K\mat D = \mat I\) up to rounding (SymPy), as lemma 10.3 says.
  5. The kinetic energy of the mass is \(T = \tfrac12 m(\dot{u}^2 + \dot{v}^2)\), so \(\mat M = m\mat I = 1000\,\mat I\) kg. The potential is \(V = \tfrac12\,\vek q^\T\mat K\vek q + m g\,v\) for displacements from the unloaded position. The equilibrium \(\nabla V = \vek 0\) is at \(\vek q_0 = -\mat K^{-1}(0, mg)\), that is \(\vek q_0 = \mat D\,(0, -mg)\) with the components \(u_0 = -2{,}669\) mm and \(v_0 = -10{,}511\) mm, and the Hessian matrix is \(\mat K\) everywhere, because \(V\) is a quadratic function of the displacements.
  6. For the displacement from equilibrium, by theorem 10.2 without damping,
    \[\begin{aligned} &1000\,\ddot{u} + 7{,}4088\cdot 10^6\,u \\ &\quad - 1{,}8816\cdot 10^6\,v = Q_{\mathrm{u}} , \\ &1000\,\ddot{v} - 1{,}8816\cdot 10^6\,u \\ &\quad + 1{,}4112\cdot 10^6\,v = Q_{\mathrm{v}} . \end{aligned} \tag{10.8}\]

Source: Not from a source. The matrix \(\mat K\) is from section 4.6.7 and from definition 7.4, the numbers are ours.

Why is the computation linear if the bars tilt under the weight? The computation from chapter 4 expresses the elongation of a bar as a projection of the displacement, \(\vek n\cdot\vek q\), so to first order. The exact geometry would add to the Hessian matrix a term due to the force in the bar: a bar with force \(N\) and length \(L\) resists a transverse displacement like a taut string with the stiffness \(N/L\). The weight loads bar \(AC\) with a compressive force of \(13\,080\) N and bar \(BC\) with a tensile force of \(16\,350\) N. Compression reduces the transverse stiffness, tension increases it, by \(|N|/L = 3270\) N/m. This changes the natural frequencies (definition 8.122) by \(-0{,}0094\ \%\) and \(+0{,}0010\ \%\) (NumPy), which is much less than the uncertainty in \(EA\). Where this term mattered, we would have to keep it. Chapter 12 will treat it.

Machine F. Chapter 9 allowed the machine on mounts only a vertical displacement (a guide) and mentioned that a real machine would also rock. Now we do it. Machine F is a rigid body of mass \(M = 250\) kg in the shape of a box \(1{,}2\ \text{m} \times 0{,}6\ \text{m}\) and with the moment of inertia about the centre of mass \(J = M(1{,}2^2 + 0{,}6^2)/12 = 37{,}5\ \text{kg m}^2\). It stands on two pairs of mounts (podložke), each pair has the stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{p}} = 123\,370\) N/m, together \(246\,740\) N/m, like the four mounts of the machine in chapter 9. The mounts are springs that act only vertically, which is an idealization: real mounts also have a shear stiffness. The machine moves vertically and rotates in the plane, like the bar on springs in section 8.13.3 (figure 10.5). The coordinates are the vertical displacement of the centre of mass \(y\) (upwards) and the rotation \(\varphi\) (counterclockwise), measured from the position in which the mounts are unstrained. A point at the horizontal distance \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) from the centre of mass moves vertically by \(y + x_{\mathrm{i}}\sin\varphi \approx y + x_{\mathrm{i}}\varphi\).

Example 10.6 Equation of motion of the machine that also rocks (gibalna enačba stroja, ki se tudi zibla)

Machine F as above, the mounts with vertical stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{p}}\) are at the horizontal distances \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) from the centre of mass. We look for \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) for \((y, \varphi)\).

  1. The kinetic energy of a rigid body in the plane is \(T = \tfrac12 M\dot{y}^2 + \tfrac12 J\dot\varphi^2\) (theorem 8.84, as for the bar on springs), so \(\mat M = \operatorname{diag}(M, J)\) with the units kg and kg m\(^2\).
  2. The potential of the springs and the weight is \(V = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \tfrac12 k_{\mathrm{p}}\,(y + x_{\mathrm{i}}\sin\varphi)^2 + M g\,y\).
  3. The Hessian matrix at \(y = \varphi = 0\), where the mounts are unstrained: \(\partial^2 V/\partial y^2 = 2k_{\mathrm{p}}\), \(\partial^2 V/\partial y\partial\varphi = k_{\mathrm{p}}(x_1 + x_2)\), \(\partial^2 V/\partial\varphi^2 = k_{\mathrm{p}}(x_1^2 + x_2^2)\). So
    \[\mat K = k_{\mathrm{p}}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & x_1 + x_2 \\ x_1 + x_2 & x_1^2 + x_2^2 \end{bmatrix} .\]
  4. The same elements we get by the column rule. We move the machine by \(y = 1\) m without rotation: each pair of mounts acts on the machine with the force \(-k_{\mathrm{p}}\), so it must be held by the forces \(2k_{\mathrm{p}}\) together and the moment about the centre of mass \(k_{\mathrm{p}}(x_1 + x_2)\). This is the first column. We rotate the machine by \(\varphi = 1\) rad without lifting: mount \(i\) moves by \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\), so the force that holds the machine is \(k_{\mathrm{p}}(x_1 + x_2)\) and the moment is \(k_{\mathrm{p}}(x_1^2 + x_2^2)\). This is the second column. The force for the rotation and the moment for the displacement are equal, \(k_{\mathrm{p}}(x_1 + x_2)\), as it must be for a symmetric matrix.
  5. Mounts at \(x_1 = -0{,}5\) m and \(x_2 = 0{,}5\) m (centre of mass in the middle): \(\mat K = \operatorname{diag}(246\,740\ \text{N/m},\ 61\,685\ \text{N m})\), the matrix is diagonal and the coordinates are not coupled. The bounce has the frequency \(\sqrt{246\,740/250}/(2\pi) = 5{,}000\) Hz, as in chapter 9, the rocking \(\sqrt{61\,685/37{,}5}/(2\pi) = 6{,}455\) Hz.
  6. The centre of mass 0,1 m from the middle between the mounts, mounts at \(x_1 = -0{,}6\) m and \(x_2 = 0{,}4\) m: \(x_1 + x_2 = -0{,}2\) m and \(x_1^2 + x_2^2 = 0{,}52\) m\(^2\), so
    \[\mat K = \begin{bmatrix} 246\,740 & -24\,674 \\ -24\,674 & 64\,152{,}4 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat M = \begin{bmatrix} 250 & 0 \\ 0 & 37{,}5 \end{bmatrix} , \tag{10.9}\]
    in the units N/m, N, N m, kg and kg m\(^2\). The off-diagonal term is not zero, because the centre of mass is not in the middle between the mounts: when the machine is lifted, both mounts resist with the same force, but their resultant lies 0,1 m from the centre of mass and gives a moment about it. The motions are coupled (sklopljeni), as for the bar on two different springs in section 8.13.3.
  7. The equilibrium of these mounts is at \(y_0 = -10{,}34\) mm and \(\varphi_0 = -3{,}98\) mrad (SymPy from \(\nabla V = \vek 0\) for the exact \(V\) with \(\sin\varphi\)). The Hessian matrix of the exact \(V\) at it differs from (10.9) by \(4{,}1\cdot 10^{-6}\) of the largest element, so we keep it. By theorem 10.2 for the displacement from equilibrium \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek Q\) holds with the matrices from (10.9).

Source: Not from a source. The same model is the bar on two springs from section 8.13.3. The numbers are ours.

For this machine the flexibility form is an example of a matrix that is not symmetric. For (10.9) the matrix \(\mat D = \mat K^{-1}\) is symmetric with \(D_{12} = 1{,}621\cdot 10^{-6}\) (NumPy), but in \(\mat D\mat M\) we have \((\mat D\mat M)_{12} = D_{12}\,J = 6{,}08\cdot 10^{-5}\) and \((\mat D\mat M)_{21} = D_{21}\,M = 4{,}05\cdot 10^{-4}\) in SI base units. The masses \(M\) and \(J\) are different, so the two elements differ, and the matrix is not symmetric.

With this we have for three systems the equation of motion (10.5), and without damping for two. In the next section we ask when all coordinates move in step.

10.2 The eigenvalue problem and natural modes (lastni problem in nihajni načini)

The two-storey frame A (okvir A) of section 10.1 is our model of a laboratory frame. Two rigid floors (stropa), each of mass \(m = 500\) kg, are joined to the ground and to each other by two steel columns (stebra) of length 1 m and cross section \(20 \times 40\) mm. The columns are clamped into the ground and into the floors, their mass is neglected and the floors move only horizontally. The column \(\vek q = (q_1, q_2)\) holds the horizontal displacements of the lower and the upper floor from equilibrium. A storey has stiffness \(k = 501\,760\) N/m, and by theorem 10.2 the equation of motion without damping and forces is

\[\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek 0 , \qquad \mat M = m\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \quad \mat K = k\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} . \tag{10.10}\]

Each floor feels both neighbouring parts of the frame: the lower one is pulled back by the spring of the storey below it and forward by the spring of the storey above it, the upper one only by the spring of the storey below it.

We ask: can the frame vibrate so that both floors move in step, that is with the same frequency, the same time dependence and so that both reach zero and the largest displacement at the same moments? For a system with one degree of freedom this is the only form of vibration (chapter 9). With two degrees of freedom we looked for it with a cosine in section 8.13.3 and called it a mode of vibration. Here we pose the question for any number \(n\) of coordinates and any stiffness matrix, because the next sections need systems with dozens of coordinates and systems with zero or negative stiffness.

First we say what "in step" means. A motion is synchronous (sinhrono) if \(\vek q(t) = \boldsymbol\varphi\,g(t)\), where \(\boldsymbol\varphi \ne \vek 0\) is a column of \(n\) numbers that fixes the ratios between the coordinates, and \(g\) is one function of time, the same for all coordinates. For frame A this means that the ratio \(q_2/q_1\) is the same at every time. We insert it into the equation of motion. Since \(\boldsymbol\varphi\) is constant, \(\ddot{\vek q} = \boldsymbol\varphi\,\ddot{g}\), and

\[(\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi)\,\ddot{g}(t) + (\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi)\,g(t) = \vek 0 . \tag{10.11}\]

The column \(\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi\) is not zero, because \(\boldsymbol\varphi^\T\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi > 0\) for a positive definite matrix \(\mat M\) (definition 6.27). Choose a row \(i\) with \((\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi)_{\mathrm{i}} \ne 0\). From it, \(\ddot{g} = -\lambda\,g\) with the number \(\lambda = (\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi)_{\mathrm{i}}/(\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi)_{\mathrm{i}}\), which does not depend on time. Inserting this back into equation (10.11) gives for every row \(j\) the equality \(\big((\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi)_{\mathrm{j}} - \lambda\,(\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi)_{\mathrm{j}}\big)\,g(t) = 0\). The function \(g\) is not zero everywhere, otherwise \(\vek q = \vek 0\), so all rows give the same condition, \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi = \lambda\,\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi\). The requirement of synchronous motion has therefore turned into an equation for the unknown \(\lambda\) and \(\boldsymbol\varphi\). We name it.

Definition 10.7 Eigenpair and eigenvalue problem (lastni par in lastni problem)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric matrix and \(\mat M\) a symmetric positive definite matrix, both with \(n\) rows and \(n\) columns. A real number \(\lambda\) and a nonzero real column \(\boldsymbol\varphi\) with \(n\) elements form an eigenpair (lastni par) of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) if

\[\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi = \lambda\,\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi . \tag{10.12}\]

The search for such pairs is the generalized eigenvalue problem (posplošeni lastni problem), the number \(\lambda\) is the eigenvalue (lastna vrednost) and the column \(\boldsymbol\varphi\) the eigencolumn (lastni stolpec). If \(\lambda \ge 0\), then \(\omega = \sqrt\lambda\) is the natural circular frequency (lastna krožna frekvenca) and \(\boldsymbol\varphi\) the mode shape (način nihanja), as in definition 8.122.

Source: CK (9.4) (PDF p. 267) and (10.4) (PDF p. 301): inserting a harmonic motion into the equation of motion gives an algebraic eigenvalue problem. GR (2.22)-(2.25) (PDF p. 85-86): synchronous motion, eigenvalue problem, "eigenmode". The route to the equation through row \(i\) is not from the source.

The definition differs from definition 8.122 in two things. First, it allows every real \(\lambda\). Chapter 8 required \(\omega > 0\), but we shall also meet \(\lambda = 0\) for systems that the supports do not hold, and \(\lambda < 0\) for unstable equilibrium (theorem 8.117). Second, in this chapter we write the mode \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), not \(\vek u_{\mathrm{r}}\) as in chapter 8, because \(\vek u\) means a displacement for bodies and for finite elements. For \(\mat M = \mat I\) equation (10.12) is the eigenvalue and eigenvector of the matrix \(\mat K\) by definition 2.59.

If \(\boldsymbol\varphi\) is an eigencolumn, so is \(c\,\boldsymbol\varphi\) for every number \(c \ne 0\), because equation (10.12) is linear in \(\boldsymbol\varphi\). A mode is therefore determined up to multiplication by a number (CK, PDF p. 301). Where we compare ratios between coordinates, we take one element equal to \(1\) and say each time which one (for frame A in this section the first, for bracket B the unit length of the column). Later we shall normalize the theorems with \(\boldsymbol\varphi^\T\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi = 1\) and say each time which normalization applies.

So far we only demanded synchronous motion. The next lemma says when the equation of motion really allows it, and that a frequency needs an eigenvalue, not an arbitrary number.

Lemma 10.8 Synchronous vibration and eigenpair (sinhrono nihanje in lastni par)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric and \(\mat M\) a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\), \(\omega > 0\) a number, \(\boldsymbol\varphi \ne \vek 0\) a real column with \(n\) elements and \((a, b) \ne (0, 0)\) a pair of real numbers. Then:

  1. The motion \(\vek q(t) = \boldsymbol\varphi\,(a\cos\omega t + b\sin\omega t)\) is a solution of \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek 0\) exactly when \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi = \omega^2\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi\).
  2. For every eigenpair \((\lambda, \boldsymbol\varphi)\) we have \(\lambda = \boldsymbol\varphi^\T\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi\,/\,\boldsymbol\varphi^\T\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi\). If \(\mat K\) is positive semidefinite (definition 7.15), then \(\lambda \ge 0\). If it is positive definite, then \(\lambda > 0\).
Proof

We show point 1 by insertion, and point 2 by multiplying the eigenvalue problem by \(\boldsymbol\varphi^\T\).

  1. Let \(g(t) = a\cos\omega t + b\sin\omega t\). By theorem 8.12 (equation (8.7) with \(c = 0\)), \(g'(t) = -a\omega\sin\omega t + b\omega\cos\omega t\), and differentiating once more, \(g''(t) = -\omega^2\,(a\cos\omega t + b\sin\omega t) = -\omega^2 g(t)\).
  2. Since \(\boldsymbol\varphi\) is constant, \(\ddot{\vek q} = \boldsymbol\varphi\,g'' = -\omega^2 g\,\boldsymbol\varphi\), hence \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = (\mat K - \omega^2\mat M)\,\boldsymbol\varphi\;g(t)\).
  3. If \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi = \omega^2\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi\), this column is zero at every time.
  4. Conversely, let the column be zero at every time. At \(t_0 = 0\) we have \(g(t_0) = a\), and at \(t_0 = \pi/(2\omega)\) we have \(g(t_0) = b\). At least one of the numbers \(a\), \(b\) is not zero, so there is a \(t_0\) with \(g(t_0) \ne 0\). At it, step 2 gives \((\mat K - \omega^2\mat M)\boldsymbol\varphi = \vek 0\). This proves point 1.
  5. Let \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi = \lambda\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi\). Multiply from the left by \(\boldsymbol\varphi^\T\): \(\boldsymbol\varphi^\T\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi = \lambda\,\boldsymbol\varphi^\T\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi\). Since \(\mat M\) is positive definite and \(\boldsymbol\varphi \ne \vek 0\), we have \(\boldsymbol\varphi^\T\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi > 0\) (definition 6.27), and dividing gives the first sentence of point 2.
  6. For positive semidefinite \(\mat K\) the numerator is \(\ge 0\) (definition 7.15), for positive definite \(> 0\) (definition 6.27). The denominator is positive, so \(\lambda\) has the same sign as the numerator. This proves point 2.

Source: GR (2.22)-(2.27) (PDF p. 85-86): the same insertion and multiplication by \(\boldsymbol\varphi^\T\), there for positive definite \(\mat K\). The proof step by step is not from the source.

The lemma says two things. The frame can vibrate synchronously only at frequencies that are square roots of eigenvalues, and at these the synchronous vibration really exists, with any phase and amplitude, since \(a\) and \(b\) fix them. For a positive definite stiffness matrix all eigenvalues are positive, because the energy of the springs is positive for every nonzero displacement: \(\tfrac12\boldsymbol\varphi^\T\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi > 0\). If \(\lambda = 0\), then \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi = \vek 0\), and \(\vek q = \boldsymbol\varphi\,(a + b\,t)\) is a solution, since \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} = \vek 0\) and \(\mat K\vek q = \vek 0\). This motion is not a vibration: the displacement grows linearly with time, the system moves like a rigid body, which we treat later in this chapter. If \(\lambda < 0\), then \(\boldsymbol\varphi^\T\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi < 0\) by point 2 of the lemma, and theorem 8.117 says that the displacement from such a starting position (in the direction \(\boldsymbol\varphi\), without initial velocity) grows at least linearly. Synchronous vibration with \(\omega > 0\) is therefore possible only at \(\lambda > 0\).

10.2.1 Frame A: the floors in step (okvir A: stropa v koraku)

We test the lemma on frame A. Equation (10.12) reads \((\mat K - \lambda\mat M)\boldsymbol\varphi = \vek 0\), that is

\[\begin{bmatrix} 2k - \lambda m & -k \\ -k & k - \lambda m \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \varphi_1 \\ \varphi_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} . \tag{10.13}\]

Two homogeneous equations in two unknowns have a nonzero solution exactly when the determinant of the matrix is zero (theorem 8.123, point 1, with the determinant by definition 2.50). The frequency equation (frekvenčna enačba) is

\[\begin{aligned} \det(\mat K - \lambda\mat M) &= (2k - \lambda m)(k - \lambda m) - k^2 \\ &= m^2\lambda^2 - 3km\,\lambda + k^2 = 0 . \end{aligned} \tag{10.14}\]

Its solutions are \(\lambda = \tfrac{3 \mp \sqrt5}{2}\,\tfrac{k}{m}\). At \(k/m = 1003{,}52\) 1/s\(^2\) we get \(\lambda_1 = 383{,}31\) 1/s\(^2\) and \(\lambda_2 = 2627{,}25\) 1/s\(^2\) (table below). Both are positive and real, as theorem 8.123 guarantees. The book has no determinant of order \(n\), so we use this route only for \(n = 2\). For larger \(n\) we shall get the eigenvalues differently, in the next section.

We get the mode from the second row of system (10.13), \(-k\varphi_1 + (k - \lambda m)\varphi_2 = 0\), hence \(r = \varphi_2/\varphi_1 = k/(k - \lambda m)\). From the first row, \(r = 2 - \lambda m/k\). At every solution of equation (10.14) the two rows agree, because its determinant is zero.

mode \(\lambda\) (1/s\(^2\)) \(\omega\) (1/s) \(f = \omega/2\pi\) (Hz) \(T\) (s) \(\boldsymbol\varphi\)
1 383,31 19,578 3,1160 0,32093 \((1;\ 1{,}618)\)
2 2627,25 51,257 8,1578 0,12258 \((1;\ -0{,}618)\)

We check the eigenpair of the first mode. With \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1 = (1;\ 1{,}618)\) we have \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_1 = (191\,655;\ 310\,105)\) N/m, and \(\lambda_1 m\,\boldsymbol\varphi_1 = 383{,}31 \cdot 500 \cdot (1;\ 1{,}618) = (191\,655;\ 310\,105)\) N/m. For the second mode both sides are \((1\,313\,625;\ -811\,865)\) N/m.

The ratios \(1{,}618\) and \(-0{,}618\) are not accidental. If we eliminate \(x\) from \(r = 2 - x\) and \(r = 1/(1 - x)\) for \(x = \lambda m/k\), we get \(r\,(r - 1) = 1\), that is \(r^2 - r - 1 = 0\), the golden ratio (zlati rez) \(r = (1 \pm \sqrt5)/2\). Why exactly this equation? The floors have equal masses, so the inertia force of a floor is proportional to its displacement, and the ratio of the inertia forces of the upper and the lower floor equals \(r\). The force of the storey on the upper floor is \(-k\,(r - 1)\,\varphi_1\) (only the spring of its storey acts, its elongation is \(q_2 - q_1\)). On the lower floor the spring below it acts with \(-k\,\varphi_1\), the spring above it with \(+k\,(r - 1)\,\varphi_1\), and the resultant is \(-k\,(2 - r)\,\varphi_1\). The ratio of these forces must also be \(r\), so \((r - 1)/(2 - r) = r\), which is the same equation. From it \(r - 1 = 1/r\): in the first mode the drift of the upper storey (storey drift), the difference \(q_2 - q_1\), is \(0{,}618\) times the drift of the lower one.

In the first mode both floors move in the same direction, the upper one \(1{,}618\) times more. In the second they move in opposite directions, the upper one \(0{,}618\) times as much as the lower. Figure 10.6 shows them.

By lemma 10.8 a vibration in one mode is \(\vek q(t) = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,(a\cos\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t + b\sin\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t)\). Figure 10.7 (left) shows it for the first mode with amplitude \(5\) mm on the lower floor: the upper floor has amplitude \(5 \cdot 1{,}618 = 8{,}09\) mm and both floors pass through zero at the same moments, first at \(T_1/4 = 0{,}0802\) s.

And what about the sum of two modes? The equation is linear in \(\vek q\), so the sum of two solutions is a solution, as in step 3 of the proof of corollary 8.124. Take \(\vek q(t) = 5\,\boldsymbol\varphi_1\cos\omega_1 t + 2\,\boldsymbol\varphi_2\cos\omega_2 t\) mm, that is the first mode with amplitude \(5\) mm on the lower floor and the second with \(2\) mm. At \(t = 0\) we have \(\vek q(0) = (7;\ 6{,}854)\) mm, the ratio \(q_2/q_1 = 0{,}979\). At \(t = 0{,}05\) s the ratio is \(4{,}97\). Since the ratio is not constant, this motion is not synchronous. The lower floor first passes through zero at \(0{,}0593\) s, the upper at \(0{,}0835\) s, so not together (figure 10.7, right). Synchronous motions are therefore special solutions, the sum of two is not synchronous. Whether every motion is a sum of modes we prove in the next sections.

10.2.2 Bracket B: modes along the principal directions (konzola B: načini vzdolž glavnih smeri)

Bracket B (konzola B) is the truss of section 4.8.1. Bar \(AC\) is horizontal and \(4\) m long, bar \(BC\) is \(5\) m long and points from the wall to \(C\) in the direction \((4;\ -3)/5\), the pins \(A\) and \(B\) are fixed to the wall, \(EA = 19{,}6\) MN. At the pin \(C\) we put a mass \(m = 1000\) kg, the bars have no mass (our model, not from the source). The column \(\vek q = (u, v)\) holds the horizontal displacement to the right and the vertical displacement upwards of the pin \(C\). The stiffness matrix of the truss in these coordinates is (definition 7.4)

\[\mat K = \begin{bmatrix} 7{,}4088 & -1{,}8816 \\ -1{,}8816 & 1{,}4112 \end{bmatrix}\cdot 10^6\ \text{N/m} , \qquad \mat M = m\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \tag{10.15}\]

and its inverse is the flexibility matrix \(\mat D = (1\ \text{m}/EA)\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 16/3 \\ 16/3 & 21 \end{bmatrix}\) from equation (4.82) (lemma 10.3). The matrix \(\mat M\) is a multiple of the identity, so equation (10.12) is the eigenvalue problem of the matrix \(\mat K\) alone with the eigenvalue \(\lambda m\).

By step 3 of the proof of theorem 8.123 the frequency equation is \((\lambda m)^2 - (\operatorname{tr}\mat K)\,\lambda m + \det\mat K = 0\) with trace (sled) \(\operatorname{tr}\mat K = 8{,}82\cdot 10^6\) N/m and \(\det\mat K = 6{,}9149\cdot 10^{12}\) N\(^2\)/m\(^2\). The solutions are \(\lambda_1 m = 869\,771\) N/m and \(\lambda_2 m = 7\,950\,229\) N/m, so

\[\lambda_1 = 869{,}77\ \text{1/s}^2 , \quad \lambda_2 = 7950{,}23\ \text{1/s}^2 , \qquad \omega_1 = 29{,}492\ \text{1/s} , \quad \omega_2 = 89{,}164\ \text{1/s} ,\]

that is \(f_1 = 4{,}6938\) Hz and \(f_2 = 14{,}191\) Hz. The unit modes are \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1 = (0{,}27653;\ 0{,}96101)\), pointing \(73{,}95^\circ\) above the axis \(x\), and \(\boldsymbol\varphi_2 = (0{,}96101;\ -0{,}27653)\), pointing \(16{,}05^\circ\) below it. We check the first: \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_1 = (240\,517;\ 835\,855)\) N/m, and \(\lambda_1 m\,\boldsymbol\varphi_1 = 869\,771\cdot(0{,}27653;\ 0{,}96101) = (240\,517;\ 835\,855)\) N/m.

The modes are perpendicular. By corollary 8.124 we have \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1^\T\mat M\boldsymbol\varphi_2 = 0\), which for \(\mat M = m\mat I\) is exactly \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1\cdot\boldsymbol\varphi_2 = 0\), and indeed \(0{,}27653 \cdot 0{,}96101 - 0{,}96101 \cdot 0{,}27653 = 0\). The motion of the pin in the first mode is therefore a straight line at the angle \(73{,}95^\circ\), in the second a line perpendicular to it. Why exactly so? The flexibility matrix gives the answer. If we multiply the equation \(\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi = \lambda m\,\boldsymbol\varphi\) from the left by \(\mat D = \mat K^{-1}\), we get

\[\boldsymbol\varphi = \lambda m\,\mat D\boldsymbol\varphi , \qquad \mat D\boldsymbol\varphi = \frac{1}{\lambda m}\,\boldsymbol\varphi . \tag{10.16}\]

A force in the direction of a mode therefore causes a displacement in the same direction. For a force of \(1\) kN in the direction \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1\) the displacement is \(1{,}1497\) mm (\(1/(\lambda_1 m) = 1{,}1497\cdot 10^{-6}\) m/N), in the direction \(\boldsymbol\varphi_2\) only \(0{,}12578\) mm. Since \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1\) and \(\boldsymbol\varphi_2\) are perpendicular unit columns, a force of magnitude \(1\) kN in an arbitrary direction is \(\vek F = 1\,\text{kN}\,(c_1\boldsymbol\varphi_1 + c_2\boldsymbol\varphi_2)\) with \(c_1^2 + c_2^2 = 1\). By equation (10.16) the displacement is \(\mat D\vek F = 1\,\text{kN}\,(c_1 d_1\boldsymbol\varphi_1 + c_2 d_2\boldsymbol\varphi_2)\) with \(d_{\mathrm{r}} = 1/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} m)\). The components of the displacement \(x_{\mathrm{r}} = c_{\mathrm{r}} d_{\mathrm{r}}\cdot 1\,\text{kN}\) in the directions of the modes satisfy \((x_1/d_1)^2 + (x_2/d_2)^2 = (1\,\text{kN})^2\). This is an ellipse (elipsa) with semi-axes \(1{,}1497\) mm and \(0{,}12578\) mm, lying in the directions of the modes (figure 10.8). The modes are therefore eigenvectors of the flexibility matrix (definition 2.59), that is its principal directions. The first mode is the direction in which the pin is most flexible, so it has the lowest frequency.

Why is the flexibility in the direction \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1\) \(9{,}14\) times larger? When the pin is displaced by \(\vek q\), bar \(AC\) lengthens by \(u\) and bar \(BC\) by \(0{,}8\,u - 0{,}6\,v\) (section 4.8.1). For a displacement of \(1\) m in the direction \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1\) these are \(0{,}277\) m and \(-0{,}355\) m, for a displacement of \(1\) m in the direction \(\boldsymbol\varphi_2\) they are \(0{,}961\) m and \(0{,}935\) m. Twice the energy of the bars is \((EA/4)\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{AC}}^2 + (EA/5)\,\Delta L_{\mathrm{BC}}^2 = \boldsymbol\varphi^\T\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi\), and it gives \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1^\T\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_1 = 869\,771\) N/m and \(\boldsymbol\varphi_2^\T\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_2 = 7\,950\,229\) N/m, that is \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} m\) by lemma 10.8. In the first mode the bars deform little and in opposite senses (a lengthening of \(0{,}277\) m and a shortening of \(0{,}355\) m), in the second both deform a lot and in the same sense, each by almost the whole displacement.

10.2.3 Other coordinates: storey drifts (druge koordinate: etažni zamiki)

For frame A we chose the displacements of the floors as coordinates. Physically the storey drift (etažni zamik) would be just as natural, that is the displacement of a floor relative to the one below it. Let \(q_1' = q_1\) and \(q_2' = q_2 - q_1\) be the drifts of the first and the second storey. What happens to the eigenvalue problem? We write \(\vek q = \mat P\vek q'\) with the invertible matrix \(\mat P = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) (\(\det\mat P = 1\)). As in section 8.13.3, the energies in the new coordinates are written with \(\mat K' = \mat P^\T\mat K\mat P\) and \(\mat M' = \mat P^\T\mat M\mat P\). We compute them:

\[\mat K' = k\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat M' = \begin{bmatrix} 2m & m \\ m & m \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1000 & 500 \\ 500 & 500 \end{bmatrix}\ \text{kg} . \tag{10.17}\]

The stiffness matrix is diagonal, because the potential energy \(\tfrac12 k\,q_1'^2 + \tfrac12 k\,q_2'^2\) is the sum of the energies of the storeys, each depending only on its own drift. The mass matrix has an off-diagonal element, because the kinetic energy is \(\tfrac12 m\,\dot{q}_1'^2 + \tfrac12 m\,(\dot{q}_1' + \dot{q}_2')^2\) and the upper floor moves with the drift of both storeys. The coupling has moved from the stiffness to the mass matrix. The eigenvalues stay the same:

  1. The frequency equation of the new coordinates is \(\det(\mat K' - \lambda\mat M') = (k - 1000\lambda)(k - 500\lambda) - (500\lambda)^2 = 250\,000\,\lambda^2 - 1500\,k\,\lambda + k^2\).
  2. At \(m = 500\) kg we have \(m^2 = 250\,000\) and \(3km = 1500\,k\), so this is the same equation as (10.14).
  3. Why? If \((\mat K' - \lambda\mat M')\,\boldsymbol\varphi' = \vek 0\), then \(\mat P^\T(\mat K - \lambda\mat M)\,\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi' = \vek 0\). The matrix \(\mat P^\T\) is invertible, so \(\mat P^\T\vek y = \vek 0\) implies \(\vek y = \vek 0\), and therefore \((\mat K - \lambda\mat M)\,\mat P\boldsymbol\varphi' = \vek 0\). The column \(\boldsymbol\varphi = \mat P\boldsymbol\varphi'\) is an eigencolumn in the old choice of coordinates with the same eigenvalue. Conversely with \(\mat P^{-1}\).
  4. The modes in drifts are \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1' = \mat P^{-1}\boldsymbol\varphi_1 = (1;\ 0{,}618)\) and \(\boldsymbol\varphi_2' = (1;\ -1{,}618)\). In the first mode the drift of the upper storey is \(0{,}618\) times the drift of the lower one, as we saw before.

The frequencies therefore depend only on the system, not on the coordinates in which we write it. The coordinates determine how we write the modes and where the coupling goes, not the physics.

10.2.4 Where next (kam naprej)

We found that frame A and bracket B have two modes each, every one with its own frequency, and that the modes are perpendicular in the sense fixed by the mass matrix (for B in the ordinary sense). We got this for \(n = 2\) with a \(2 \times 2\) determinant. A bar of \(16\) finite elements, which we meet as an example in this chapter (in chapter 7 we divided the bar into only a few elements), has \(16\) coordinates, and a \(2 \times 2\) determinant does not suffice for it. So we ask: does every such system have \(n\) modes? Are the eigenvalues always real? How are two modes related if their eigenvalues differ, and what if they are equal? And is every motion a sum of modes, as it was for \(n = 2\)? The next section answers all these questions.

10.3 Mathematics: the spectral theorem

In section 10.2 we obtained, for frame A, two natural frequencies and two modes from a determinant of order 2, and vibration in one mode was a motion in which all coordinates move in step (lemma 10.8). For a system with 16 coordinates, such as the bar made of finite elements will be, we have no determinant of order 16, since the book has determinants only up to order 3 (definition 2.50). Even if we had one, we would obtain an equation of degree 16 for \(\lambda\), and we would not know whether it has 16 real solutions. So four questions arise for a pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) of order \(n\).

  1. Does the pair always have \(n\) eigenpairs (definition 10.7)?
  2. Are the eigenvalues real, even if we admit complex numbers? A complex eigenvalue would give a motion in which vibration is mixed with growth or decay.
  3. How are the modes related to each other?
  4. Is every column a sum of modes, so that every motion can be built from them?

The answer is theorem 10.13 of this section. We prove it without determinants, with the smallest value, along the same path by which we proved theorem 2.61 for a \(3 \times 3\) matrix with the largest value in chapter 2.

10.3.1 Idea: successive minima

For the principal directions we looked for the unit vector at which \(\vek n^\T\mat A\,\vek n\) is largest and showed that it is an eigenvector. We do the same here, with three changes. First: instead of the unit sphere \(\vek v^\T\vek v = 1\) we take the set of columns with \(\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v = 1\). At velocities \(\dot{\vek q}\) the kinetic energy is \(\tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek q}\) (theorem 8.84), so all columns of this set, read as velocities, have the same kinetic energy. By lemma 10.8 the eigenvalue is the quotient \(\lambda = \vek\varphi^\T\mat K\,\vek\varphi/\vek\varphi^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi\), the ratio of twice the potential energy at displacements \(\vek\varphi\) to twice the kinetic energy at velocities \(\vek\varphi\). So we expect the lowest frequency to belong to the shape that strains the structure least at a given kinetic energy, and we look for the smallest value of \(\vek v^\T\mat K\,\vek v\) on this set. Second change: we look for the smallest, not the largest value, because the lowest frequency interests us first. Third change: we cannot get the third direction from a cross product, which we do not have for more coordinates, so we will need another argument, lemma 10.9.

Let us look at the set and its smallest value for frame A. In the coordinates \((q_1, q_2)\) of section 10.1 we have \(\mat M = m\mat I\) and the set \(\vek q^\T\mat M\,\vek q = 1\) is a circle. In the coordinates \((q_1, q_2 - q_1)\) of section 10.2 \(\mat K\) is a multiple of the identity matrix, the curves of constant value of \(\vek v^\T\mat K\,\vek v\) are circles, and the modes \((1,\ 0{,}618)\) and \((1,\ -1{,}618)\) are perpendicular, since \(1 \cdot 1 + 0{,}618 \cdot (-1{,}618) = 0\) up to rounding. In both cases this comes from the coordinates, not from a general rule. So we take coordinates in which neither matrix is diagonal: the displacement of the upper floor \(y_1 = q_2\) and the drift of the upper storey \(y_2 = q_2 - q_1\). From \(\vek q = \mat P\,\vek y\) with \(\mat P = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) we get \(\vek q^\T\mat K\,\vek q = \vek y^\T(\mat P^\T\mat K\mat P)\,\vek y\) (lemma 1.101), hence

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{y}} = \mat P^\T\mat K\mat P = k\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat M_{\mathrm{y}} = \mat P^\T\mat M\mat P = m\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \tag{10.18}\]

with \(k = 501\,760\) N/m and \(m = 500\) kg. The set \(\vek y^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek y = 1\) is an ellipse with semi-axes \(0{,}0724\) and \(0{,}0276\) kg\(^{-1/2}\) (figure 10.9). The curves of constant value \(\vek y^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek y = c\) are ellipses about the origin that grow as \(c\) increases. The smallest value of \(\vek y^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek y\) on the ellipse is reached by the smallest ellipse of this family that still reaches the ellipse (it touches it from inside), and the largest by the largest one that still reaches it (it touches it from outside). The two touchings occur at \(c = 383{,}311\) 1/s\(^2\) (blue) and \(c = 2627{,}249\) 1/s\(^2\) (orange), which are exactly the eigenvalues of section 10.2. The points of contact are \(\pm\vek\varphi_1\) and \(\pm\vek\varphi_2\) with \(\vek\varphi_1 = (0{,}038042,\ 0{,}014531)\) and \(\vek\varphi_2 = (-0{,}023511,\ -0{,}061554)\) kg\(^{-1/2}\). At \(c = 900\) 1/s\(^2\) (grey dashed) the curve cuts the ellipse at four points. The smallest value is not reached there, because from an intersection point we can move along the ellipse to the side where \(\vek y^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek y < 900\) 1/s\(^2\).

At the point of contact \(\vek\varphi_1\) must be an eigencolumn: if the two curves crossed at this point, we could move along the ellipse to the side with a smaller value. This is the idea of section 2.11.2, here for a pair of matrices. The proof will make it precise and for every order \(n\).

The assumptions are as follows. The matrix \(\mat K\) is symmetric with real entries, while \(\vek v^\T\mat K\,\vek v\) may have either sign, so that we also cover unstable equilibrium (\(\lambda < 0\)) and a mechanism (\(\lambda = 0\)). The matrix \(\mat M\) is symmetric and positive definite (definition 6.27), both of order \(n\), as in theorem 10.2. Columns have \(n\) real entries.

10.3.2 Tools: more unknowns than equations, and \(\mat M\)-orthogonality

In theorem 2.61 we obtained the third direction as the cross product of two perpendicular vectors. For any order \(n\) we need another statement: when we impose fewer conditions than there are unknowns, something nonzero still satisfies them.

Lemma 10.9 Homogeneous system with more unknowns than equations (homogeni sistem z več neznankami kot enačbami)

Let \(\mat A\) be a real matrix with \(k\) rows and \(n\) columns, \(n > k\). Then there is a column \(\vek w \ne \vek 0\) with \(n\) entries for which \(\mat A\,\vek w = \vek 0\).

Proof

We must show that the elimination of definition 8.20 leaves some column without a pivot, and that the unknown of this column can be set to \(1\). The idea comes from the proof of lemma 8.21.

  1. Gaussian elimination with row exchanges as in definition 8.20 finds \(r\) pivots, one in each of the rows \(1, \dots, r\), in the columns \(c_1 < c_2 < \dots < c_{\mathrm{r}}\) (each pivot lies to the right of the previous one). There are \(k\) rows, so \(r \le k\). Each step of the elimination, an exchange of two rows or the subtraction of a multiple of one row from another, gives a system with the same solutions (step 1 of the proof of lemma 8.21). We obtain a system \(\mat U\,\vek w = \vek 0\) with the same set of solutions as \(\mat A\,\vek w = \vek 0\).
  2. By definition 8.20 the pivot \(U_{\mathrm{i} \mathrm{c}_\mathrm{i}}\) in row \(i \le r\) is nonzero, and all entries of row \(i\) to its left are zero. Indeed, column \(c_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the first column to the right of \(c_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) that has a nonzero number in the rows from \(i\) on. The columns before it have zeros in these rows: the pivot columns because of the subtractions in earlier steps, the columns in between because of the choice of the pivot. Later steps do not spoil these zeros, because they exchange and subtract only rows that already have zeros in these columns. If \(r < k\), the rows \(r + 1, \dots, k\) are all zeros for the same reason: the elimination stopped because none of these rows has a nonzero number in the columns to the right of \(c_{\mathrm{r}}\) (for \(r = 0\) in all columns), and in the columns up to \(c_{\mathrm{r}}\) they have zeros from earlier steps.
  3. There are \(r \le k < n\) pivots and \(n\) columns, so there is a column \(j\) that is not a pivot column. We set \(w_{\mathrm{j}} = 1\) and \(w_{\mathrm{l}} = 0\) for every other column \(l\) without a pivot.
  4. We determine the unknowns in the pivot columns in the order \(i = r, r - 1, \dots, 1\) (back substitution). Row \(i\) contains only unknowns \(w_{\mathrm{l}}\) with \(l \ge c_{\mathrm{i}}\), so equation \(i\) gives \(w_{\mathrm{c}_\mathrm{i}} = -\sum_{\mathrm{l} > \mathrm{c}_\mathrm{i}} U_{\mathrm{il}}\,w_{\mathrm{l}}/U_{\mathrm{i} \mathrm{c}_\mathrm{i}}\), where all \(w_{\mathrm{l}}\) with \(l > c_{\mathrm{i}}\) are already known: either they come from step 3, or they are unknowns \(w_{\mathrm{c}_{\mathrm{i}'}}\) of rows \(i' > i\), determined earlier.
  5. The rows \(1, \dots, r\) are thus satisfied, and the rows \(r + 1, \dots, k\) are all zeros and are satisfied for every \(\vek w\). Hence \(\mat U\,\vek w = \vek 0\), by step 1 also \(\mat A\,\vek w = \vek 0\), and \(w_{\mathrm{j}} = 1\) says \(\vek w \ne \vek 0\).

Source: KREYSZIG §7.5, Theorem 3 (PDF p. 317) states the claim. The proof is not from the source.

We test the statement on a system of two equations in three unknowns, \(x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 0\) and \(4x_1 + 5x_2 + 6x_3 = 0\). Subtracting four times the first row from the second gives \(-3x_2 - 6x_3 = 0\). The pivots are in columns \(1\) and \(2\), column \(3\) is free, so we set \(x_3 = 1\). The second row gives \(x_2 = -2\), the first \(x_1 = -2x_2 - 3x_3 = 1\). The column \((1, -2, 1)\) indeed solves both equations: \(1 - 4 + 3 = 0\) and \(4 - 10 + 6 = 0\).

For \(\mat M = \mat I\) we measured the perpendicularity of columns with the scalar product. For the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) it is replaced by the product with the matrix \(\mat M\), because \(\mat M\) determines the kinetic energy.

Definition 10.10 Orthogonality and normalization with respect to the mass matrix (ortogonalnost in normiranost glede na masno matriko)

Let \(\mat M\) be a symmetric, positive definite matrix of order \(n\). Real columns \(\vek\varphi\) and \(\vek\psi\) with \(n\) entries are \(\mat M\)-orthogonal (\(\mat M\)-ortogonalna), if \(\vek\varphi^\T\mat M\,\vek\psi = 0\). A column \(\vek\varphi\) is \(\mat M\)-normalized (\(\mat M\)-normiran), if \(\vek\varphi^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi = 1\). A set of columns is \(\mat M\)-orthonormal (\(\mat M\)-ortonormirana), if all its columns are \(\mat M\)-normalized and any two different ones are \(\mat M\)-orthogonal, that is \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = 1\) for \(r = s\) and \(0\) for \(r \ne s\).

Source: CK (10.20) and the text below it, "orthogonal with respect to the mass matrix" (PDF p. 307), CK (10.31) for the normalization (PDF p. 312).

The condition does not depend on the order of the two columns. For a symmetric matrix \(\mat A\) of order \(n\) and columns \(\vek v\), \(\vek w\) with \(n\) entries, \(\vek v^\T\mat A\,\vek w\) is a \(1 \times 1\) matrix, which equals its transpose, so by lemma 1.101 (points 1 and 3)

\[\vek v^\T\mat A\,\vek w = (\vek v^\T\mat A\,\vek w)^\T = \vek w^\T\mat A^\T\vek v = \vek w^\T\mat A\,\vek v . \tag{10.19}\]

This is equation (2.60) of chapter 2 for any order \(n\). For \(\mat A = \mat M\) it says that \(\vek\varphi^\T\mat M\,\vek\psi = 0\) exactly when \(\vek\psi^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi = 0\).
