For \(\mat M = \mat I\) this is ordinary perpendicularity, for frame A in the coordinates \(\vek q\) (\(\mat M = m\mat I\)) too, but for frame A in the coordinates \(\vek y\) it is not (figure 10.9). The unit of the entries of an \(\mat M\)-normalized column is kg\(^{-1/2}\), because \(\vek\varphi^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi = 1\) is a number without a unit. Meaning of the normalization: the velocities \(\dot{\vek q} = \sqrt{1\ \text{J}}\,\vek\varphi\) have kinetic energy \(\tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek q} = \tfrac12\) J.

Corollary 10.11 At most as many nonzero mass-orthogonal columns as coordinates (največ toliko neničelnih masno ortogonalnih stolpcev, kolikor je koordinat)

Let \(\mat M\) be a symmetric, positive definite matrix of order \(n\) and \(\vek\psi_1, \dots, \vek\psi_{\mathrm{p}}\) nonzero, pairwise \(\mat M\)-orthogonal columns with \(n\) entries. Then:

  1. From \(c_1\vek\psi_1 + \dots + c_{\mathrm{p}}\vek\psi_{\mathrm{p}} = \vek 0\) it follows that \(c_1 = \dots = c_{\mathrm{p}} = 0\).
  2. \(p \le n\).
  3. If \(p = n\) and the column \(\vek w\) is \(\mat M\)-orthogonal to all of \(\vek\psi_1, \dots, \vek\psi_{\mathrm{n}}\), then \(\vek w = \vek 0\).
Proof

We must show three points. The first is a computation with the product with \(\mat M\), the second and third follow from lemma 10.9.

  1. Let \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} c_{\mathrm{i}}\vek\psi_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek 0\). For each \(j\) we multiply the equation from the left by the row \(\vek\psi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat M\) (lemma 1.99, point 3), and since \(\vek\psi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\psi_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) for \(i \ne j\), there remains \(c_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek\psi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\psi_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\). Since \(\vek\psi_{\mathrm{j}} \ne \vek 0\) and \(\mat M\) is positive definite, \(\vek\psi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\psi_{\mathrm{j}} > 0\), hence \(c_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\).
  2. Suppose \(p > n\). The matrix \(\mat A\) with the columns \(\vek\psi_1, \dots, \vek\psi_{\mathrm{p}}\) has \(n\) rows and \(p > n\) columns, so by lemma 10.9 there is \(\vek c \ne \vek 0\) with \(\mat A\,\vek c = \vek 0\). By (1.38) entry \(l\) of the column \(\mat A\,\vek c\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} (\vek\psi_{\mathrm{i}})_{\mathrm{l}}\,c_{\mathrm{i}}\), so \(\mat A\,\vek c = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} c_{\mathrm{i}}\vek\psi_{\mathrm{i}} = \vek 0\). This contradicts point 1.
  3. Let \(\vek w \ne \vek 0\) be \(\mat M\)-orthogonal to all \(\vek\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\). Then \(\vek\psi_1, \dots, \vek\psi_{\mathrm{n}}, \vek w\) is a set of \(n + 1\) nonzero pairwise \(\mat M\)-orthogonal columns, which contradicts point 2.

Source: The proof is not from a source. CK (PDF p. 313) states that the modes are linearly independent and refers to Problem 10.8.

For \(\mat M = \mat I\) and \(n = 3\) the corollary says that space has no four nonzero pairwise perpendicular vectors. Before we state the theorem, we need the set on which we look for the minimum. It must be nonempty, closed and bounded, so that theorem 8.26 guarantees that the minimum exists.

Lemma 10.12 The set of mass-normalized columns (množica masno normiranih stolpcev)

Let \(\mat M\) be a symmetric, positive definite matrix of order \(n\) and \(\vek b_1, \dots, \vek b_{\mathrm{k}}\) arbitrary columns with \(n\) entries, \(k < n\). The set

\[S = \{\vek v :\ \vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v = 1 ,\ \vek b_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\vek v = 0 \text{ for } j = 1, \dots, k\}\]

is nonempty, closed and bounded. For \(k = 0\) there are no conditions \(\vek b_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\vek v = 0\). For \(\vek b_{\mathrm{j}} = \mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\) they are the \(\mat M\)-orthogonality conditions \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v = 0\), since \(\mat M\) is symmetric.

Proof

We must show three properties. Nonemptiness comes from lemma 10.9, boundedness from the smallest value of \(\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v\) on the unit sphere, closedness from the continuity of polynomials.

  1. Nonempty. The conditions \(\vek b_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\vek w = 0\) are \(k\) equations in \(n > k\) unknowns \(w_1, \dots, w_{\mathrm{n}}\), with the rows \(\vek b_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\) as coefficients. By lemma 10.9 there is \(\vek w \ne \vek 0\) that satisfies them. For \(k = 0\) there are no conditions and we take \(\vek w = \vek e_1\). Since \(\mat M\) is positive definite, \(\vek w^\T\mat M\,\vek w > 0\), and \(\vek v = \vek w/\sqrt{\vek w^\T\mat M\,\vek w}\) lies in \(S\), since \(\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v = 1\) and the orthogonality conditions are homogeneous.
  2. Bounded. As in step 1 of the proof of theorem 8.61, the polynomial \(\vek u \mapsto \vek u^\T\mat M\,\vek u\) has a smallest value \(\mu\) on the unit sphere \(|\vek u| = 1\) (theorem 8.26, lemma 8.24, points 3 and 4), and \(\mu > 0\) because \(\mat M\) is positive definite. Every \(\vek v \ne \vek 0\) is \(|\vek v|\,\vek u\) with \(\vek u = \vek v/|\vek v|\) on the sphere, and since the quadratic form is multiplied by \(c^2\) when the column is multiplied by a number \(c\), \(\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v = |\vek v|^2\,\vek u^\T\mat M\,\vek u \ge \mu\,|\vek v|^2\). For \(\vek v\) in \(S\) therefore \(1 \ge \mu\,|\vek v|^2\), hence \(|\vek v| \le 1/\sqrt\mu\).
  3. Closed. Each of the functions \(\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v\) and \(\vek b_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\vek v\) is a polynomial in the coordinates \(v_1, \dots, v_{\mathrm{n}}\), hence continuous (lemma 8.24, point 3). By point 4 of the same lemma the sets where a continuous function has the value \(1\) or \(0\) are closed. By the same point the intersection of these \(k + 1\) sets is closed too, since we obtain it by \(k\) successive intersections of two closed sets.

Source: The proof is not from a source, apart from the lemmas and theorems used.

10.3.3 The theorem

Theorem 10.13 Spectral theorem for the stiffness and mass matrix (spektralni izrek za togostno in masno matriko)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric matrix of order \(n\) with real entries and \(\mat M\) a symmetric, positive definite matrix of order \(n\). Then there are real numbers \(\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) and real columns \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) with \(n\) entries that are \(\mat M\)-orthonormal (definition 10.10) and for which

\[\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} \qquad (r = 1, \dots, n) . \tag{10.20}\]

The number \(\lambda_1\) is the smallest value of \(\vek v^\T\mat K\,\vek v\) among the columns with \(\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v = 1\). The number \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the smallest value of the same expression among the columns with \(\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v = 1\) that are \(\mat M\)-orthogonal to \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}-1}\).

Proof

We find the eigenpairs one after the other, as in theorem 2.61, but with the smallest value. We must show that the smallest value on the set \(S_{\mathrm{r}}\) exists, that the column \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) at which it is reached is an eigencolumn, and that the procedure runs up to \(r = n\). We write \(q(\vek v) = \vek v^\T\mat K\,\vek v\) and \(p(\vek v) = \vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v\). Let \(W_{\mathrm{r}}\) be the set of columns \(\vek v\) with \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v = 0\) for \(j < r\) (\(W_1\) is the set of all columns) and \(S_{\mathrm{r}}\) the set of columns in \(W_{\mathrm{r}}\) with \(p(\vek v) = 1\). The induction step \(r\) assumes that \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}-1}\) have already been chosen, \(\mat M\)-orthonormal, with \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\). For \(r = 1\) there is no assumption. The set \(S_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the set \(S\) of lemma 10.12 with \(k = r - 1\) and \(\vek b_{\mathrm{j}} = \mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\).

  1. By lemma 10.12 \(S_{\mathrm{r}}\) is nonempty, closed and bounded when \(r - 1 < n\), and \(q\) is continuous (lemma 8.24, point 3). By theorem 8.26 there is \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) in \(S_{\mathrm{r}}\) such that \(q(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}) = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \le q(\vek v)\) for every \(\vek v\) in \(S_{\mathrm{r}}\). Since \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) lies in \(S_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 1\) and \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is \(\mat M\)-orthogonal to \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}-1}\). This is the last sentence of the theorem.
  2. Since \(q(c\,\vek v) = c^2\,q(\vek v)\) and \(p(c\,\vek v) = c^2\,p(\vek v)\), every nonzero \(\vek v\) in \(W_{\mathrm{r}}\) gives \(\vek v/\sqrt{p(\vek v)}\) in \(S_{\mathrm{r}}\) (the set \(W_{\mathrm{r}}\) is closed under multiplication by a number, \(p(\vek v) > 0\)). By step 1 \(q(\vek v)/p(\vek v) \ge \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). Let \(\mat B = \mat K - \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\mat M\), a symmetric matrix (lemma 1.101, point 2). By lemma 1.99, point 3, then
    \[\vek v^\T\mat B\,\vek v = q(\vek v) - \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,p(\vek v) \ge 0 \quad \text{for every } \vek v \text{ in } W_{\mathrm{r}} , \qquad \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = 0 ,\]
    where for \(\vek v = \vek 0\) both sides of the inequality are zero.
  3. Let \(\vek z\) be a column in \(W_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(t\) a number. Then \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} + t\,\vek z\) lies in \(W_{\mathrm{r}}\), because the conditions \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v = 0\) are linear in \(\vek v\). We expand with the properties of the matrix product (lemmas 1.99 and 1.101). The first term of the expansion is \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) by step 2, the two middle terms are equal by (10.19), \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat B\,\vek z = \vek z^\T\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), and by step 2
    \[(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} + t\,\vek z)^\T\mat B\,(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} + t\,\vek z) = 2t\,\alpha + t^2\beta \ge 0 , \qquad \alpha = \vek z^\T\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} , \quad \beta = \vek z^\T\mat B\,\vek z \ge 0 ,\]
    for every number \(t\). As in step 6 of the proof of theorem 2.61 it follows that \(\alpha = 0\): if \(\alpha \ne 0\), the expression would have the value \(-\alpha^2(\beta + 2)/(\beta + 1)^2 < 0\) at \(t = -\alpha/(\beta + 1)\) (figure 2.72). Hence \(\vek z^\T\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) for every \(\vek z\) in \(W_{\mathrm{r}}\).
  4. Let \(\vek w\) be any column, \(c_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat M\,\vek w\) for \(j < r\) and \(\vek z = \vek w - \sum_{\mathrm{j}<\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\). By \(\mat M\)-orthonormality \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}^\T\mat M\,\vek z = c_{\mathrm{i}} - \sum_{\mathrm{j}<\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = c_{\mathrm{i}} - c_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) for every \(i < r\), so \(\vek z\) lies in \(W_{\mathrm{r}}\).
  5. For \(j < r\) we have \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\). The matrices \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) are symmetric, so by lemma 1.101 and the induction assumption \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = (\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}})^\T\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = (\lambda_{\mathrm{j}}\,\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}})^\T\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), and this is zero because \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) lies in \(W_{\mathrm{r}}\). Also \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\), so \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 0 - \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \cdot 0\).
  6. By step 4 \(\vek w = \vek z + \sum_{\mathrm{j}<\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\), so by lemma 1.101, point 2, and steps 3 and 5, for every column \(\vek w\)
    \[\vek w^\T\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek z^\T\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}<\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 0 .\]
    For \(\vek w = \mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) this is \((\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}})^\T(\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}) = |\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}|^2 = 0\). A sum of squares of entries is zero only if every entry is zero, so \(\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek 0\) and \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\). Step \(r\) is complete.
  7. Since \(W_{\mathrm{r}} \subset W_{\mathrm{r}-1}\), also \(S_{\mathrm{r}} \subset S_{\mathrm{r}-1}\), and the smallest value on the smaller set is not smaller: \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}-1} \le \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\).
  8. By lemma 10.12 \(S_{\mathrm{r}}\) is nonempty for every \(r \le n\), so all the steps \(r = 1, 2, \dots, n\) can be carried out. This gives \(\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\), the \(\mat M\)-orthonormal \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) and the equations (10.20).

Source: CK (10.20) and (10.21) (PDF p. 307) for the \(\mat M\)-orthogonality of modes with different frequencies, CM §2.5.6.2 and §2.5.6.3 (PDF pp. 92 and 93) for \(\mat M = \mat I\), KREYSZIG §8.4, Theorem 2 (PDF p. 366) the statement for symmetric matrices without proof ("For a proof (which is involved) see Ref. [B3]"), GR (PDF p. 93) for \(\mat M\)-orthonormal modes. The proof by successive minima is not from the sources, just like the proof of theorem 2.61.

Without determinants, the proof has shown that every pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) of order \(n\) has as many real eigenpairs with \(\mat M\)-orthonormal eigencolumns as there are coordinates: an eigencolumn is the point at which \(\vek v^\T\mat K\,\vek v\) takes the smallest value that the extreme value theorem guarantees, and equation (10.20) follows from its being the smallest. Step 3 is the precise form of the idea of figure 10.9: if \(\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) were not zero, we could move along the set \(S_{\mathrm{r}}\) to the side where \(\vek v^\T\mat K\,\vek v\) is smaller. For the first eigenpair (\(r = 1\)) \(W_1\) is the set of all columns and step 3 holds for every \(\vek z\), for the later ones only for columns in \(W_{\mathrm{r}}\). So step 4 splits every column into a part in \(W_{\mathrm{r}}\) and multiples of the eigencolumns already found, and step 5 shows that \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}^\T\mat B\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is zero for these as well. Later in this chapter we will use the last sentence of the theorem to estimate eigenvalues: the eigenvalues are the smallest values of the quotient of energies.

From history

Rayleigh, in his treatise Theory of Sound, published in 1877, introduced the fundamental concept of oscillation of a linear system about an equilibrium configuration and showed that eigenmodes and eigenfrequencies exist for discrete and for continuous systems (GR, PDF p. 19). He was concerned with acoustics, not with structural mechanics (GR, PDF p. 19). The pioneers of aeronautics were the first structural designers who had to get vibration under control, because they constantly aimed to reduce the weight of flying structures (GR, PDF p. 19). From the 1920s onwards aeronautical engineers had to admit the importance of the mechanics of vibration for predicting the aeroelastic behaviour of aircraft (GR, PDF p. 19). During the next forty years they had to limit the scope of their analysis to methods that the computational means of the time could handle (GR, PDF p. 19). The structural models were therefore either analytical or described by a small number of degrees of freedom, obtained by transfer (prenosnimi) or Rayleigh-Ritz methods (GR, PDF p. 19). The appearance and spread of computers since 1960 led to a reconsideration of all methods of analysis, and the traditional methods were replaced by matrix methods arising from the discretization of variational expressions (GR, PDF p. 19).

We met the methods of Rayleigh and Ritz in section 6.4.1, and the beginnings of the finite element method in section 7.2.2. Back to the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) and the theorem. For a symmetric \(\mat K\) and a positive definite \(\mat M\) of order \(n\) there are \(n\) real eigenpairs with \(\mat M\)-orthonormal modes, which the proof found one after the other as successive smallest values of the quotient of energies on the sets \(S_{\mathrm{r}}\).

10.3.4 Frame with two and three storeys

Let us look at the steps of the proof for frame A. For \(r = 1\), \(W_1\) is the plane of all columns \(\vek y\), and we saw the smallest value of \(\vek y^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek y\) on the ellipse \(\vek y^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek y = 1\) in figure 10.9: \(\lambda_1 = 383{,}311\) 1/s\(^2\) at \(\vek\varphi_1 = (0{,}038042,\ 0{,}014531)\) kg\(^{-1/2}\), which in the coordinates \(\vek q\) is the column \((0{,}023511,\ 0{,}038042)\) with the ratio of floor displacements \(1{,}618\), the first mode of section 10.2. For \(r = 2\), \(W_2\) is the line of columns with \(\vek\varphi_1^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{y}}\,\vek y = 0\), that is \(30{,}777\,y_1 - 11{,}756\,y_2 = 0\), hence \(y_2 = 2{,}618\,y_1\) (figure 10.10). This line cuts the ellipse at two points, \(\pm\vek\varphi_2\) with \(\vek\varphi_2 = (-0{,}023511,\ -0{,}061554)\) kg\(^{-1/2}\), which in the coordinates \(\vek q\) is the column \((0{,}038042,\ -0{,}023511)\) with the ratio \(-0{,}618\), the second mode. The set \(S_2\) therefore has two elements and the smallest value on it is \(\lambda_2 = 2627{,}249\) 1/s\(^2\). The procedure ends at \(r = n = 2\).

With a third storey we see why lemma 10.9 is needed. Let the frame have three equal storeys: three rigid floors of mass \(m = 500\) kg and three storeys of stiffness \(k = 501\,760\) N/m (our model, frame A with a third storey added). The floors have displacements \(q_1\), \(q_2\), \(q_3\) from the bottom up. By the same rule as for A (example 10.1, steps 2 and 3) the columns act on the floors with the forces \(-k(2q_1 - q_2)\), \(-k(-q_1 + 2q_2 - q_3)\) and \(-k(q_3 - q_2)\). Row \(i\) of the matrix \(\mat K\) holds the coefficients of the force on floor \(i\) with the opposite sign, hence

\[\mat K = k\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat M = m\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} . \tag{10.21}\]

Since \(\mat M = m\mat I\), we compute in units: we measure \(\lambda\) in the unit \(k/m = 1003{,}52\) 1/s\(^2\) and the entries of columns in the unit \(m^{-1/2}\). In these units \(\mat M\) plays the role of the identity matrix and \(\mat K\) the role of the matrix \(\mat K/k\), an \(\mat M\)-normalized column is a unit column, and the set \(S_1\) is the unit sphere. The numbers come from a NumPy computation.

  1. Step 1. The smallest value of \(\vek v^\T(\mat K/k)\,\vek v\) on the unit sphere is \(\lambda_1 = 0{,}198062\) at \(\vek\varphi_1 = (0{,}327985,\ 0{,}591009,\ 0{,}736976)\). We check equation (10.20): \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi_1/k = (0{,}064962,\ 0{,}117057,\ 0{,}145967)\) and \(\lambda_1\,\vek\varphi_1 = (0{,}064962,\ 0{,}117057,\ 0{,}145967)\).
  2. Step 2. The set \(W_2\) is the plane of columns perpendicular to \(\vek\varphi_1\), and \(S_2\) is the unit circle in it. The smallest value on this circle is \(\lambda_2 = 1{,}554958\) at \(\vek\varphi_2 = (0{,}736976,\ 0{,}327985,\ -0{,}591009)\). On the circle the value varies between \(1{,}554958\) and \(3{,}246980\).
  3. Step 3. The set \(W_3\) is given by two equations, \(\vek\varphi_1^\T\vek v = 0\) and \(\vek\varphi_2^\T\vek v = 0\), in three unknowns. By lemma 10.9 the system has a nonzero solution. We take the rows \((1,\ 1{,}801938,\ 2{,}24698)\) and \((1,\ 0{,}445042,\ -0{,}801938)\), multiples of \(\vek\varphi_1^\T\) and \(\vek\varphi_2^\T\). Subtracting the first row from the second gives \(-1{,}356896\,v_2 - 3{,}048917\,v_3 = 0\). The pivots are in columns \(1\) and \(2\), column \(3\) is free: \(v_3 = 1\), \(v_2 = -2{,}246980\), \(v_1 = -1{,}801938 \cdot (-2{,}246980) - 2{,}24698 = 1{,}801938\). Since \(v_3\) is the only free unknown, all solutions are multiples of this column. The length of this column is \(3{,}048917\), and \(\vek\varphi_3 = (0{,}591009,\ -0{,}736976,\ 0{,}327985)\) lies in \(S_3\). The set \(S_3\) has only two elements, \(\pm\vek\varphi_3\), and the value \(\vek\varphi_3^\T\mat K\,\vek\varphi_3/k = 3{,}246980 = \lambda_3\). The deviation \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi_3/k - \lambda_3\,\vek\varphi_3\) is below \(10^{-15}\).

The natural frequencies \(f_{\mathrm{r}} = \tfrac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}\) are \(2{,}2438\), \(6{,}2870\) and \(9{,}0850\) Hz. The ratios of the floor displacements, with the first one normalized to \(1\), are \((1,\ 1{,}8019,\ 2{,}2470)\), \((1,\ 0{,}4450,\ -0{,}8019)\) and \((1,\ -1{,}2470,\ 0{,}5550)\). In the first mode all floors move in the same direction and the top one the most, in the third the sign of the displacements alternates between neighbouring floors.

10.3.5 Expansion in modes and the modal matrix

The answer to the fourth question: every column is a sum of modes.

Corollary 10.14 Expansion theorem for any number of coordinates (razvoj po načinih za poljubno število koordinat)

Let \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) be as in theorem 10.13. Then:

  1. Every column \(\vek v\) with \(n\) entries is \(\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^n c_{\mathrm{r}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), and the coefficients are unique, \(c_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v\).
  2. If \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi = \lambda\,\mat M\,\vek\varphi\) for a real number \(\lambda\) and a column \(\vek\varphi \ne \vek 0\), then \(\lambda = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for some \(r\), and \(\vek\varphi\) is a sum of multiples of those \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) for which \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda\).
  3. The number of indices \(r\) with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda\) does not depend on the choice of columns in the proof of the theorem: every other choice according to the theorem gives the same list of eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\).
Proof

We must show the expansion, then what follows for other eigenpairs, and finally that the list of eigenvalues does not depend on the choice.

  1. Let \(\vek w = \vek v - \sum_{\mathrm{r}} (\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v)\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\). By \(\mat M\)-orthonormality \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\,\vek w = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v - \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v = 0\) for every \(s\). The columns \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) are nonzero, since they are \(\mat M\)-normalized, so by point 3 of corollary 10.11 \(\vek w = \vek 0\). If \(\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{r}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), we multiply from the left by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\) and obtain \(c_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v\) (again by \(\mat M\)-orthonormality).
  2. By point 1 \(\vek\varphi = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{r}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) with \(c_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi\). Since \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) are symmetric, by lemma 1.101 \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\,\vek\varphi = (\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}})^\T\vek\varphi = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,c_{\mathrm{r}}\), while by assumption \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\,\vek\varphi = \lambda\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi = \lambda\,c_{\mathrm{r}}\). Hence \((\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - \lambda)\,c_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) for every \(r\). Since \(\vek\varphi \ne \vek 0\), some \(c_{\mathrm{r}} \ne 0\), and for this \(r\) we have \(\lambda = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). Only the \(c_{\mathrm{r}}\) with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda\) can be nonzero.
  3. Let \(E_\lambda\) be the set of solutions of \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi = \lambda\,\mat M\,\vek\varphi\) (including \(\vek 0\)) and \(p\) the number of indices \(r\) with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda\). By step 2 every nonzero element of \(E_\lambda\) is a sum of multiples of the columns \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda\). For \(p = 0\) therefore \(E_\lambda = \{\vek 0\}\).
  4. Let \(\vek\psi_1, \dots, \vek\psi_{\mathrm{p}'}\) be \(\mat M\)-orthonormal columns in \(E_\lambda\). We show \(p' \le p\). For \(p = 0\) this holds, because an \(\mat M\)-normalized column is not \(\vek 0\). Let \(p \ge 1\) and suppose \(p' > p\). By step 3 \(\vek\psi_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} a_{\mathrm{ji}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\), a sum over the \(p\) indices \(j\) with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} = \lambda\). The system \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} a_{\mathrm{ji}}\,x_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\) has \(p\) equations and \(p' > p\) unknowns, so by lemma 10.9 there is \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\) for which \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} x_{\mathrm{i}}\,\vek\psi_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}}\big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} a_{\mathrm{ji}}\,x_{\mathrm{i}}\big)\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek 0\). This contradicts point 1 of corollary 10.11. Hence \(p' \le p\).
  5. Let another choice of columns in the proof of the theorem give the eigenvalues \(\lambda'_1 \le \dots \le \lambda'_{\mathrm{n}}\) and the columns \(\vek\varphi'_{\mathrm{r}}\). The columns \(\vek\varphi'_{\mathrm{r}}\) with \(\lambda'_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda\) are \(\mat M\)-orthonormal and lie in \(E_\lambda\), so by step 4 there are at most \(p\) of them. The other choice satisfies the theorem as well, so steps 1 to 4 also hold with the roles of the two choices exchanged, and there are at least \(p\) of them. Every real number therefore appears equally often in both lists. Both lists have \(n\) members and are in increasing order, so they are equal.

Source: CK (10.33) and (10.34) (PDF p. 313): "An expansion theorem can be stated for MDOF systems", GR (PDF p. 93) for the choice of \(\mat M\)-orthonormal modes for a repeated eigenvalue. The proof is not from a source.

The corollary says that there are no more than \(n\) eigenvalues and that we find them nowhere else than in the list of the theorem. For a repeated eigenvalue the choice of modes is not unique: for \(\mat K = k\mat I\) and \(\mat M = m\mat I\) we have \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = k/m\) for every \(r\), and every \(\mat M\)-orthonormal set of columns is a valid choice. The list of eigenvalues, however, is uniquely determined (point 3).

Frame A, initial shape \(\vek q(0) = (5,\ 10)\) mm (the shape under a force on the upper floor, for which by the second column of the flexibility matrix (10.6) \(q_2 = 2q_1\)): the coefficients are \(c_1 = \vek\varphi_1^\T\mat M\,\vek q(0) = 0{,}24899\) and \(c_2 = -0{,}022451\) in the unit m kg\(^{1/2}\). The parts in the modes are \(c_1\,\vek\varphi_1 = (5{,}854,\ 9{,}472)\) mm and \(c_2\,\vek\varphi_2 = (-0{,}854,\ 0{,}528)\) mm, their sum is \((5,\ 10)\) mm (figure 10.11, in the coordinates \(\vek y\) the parts are \((9{,}472,\ 3{,}618)\) and \((0{,}528,\ 1{,}382)\) mm). We obtained the coefficients with one multiplication by the matrix \(\mat M\) per mode, without solving a system.

Definition 10.15 Modal matrix (modalna matrika)

Let \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) be as in theorem 10.13. The modal matrix (modalna matrika) \(\mat\Phi\) is the matrix of order \(n\) whose columns are \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(\mat\Phi = [\vek\varphi_1\ \dots\ \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}]\). We write \(\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{n}})\) for the diagonal matrix with the entries \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) on the diagonal.

Source: CK (10.26) to (10.28) (PDF p. 312).

Lemma 10.16 Properties of the modal matrix (lastnosti modalne matrike)

For the modal matrix \(\mat\Phi\), \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat M\,\mat\Phi = \mat I\), \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat K\,\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{n}})\), the matrix \(\mat\Phi\) is invertible and \(\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat\Phi^\T\mat M\).

Proof

We must show two equalities, invertibility and the form of the inverse matrix. The equalities are a statement about the entries, invertibility follows from lemma 8.21.

  1. The entry \((r, s)\) of the matrix \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat M\,\mat\Phi\) is \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) (definition 1.98), which by \(\mat M\)-orthonormality is \(1\) for \(r = s\) and \(0\) for \(r \ne s\), the entry \((r, s)\) of the identity matrix.
  2. The entry \((r, s)\) of the matrix \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat K\,\mat\Phi\) is by (10.20) \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\), which by step 1 is \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for \(r = s\) and \(0\) for \(r \ne s\).
  3. Let \(\mat\Phi\,\vek w = \vek 0\). By step 1 and lemma 1.99, point 1, then \(\vek w = \mat I\,\vek w = (\mat\Phi^\T\mat M\,\mat\Phi)\,\vek w = \mat\Phi^\T\mat M\,(\mat\Phi\,\vek w) = \vek 0\). By lemma 8.21 \(\mat\Phi\) is invertible, with the inverse matrix \(\mat\Phi^{-1}\), for which \(\mat\Phi\,\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat I\).
  4. By step 1 and lemma 1.99, point 2, \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat M = (\mat\Phi^\T\mat M)\,(\mat\Phi\,\mat\Phi^{-1}) = (\mat\Phi^\T\mat M\,\mat\Phi)\,\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat\Phi^{-1}\).

Source: CK (10.29) to (10.32) (PDF p. 312). The proof is not from a source.

In the coordinates \(\vek q\) frame A has the modal matrix \(\mat\Phi = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0{,}023511 & 0{,}038042 \\ 0{,}038042 & -0{,}023511 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) kg\(^{-1/2}\). For it \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat M\,\mat\Phi = \mat I\) and \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat K\,\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(383{,}31,\ 2627{,}25)\) 1/s\(^2\), which we checked by computation. Bracket B of section 10.1 (the truss of chapter 4 with a mass of \(1000\) kg at the joint C) has \(\mat K = 10^6\left[\begin{smallmatrix} 7{,}4088 & -1{,}8816 \\ -1{,}8816 & 1{,}4112 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) N/m, \(\mat M = 1000\,\mat I\) kg and \(\mat\Phi = \left[\begin{smallmatrix} 0{,}008745 & 0{,}030390 \\ 0{,}030390 & -0{,}008745 \end{smallmatrix}\right]\) kg\(^{-1/2}\). Here too \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat M\,\mat\Phi = \mat I\), \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat K\,\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(869{,}77,\ 7950{,}23)\) 1/s\(^2\), hence \(\omega = 29{,}492\) and \(89{,}164\) 1/s. Since \(\mat M = 1000\,\mat I\), \(\mat M\)-orthogonality is ordinary perpendicularity, and indeed \(0{,}008745 \cdot 0{,}030390 + 0{,}030390 \cdot (-0{,}008745) = 0\).

The special case \(\mat M = \mat I\) is the theorem that chapter 6 promised for any symmetric matrix of order \(n\).

Corollary 10.17 Spectral theorem for a symmetric matrix (spektralni izrek za simetrično matriko)

A symmetric matrix \(\mat A\) of order \(n\) with real entries has \(n\) real eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(n\) pairwise perpendicular unit columns \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) with \(\mat A\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\). Every column \(\vek v\) is \(\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} (\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek v)\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\).

Proof

We must show that this is theorem 10.13 and corollary 10.14 for a special choice.

  1. The matrix \(\mat I\) is symmetric and positive definite, since \(\vek v^\T\mat I\,\vek v = |\vek v|^2 > 0\) for \(\vek v \ne \vek 0\).
  2. For \(\mat K = \mat A\) and \(\mat M = \mat I\), \(\mat M\)-orthogonality is ordinary perpendicularity, \(\mat M\)-normalization is length \(1\), and the theorem gives the statement on the eigenpairs. Corollary 10.14 gives the expansion.

Source: The proof is not from a source. CM §2.5.6.3 (PDF p. 93), SADD §1.6 (PDF pp. 21 and 22), as for theorem 2.61.

For \(n = 3\) this is theorem 2.61 with the eigenvalues in reverse order: there they are ordered from the largest, here from the smallest.

10.3.6 The eigenvalues are real

The theorem speaks of real columns and real numbers \(\lambda\). Could some complex pair \((\lambda, \vek\varphi)\) show a vibration that the theorem does not cover? We introduced complex numbers in section 9.3: a complex column has complex entries, \(\vek\varphi = \vek a + \mathrm i\,\vek b\) with real columns \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\). We compute the product of a real matrix with a complex column by equation (1.38), with complex numbers in place of real ones.

Lemma 10.18 The eigenvalues are real (lastne vrednosti so realne)

Let \(\mat K\) be symmetric and \(\mat M\) symmetric positive definite matrices of order \(n\), both with real entries. If for a complex number \(\lambda\) and a complex column \(\vek\varphi \ne \vek 0\) we have \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi = \lambda\,\mat M\,\vek\varphi\), then \(\lambda\) is a real number.

Proof

We must show that the imaginary part of \(\lambda\) is zero. We split the equation into its real and imaginary parts and eliminate the same expression by the symmetry of the matrices.

  1. Let \(\lambda = \sigma + \mathrm i\tau\) and \(\vek\varphi = \vek a + \mathrm i\,\vek b\). Since the matrices are real, \(\mat M\,\vek\varphi = \mat M\,\vek a + \mathrm i\,\mat M\,\vek b\), and by the rules of arithmetic (lemma 9.20) \(\lambda\,\mat M\,\vek\varphi = (\sigma\,\mat M\,\vek a - \tau\,\mat M\,\vek b) + \mathrm i\,(\tau\,\mat M\,\vek a + \sigma\,\mat M\,\vek b)\), and \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi = \mat K\,\vek a + \mathrm i\,\mat K\,\vek b\) (the matrix is real). The real parts and the imaginary parts are equal: \(\mat K\,\vek a = \sigma\,\mat M\,\vek a - \tau\,\mat M\,\vek b\) and \(\mat K\,\vek b = \tau\,\mat M\,\vek a + \sigma\,\mat M\,\vek b\).
  2. We multiply the first equation from the left by \(\vek b^\T\), the second by \(\vek a^\T\): \(\vek b^\T\mat K\,\vek a = \sigma\,\vek b^\T\mat M\,\vek a - \tau\,\vek b^\T\mat M\,\vek b\) and \(\vek a^\T\mat K\,\vek b = \tau\,\vek a^\T\mat M\,\vek a + \sigma\,\vek a^\T\mat M\,\vek b\).
  3. The matrices are symmetric, so \(\vek b^\T\mat K\,\vek a = \vek a^\T\mat K\,\vek b\) and \(\vek b^\T\mat M\,\vek a = \vek a^\T\mat M\,\vek b\) (equation (10.19)). When we subtract the second equation of step 2 from the first, the left sides and the terms with \(\sigma\) cancel: \(0 = -\tau\,(\vek a^\T\mat M\,\vek a + \vek b^\T\mat M\,\vek b)\).
  4. Since \(\vek\varphi \ne \vek 0\), \(\vek a \ne \vek 0\) or \(\vek b \ne \vek 0\). Since \(\mat M\) is positive definite, \(\vek a^\T\mat M\,\vek a + \vek b^\T\mat M\,\vek b > 0\), hence \(\tau = 0\).

Source: CM (2.5.34) to (2.5.36) (PDF pp. 92-93) proves the same for a symmetric matrix (\(\mat M = \mat I\)) with complex conjugate pairs. The proof above with real and imaginary parts is not from a source.

Meaning: we look for solutions \(\vek q = \mathrm e^{st}\vek\varphi\) of \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek 0\) with complex \(s\). Since \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\,\mathrm e^{st} = s\,\mathrm e^{st}\) and \(\mathrm e^{st} \ne 0\) (theorem 9.28, points 2 and 3), we need \((s^2\mat M + \mat K)\,\vek\varphi = \vek 0\), hence \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi = -s^2\,\mat M\,\vek\varphi\). By the lemma \(\lambda = -s^2\) is real. With \(s = \sigma + \mathrm i\tau\) we have \(s^2 = \sigma^2 - \tau^2 + 2\mathrm i\,\sigma\tau\), so \(\sigma\tau = 0\): \(s\) is real or purely imaginary. For \(\lambda > 0\), \(s = \pm\mathrm i\sqrt\lambda\), a pure vibration. For \(\lambda = 0\), \(s = 0\). For \(\lambda < 0\), \(s = \pm\sqrt{-\lambda}\) is real, growth or decay without vibration. So an undamped system has no solution \(\mathrm e^{st}\vek\varphi\) with an \(s\) whose real and imaginary parts are both nonzero. With damping, later in this chapter, this will change.

The spectral theorem has thus answered all four questions from the beginning of the section. A pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) of order \(n\) has \(n\) real eigenpairs, the modes are \(\mat M\)-orthonormal, every column is their sum, and the eigenvalues are successive minima of the quotient of energies. In the next section we use them to decouple the equations of motion, and later in the chapter we estimate the eigenvalues without computing them.

10.4 Modal coordinates and free vibration (modalne koordinate in prosto nihanje)

Two-storey frame A (okvir A) from section 10.1 has two floors of mass \(m = 500\) kg and storey stiffness \(k = 501\,760\) N/m, so \(\mat M = m\,\mat I\) and \(\mat K = k\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). We push on the upper floor with the force \(F = 2508{,}8\) N. The floors then move statically by \(q_1 = 5\) mm and \(q_2 = 10\) mm, because \(\mat K\vek q = k\,(2 \cdot 5 - 10,\ -5 + 10)\) mm \(= (0,\ k \cdot 5\ \text{mm}) = (0,\ 2508{,}8\ \text{N})\), as it must be for a force on the upper floor only. Then we suddenly remove the force, with no initial velocity. How does each floor move, and which part of the motion belongs to which mode?

Section 10.2 showed that the frame can vibrate in a single mode: both floors move along the same cosine with the same frequency. The initial shape (5 mm, 10 mm) is along neither of the two modes, so the motion is not that simple. Section 10.3, however, showed that every column with \(n\) elements is a sum of modes. So at every time \(t\) we can write the column \(\vek q(t)\) as the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}} \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\), except that the number \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\) at each mode now depends on time. These numbers are the new coordinates. We will show that each of them satisfies its own equation, which contains no other, and that it is the equation of a system with one degree of freedom, known from chapter 9. The coupling that looks like a property of the frame in the coordinates \(q_1\), \(q_2\) is therefore a consequence of the choice of coordinates.

10.4.1 Modal coordinates (modalne koordinate)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric and \(\mat M\) a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\), and \(\Phi = [\boldsymbol\varphi_1\ \dots\ \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}]\) their modal matrix (definition 10.15), so \(\Phi^\T\mat M\,\Phi = \mat I\) and \(\Phi^\T\mat K\,\Phi = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{n}})\) by lemma 10.16. By the same lemma \(\Phi^{-1} = \Phi^\T\mat M\). Hence for every column \(\vek q\) there is exactly one column \(\boldsymbol\eta\) with \(\vek q = \Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta\), namely \(\boldsymbol\eta = \Phi^\T\mat M\,\vek q\). This is the expansion in modes from corollary 10.14, written with a matrix.

Definition 10.19 Modal coordinates (modalne koordinate)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\) and \(\Phi\) be as above and \(\vek q(t) \in \mathbb R^n\) the column of generalized coordinates of a system with \(n\) degrees of freedom. The modal coordinates (modalne koordinate, also principal coordinates, glavne koordinate) of the system are the numbers

\[\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(t) = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek q(t) , \qquad r = 1, \dots, n , \tag{10.22}\]

collected in the column \(\boldsymbol\eta(t) = \Phi^\T\mat M\,\vek q(t)\). It holds that \(\vek q(t) = \Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{n}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(t)\).

Source: CK (11.8)-(11.9) PDF str. 344-345: "The coordinates \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(t)\) will be referred to as principal coordinates or modal coordinates." GR (2.64) PDF str. 95-96: "vector of modal coordinates (also called normal coordinates)".

The number \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\) tells how much of the mode \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is in the current column \(\vek q\). We normalized the modes with \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 1\), so with \(\mat M\) in kg and \(\vek q\) in m they have the unit kg\(^{-1/2}\) and the modal coordinates have m kg\(^{1/2}\). We introduced this unit ourselves by the normalization, so we always state it. If we instead normalize the modes so that the largest component equals 1, the number in front of the mode is in metres, and the share \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\) in the sum \(\vek q\) is the same (GR PDF str. 97: the contribution of a mode does not depend on the scale of the mode).

Let us look at this for frame A. The normalized modes from section 10.2 are the columns of the modal matrix

\[\Phi = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}023511 & 0{,}038042 \\ 0{,}038042 & -0{,}023511 \end{bmatrix}\ \text{kg}^{-1/2} ,\]

and with the largest component 1 they are \((0{,}618034,\ 1)\) and \((1,\ -0{,}618034)\), where \(0{,}618034 = 1/1{,}618034\) and \(1{,}618034\) is the ratio \(q_2/q_1\) of mode 1. For the initial displacement \(\vek q(0) = (5\ \text{mm},\ 10\ \text{mm})\) equation (10.22) gives \(\eta_1(0) = 0{,}24899\) m kg\(^{1/2}\) and \(\eta_2(0) = -0{,}022451\) m kg\(^{1/2}\). If \(\boldsymbol\psi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the mode with the largest component 1, the coefficient in front of it is \(a_{\mathrm{r}} = \boldsymbol\psi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek q(0)\,/\,\boldsymbol\psi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\boldsymbol\psi_{\mathrm{r}}\) (we divide by the norm of the mode, because \(\boldsymbol\psi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\boldsymbol\psi_{\mathrm{r}} \ne 1\)). We get \(a_1 = 9{,}472\) mm and \(a_2 = -0{,}854\) mm, which is the displacement of the upper floor in each mode. In both cases the contributions of the modes are equal, \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1\eta_1(0) = (5{,}854\ \text{mm},\ 9{,}472\ \text{mm})\) and \(\boldsymbol\varphi_2\eta_2(0) = (-0{,}854\ \text{mm},\ 0{,}528\ \text{mm})\). They add up to (5 mm, 10 mm), as they must (figure 10.12).

10.4.2 Decoupling of the equations (razklopitev enačb)

The question remains what the equation of motion does in the new coordinates. We write the linear equation from section 10.1 without damping as \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek Q(t)\), where \(\vek Q(t)\) is the column of generalized forces. We insert \(\vek q = \Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta\) and multiply the equation from the left by \(\Phi^\T\). The matrices \(\Phi^\T\mat M\,\Phi = \mat I\) and \(\Phi^\T\mat K\,\Phi = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}})\) appear. Both are diagonal, so row \(r\) contains only \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\).

Theorem 10.20 Decoupling of the equations of motion (razklopitev gibalnih enačb)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric and \(\mat M\) a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\), \(\Phi\) their modal matrix with eigenvalues \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(\vek Q(t)\) a column of \(n\) functions of time and \(\vek q(t)\) a twice differentiable column with modal coordinates \(\boldsymbol\eta = \Phi^\T\mat M\,\vek q\). Then

\[\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek Q(t)\]

holds at every time if and only if at every time

\[\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek Q(t) , \qquad r = 1, \dots, n . \tag{10.23}\]

The kinetic energy \(T = \tfrac12\,\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek q}\) and the potential energy \(V = \tfrac12\,\vek q^\T\mat K\,\vek q\) are

\[T = \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{n}\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}^2 , \qquad V = \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{n}\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{r}}^2 . \tag{10.24}\]
Proof

We must show that multiplication by \(\Phi^\T\) turns the equation of motion into \(n\) separate equations and that nothing is lost in the process.

  1. By definition 10.19 \(\vek q = \Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta\). The matrix \(\Phi\) does not depend on time, so \(\ddot{\vek q} = \Phi\,\ddot{\boldsymbol\eta}\), and the equation of motion is \(\mat M\Phi\,\ddot{\boldsymbol\eta} + \mat K\Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta = \vek Q\).
  2. We multiply from the left by \(\Phi^\T\): \(\Phi^\T\mat M\Phi\,\ddot{\boldsymbol\eta} + \Phi^\T\mat K\Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta = \Phi^\T\vek Q\). By lemma 10.16 this is \(\ddot{\boldsymbol\eta} + \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{n}})\,\boldsymbol\eta = \Phi^\T\vek Q\). Row \(r\) is equation (10.23), because the \(r\)-th component of the column \(\Phi^\T\vek Q\) is \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek Q\). This proves one direction.
  3. The converse needs that multiplication by \(\Phi^\T\) loses nothing. From \(\Phi^{-1} = \Phi^\T\mat M\) (lemma 10.16) it follows that \(\Phi\,\Phi^\T\mat M = \mat I\). We multiply this from the left by \(\mat M\) and from the right by \(\mat M^{-1}\) and get \(\mat M\,\Phi\,\Phi^\T = \mat I\). Together with \(\Phi^\T\mat M\,\Phi = \mat I\) this means \(\Phi^\T\) has the inverse \(\mat M\Phi\) from both sides.
  4. If equation (10.23) holds for all \(r\), then by step 2 \(\Phi^\T\big(\mat M\Phi\,\ddot{\boldsymbol\eta} + \mat K\Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta - \vek Q\big) = \vek 0\). We multiply from the left by \(\mat M\Phi\) and by step 3 get \(\mat M\Phi\,\ddot{\boldsymbol\eta} + \mat K\Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta - \vek Q = \vek 0\). This is the equation of motion from step 1.
  5. The energies: \(T = \tfrac12\,(\Phi\dot{\boldsymbol\eta})^\T\mat M\,(\Phi\dot{\boldsymbol\eta}) = \tfrac12\,\dot{\boldsymbol\eta}^\T\Phi^\T\mat M\Phi\,\dot{\boldsymbol\eta} = \tfrac12\,\dot{\boldsymbol\eta}^\T\dot{\boldsymbol\eta}\), and likewise \(V = \tfrac12\,\boldsymbol\eta^\T\Phi^\T\mat K\Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta = \tfrac12\,\boldsymbol\eta^\T\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}})\,\boldsymbol\eta\).

Source: CK (11.8)-(11.10) PDF str. 344-345 (decoupling), GR (2.64)-(2.68) PDF str. 95-96, (2.72)-(2.73) PDF str. 97 (energies). Steps 3 and 4 (converse direction) are not from the source.

The proof showed that each mode acts as an independent oscillator with one degree of freedom, with mass 1 and stiffness \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), and that the system vibrates as if it were composed of \(n\) independent oscillators (GR PDF str. 96). The coupling has disappeared because we chose coordinates in which the energies are a sum of squares without mixed terms, and not because the system changed (GR PDF str. 97).

Let us test this on frame A. With \(\lambda_1 = 383{,}31\) 1/s\(^2\) and \(\lambda_2 = 2627{,}25\) 1/s\(^2\) (section 10.2) the equations

\[\ddot\eta_1 + 383{,}31\,\eta_1 = 0 , \qquad \ddot\eta_2 + 2627{,}25\,\eta_2 = 0\]

are for free vibration. Before the release the frame was at rest under the force \(F = 2508{,}8\) N on the upper floor, that is with \(\vek Q = (0,\ F)\). The modal forces (modalni sili), the right-hand sides of equation (10.23), are \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1^\T\vek Q = 0{,}038042\,F = 95{,}44\) N kg\(^{-1/2}\) and \(\boldsymbol\varphi_2^\T\vek Q = -0{,}023511\,F = -58{,}99\) N kg\(^{-1/2}\). At rest \(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\), so \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek Q/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), which is \(0{,}24899\) and \(-0{,}022451\) m kg\(^{1/2}\). We obtained the same numbers from equation (10.22). The initial condition for each mode is therefore its rest position under the force, and the release is, for each of them, a release from rest. Mode 1 dominates for two reasons that multiply: its stiffness \(\lambda_1\) is 6,854 times smaller than \(\lambda_2\), so for the same force its coordinate is larger, and its element \(\varphi_{21}\) is larger than \(|\varphi_{22}|\) in the ratio 1,618 (the golden ratio from section 10.2). The ratio of the coordinates is \(6{,}854 \cdot 1{,}618 = 11{,}09\), which is \(0{,}24899 / 0{,}022451\).

10.4.3 Free vibration (prosto nihanje)

What does the frame do after the release? Each modal coordinate is a solution of equation (10.23) with \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) and its two initial conditions. We know the equation \(\ddot\eta + \lambda\eta = 0\): for \(\lambda > 0\) it is solved by \(\cos\omega t\) and \(\sin\omega t\) with \(\omega = \sqrt\lambda\) (theorem 8.12). We took the matrix \(\mat K\) of arbitrary sign, so \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) need not be positive either. Then the solutions are different, and the theorem lists all three.

Theorem 10.21 Free vibration of a system with several degrees of freedom (prosto nihanje sistema z več prostostnimi stopnjami)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric and \(\mat M\) a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\), \(\Phi\) their modal matrix with eigenvalues \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(t_1 > 0\) and \(\vek q_0\), \(\vek v_0\) arbitrary columns. Then the equation \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek 0\) has on \([0, t_1]\) exactly one twice differentiable solution with \(\vek q(0) = \vek q_0\) and \(\dot{\vek q}(0) = \vek v_0\), namely

\[\vek q(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{n}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(t) , \qquad \eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek q_0 , \quad \dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v_0 , \tag{10.25}\]

where

  1. for \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} = \sqrt{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}\): \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(t) = \eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\cos\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t + \dfrac{\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)}{\omega_{\mathrm{r}}}\sin\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t\),
  2. for \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\): \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(t) = \eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) + \dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\,t\),
  3. for \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} < 0\) and \(\nu_{\mathrm{r}} = \sqrt{-\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}\): \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(t) = \eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\cosh\nu_{\mathrm{r}} t + \dfrac{\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)}{\nu_{\mathrm{r}}}\sinh\nu_{\mathrm{r}} t\).

The energy of each mode, \(E_{\mathrm{r}} = \tfrac12\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}^2 + \tfrac12\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}^2\), is constant, and \(T + V = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} E_{\mathrm{r}}\).

Proof

We must show that every solution gives modal coordinates with the stated properties, that the stated functions really solve the equations, and that the \(\vek q\) assembled from them solves the initial value problem.

  1. Let \(\vek q\) be a twice differentiable solution. By theorem 10.20 with \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) every modal coordinate \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek q\) satisfies \(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\). The initial values are \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek q_0\) and \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v_0\), since \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek q}\).
  2. The equation \(\ddot\eta + \lambda\eta = 0\) is linear with constant coefficients of order 2 and characteristic polynomial \(s^2 + \lambda\). By theorem 9.36 it has exactly one solution for given values \(\eta(0)\), \(\dot\eta(0)\). So \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\) from step 1 is this solution.
  3. The stated functions are solutions. For \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\), by theorem 8.12 \((\cos\omega t)'' = -\omega^2\cos\omega t\) and \((\sin\omega t)'' = -\omega^2\sin\omega t\), so \(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = -\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\). For \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\), \(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\). For \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} < 0\), by lemma 9.42, item 1, \((\cosh\nu t)'' = \nu^2\cosh\nu t\) and the same for \(\sinh\), so \(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \nu_{\mathrm{r}}^2\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = -\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\).
  4. The initial values. For \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) the formula at \(t = 0\) gives \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\cos 0 + \dfrac{\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)}{\omega_{\mathrm{r}}}\sin 0 = \eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\), and its derivative gives \(-\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\sin 0 + \dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\cos 0 = \dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\). For \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} < 0\) the same with \(\cosh 0 = 1\), \(\sinh 0 = 0\) and the derivatives from item 1 of lemma 9.42. For \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) the function \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) + \dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\,t\) at \(t = 0\) equals \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\) and has the derivative \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\). By step 2 the stated functions are the only solutions.
  5. Existence. With the stated \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\) we assemble \(\vek q = \Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta\). By step 3 and the converse direction of theorem 10.20 (with \(\vek Q = \vek 0\)) \(\vek q\) solves the equation of motion. At \(t = 0\), \(\vek q(0) = \sum_{\mathrm{r}}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek q_0 = \vek q_0\) by corollary 10.14, and with the same expansion for \(\vek v_0\) we get \(\dot{\vek q}(0) = \vek v_0\).
  6. Uniqueness. If \(\vek q\) and \(\tilde{\vek q}\) are solutions with the same initial values, by step 1 they have the same modal coordinates, so \(\vek q = \Phi\,\boldsymbol\eta = \tilde{\vek q}\).
  7. Energy: \(\dot{E}_{\mathrm{r}} = \dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\,(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}) = 0\), so \(E_{\mathrm{r}}\) is constant (corollary 1.85). The sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}} E_{\mathrm{r}}\) equals \(T + V\) by equation (10.24).

Source: CK (11.14)-(11.18) PDF str. 345-346, GR razdelek 2.5, (2.64)-(2.71) PDF str. 95-97 (case \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) with unwinding from the sine and cosine), GR PDF str. 99-100 (constant energy). The cases \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \le 0\) and the proof of uniqueness by theorem 9.36 are not from the source.

The proof showed that the \(2n\) numbers in \(\vek q_0\) and \(\vek v_0\) determine exactly the \(2n\) coefficients \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\) and \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\), and that the motion of a system with \(n\) degrees of freedom arises from \(n\) independent oscillators. The case \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) is in section 10.5. The case \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} < 0\) corresponds to unstable equilibrium: since \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} < 0\), the matrix \(\mat K\) has a column with negative quadratic form, and theorem 8.117 says that the equilibrium is not stable. The formula from item 3 shows how: for \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) = 0\) and \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) \ne 0\), \(|\eta_{\mathrm{r}}|\) grows for large \(t\) like \(\tfrac12\,|\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)|\,\mathrm e^{\nu_{\mathrm{r}} t}\), because \(\cosh\nu t\) is close to \(\tfrac12\,\mathrm e^{\nu t}\).

10.4.4 Frame A after the release (okvir A po sprostitvi)

The initial conditions are \(\vek q_0 = (5\ \text{mm},\ 10\ \text{mm})\) and \(\vek v_0 = \vek 0\), so \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) = 0\). By item 1 of theorem 10.21, \(\eta_1(t) = 0{,}24899\cos(19{,}578\,t)\) and \(\eta_2(t) = -0{,}022451\cos(51{,}257\,t)\) in m kg\(^{1/2}\), where \(t\) is in seconds, and the motion of the floors by equation (10.25) is

\[\vek q(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 5{,}854 \\ 9{,}472 \end{bmatrix}\cos(19{,}578\,t)\ \text{mm} + \begin{bmatrix} -0{,}854 \\ 0{,}528 \end{bmatrix}\cos(51{,}257\,t)\ \text{mm} . \tag{10.26}\]

Figure 10.13 shows both floors and both modal coordinates in the first two seconds. Above, the motion looks complicated: the excursions of the floors are not equal, the curves do not repeat with the same shape. Below, the modal coordinates are two pure cosines: the large one with period \(T_1 = 0{,}32093\) s and the small one with period \(T_2 = 0{,}12258\) s.

The motion never repeats exactly. It would repeat at a time \(\tau > 0\) if \(\vek q(\tau) = \vek q(0)\) (and \(\dot{\vek q}(\tau) = \vek 0\)). From \(\vek q(\tau) = \vek q(0)\) by equation (10.26) we get \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\,(\cos\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\tau - 1) = \vek 0\). Since \(\boldsymbol\varphi_1\) and \(\boldsymbol\varphi_2\) are independent (corollary 10.14) and both numbers \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\) are nonzero, \(\cos\omega_1\tau = \cos\omega_2\tau = 1\). So \(\omega_1\tau = 2\pi p\) and \(\omega_2\tau = 2\pi s\) with integers \(p\), \(s\), and the ratio \(\omega_2/\omega_1 = s/p\) is a fraction. For A, \(\omega_2/\omega_1 = (3 + \sqrt5)/2 = 2{,}618034\). Let us show that this is not a fraction.

  1. If \((3 + \sqrt5)/2 = s/p\), then \(\sqrt5 = 2s/p - 3\), so a fraction \(a/b\) with integers \(a\), \(b > 0\). Among all such representations we choose the one with the smallest \(b\) (every nonempty set of natural numbers has a smallest element).
  2. From \(a^2 = 5b^2\), \(a^2\) is divisible by \(5\). If \(a\) is not divisible by \(5\), then \(a = 5k + j\) with \(j \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) and \(a^2 = 5\,(5k^2 + 2jk) + j^2\), where \(j^2 \in \{1, 4, 9, 16\}\) leaves the remainder \(1\) or \(4\) on division by \(5\). This contradicts the divisibility. So \(a = 5k\).
  3. From \(25k^2 = 5b^2\) it follows that \(b^2 = 5k^2\), so by the same argument as in step 2 also \(b\) is divisible by \(5\), and \(\sqrt5 = (a/5)/(b/5)\) has a smaller denominator. This contradicts the choice in step 1.

So the ratio \(\omega_2/\omega_1\) is not a fraction and the motion never repeats. For example, after the first period \(T_1\) mode 1 is again at its start, but mode 2 has made 2,618 oscillations, so its phase is \(222{,}49^\circ\) and \(\cos 222{,}49^\circ = -0{,}7374\), hence \(\vek q(T_1) = (6{,}484\ \text{mm},\ 9{,}083\ \text{mm})\) and not \((5\ \text{mm},\ 10\ \text{mm})\). After half a period, \(\vek q(T_1/2) = (-5{,}545\ \text{mm},\ -9{,}663\ \text{mm})\).

Which part of the motion belongs to which mode is told by the energy. By theorem 10.21 the energy of mode 1 is \(E_1 = \tfrac12\cdot 383{,}31\cdot 0{,}24899^2 = 11{,}882\) J and of mode 2 \(E_2 = \tfrac12\cdot 2627{,}25\cdot 0{,}022451^2 = 0{,}662\) J. The sum is \(12{,}544\) J, the strain energy of the frame under the force, \(\tfrac12\,F\,q_2 = \tfrac12\cdot 2508{,}8\ \text{N}\cdot 0{,}010\ \text{m} = 12{,}544\) J. The share of mode 1 is 94,72 %, of mode 2 5,28 %, and these shares do not change. The kinetic and potential energy of the whole system, however, oscillate: within each mode the energy is exchanged between \(\tfrac12\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) and \(\tfrac12\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}^2\), and between the modes nothing passes (figure 10.14).

10.4.5 Bracket B after the weight is removed (konzola B po odstranitvi teže)

Another example where the initial displacement is not along a mode. Bracket B (konzola B) from section 10.1 has bars \(AC\) and \(BC\) with \(EA = 19{,}6\) MN (from chapter 4) and a mass \(m = 1000\) kg in the pin \(C\). The motion is in the plane, the coordinates are the horizontal and vertical displacement of the pin \(C\), and \(\mat M = m\,\mat I\). The weight \(m g = 9{,}81\) kN, close to the load of 10 kN from chapter 4, displaces \(C\) by \((-2{,}669\ \text{mm},\ -10{,}511\ \text{mm})\) relative to the position without the weight, that is \(\vek q_0 = \mat D\,(0,\ -m g)\) with the flexibility matrix \(\mat D\) from section 10.1. What happens if we suddenly remove the weight, as if the rope holding the load snapped? The bracket returns towards the position \(\vek q = \vek 0\), from which the displacement is measured, and vibrates.

The modes from section 10.2.2 are the unit columns \(\vek e_1 = (0{,}27653,\ 0{,}96101)\) at \(\omega_1 = 29{,}492\) 1/s and \(\vek e_2 = (0{,}96101,\ -0{,}27653)\) at \(\omega_2 = 89{,}164\) 1/s. For \(\mat M = m\,\mat I\), \(\mat M\)-orthogonality is ordinary orthogonality, so the contribution of mode \(r\) to \(\vek q_0\) equals \((\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\cdot\vek q_0)\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\), regardless of the normalization of the mode (normalization multiplies \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) and divides \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\) by the same value). We get

\[\vek e_1\cdot\vek q_0 = -10{,}839\ \text{mm} , \qquad \vek e_2\cdot\vek q_0 = +0{,}341\ \text{mm} .\]

The excursion of mode 2 is therefore only 3,15 % of the excursion of mode 1. The reason is the direction: the static displacement lies at the angle \(-104{,}25^\circ\) to the \(x\) axis, while the line of mode 1 is at \(-106{,}05^\circ\) (the direction of \(\vek e_1\) is \(73{,}947^\circ\), the opposite direction \(-106{,}053^\circ\)). The angle between them is \(1{,}80^\circ\) and \(\tan 1{,}80^\circ = 0{,}0315\), which is the ratio of the two contributions, since the contribution of mode 2 is the component of the static displacement perpendicular to the line of mode 1.

The energy of the modes is \(E_{\mathrm{r}} = \tfrac12\,m\,\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\cdot\vek q_0)^2\) and gives \(E_1 = 51{,}092\) J and \(E_2 = 0{,}463\) J. The sum \(51{,}555\) J is the strain energy under the weight, \(\tfrac12\,m g\cdot 10{,}511\ \text{mm}\). The share of mode 2 is therefore \(0{,}90\ \%\), and of mode 1 \(99{,}10\ \%\). The square of the ratio of excursions, \(0{,}0315^2 = 0{,}099\ \%\), would give nine times less. The difference is in the ratio \(\lambda_2/\lambda_1 = 9{,}14\): for the same excursion the stiff direction stores nine times more energy than the compliant one. The coordinate \(\vek q\) therefore soon after the release vibrates almost along the line of mode 1 with period \(T_1 = 0{,}21305\) s. A small transverse vibration with period \(T_2 = 0{,}07047\) s and amplitude \(0{,}341\) mm, however, prevents the pin \(C\) in the plane from moving along an exact line. In section 10.5 the same system without bar \(AC\) awaits us, where one of the eigenvalues falls to zero.

10.5 Zero frequencies and rigid-body modes (ničelne frekvence in togi načini)

So far every system has had supports that prevent every displacement without deformation. What if the supports are missing? Take bracket B (konzola B) from section 10.2: bar AC is horizontal and 4 m long, bar BC is 5 m long and points from the wall to C in the direction \((4, -3)/5\), both have axial stiffness \(EA = 19{,}6\) MN, and the pin C carries a weight of mass \(m = 1000\) kg (the truss of section 4.8.1, the stiffness matrix from section 4.6.7). We remove bar AC (figure 10.15). The pin C can now leave its former position without bar BC lengthening, at least to first order. What does the theory say about a motion that costs no energy?

First we compute the stiffness matrix. The pin C is displaced by \(\vek d = (u, v)\). By lemma 7.28 bar BC lengthens by the scalar product \(\vek n\cdot\vek d\) with the unit vector \(\vek n = (0{,}8,\ -0{,}6)\) along the bar, and its energy is \(\tfrac12 k\,(\vek n\cdot\vek d)^2\) with bar stiffness \(k = EA/L = 19{,}6\cdot 10^6\ \text{N}/5\ \text{m} = 3{,}92\) MN/m. Hence \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = k\,(\vek n\cdot\vek d)^2\), so

\[\mat K = k\,\vek n\,\vek n^\T = 10^6\begin{pmatrix} 2{,}5088 & -1{,}8816 \\ -1{,}8816 & 1{,}4112 \end{pmatrix}\ \text{N/m} . \tag{10.27}\]

This is the matrix of definition 7.4 without the contribution of bar AC, since the matrix of the whole truss has the entry \((1, 1)\) equal to \(7{,}4088\cdot 10^6\) N/m, bar AC contributes \(EA/4\ \text{m} = 4{,}9\cdot 10^6\) N/m to this entry, and \(2{,}5088\cdot 10^6\) N/m remains. The matrix is symmetric and \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = k\,(\vek n\cdot\vek d)^2 \ge 0\), so it is positive semidefinite (definition 7.15). The mass matrix is still \(\mat M = m\,\mat I\), positive definite. For the column \(\vek t = (0{,}6,\ 0{,}8)\) we have \(\vek n\cdot\vek t = 0{,}48 - 0{,}48 = 0\), hence \(\mat K\,\vek t = k\,\vek n\,(\vek n\cdot\vek t) = \vek 0\). For \(\vek n\) itself \(\mat K\,\vek n = k\,\vek n\), since \(\vek n\cdot\vek n = 1\). So we have two eigenpairs of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) (definition 10.7):

\[\lambda_1 = 0 ,\ \vek\varphi_1 \parallel \vek t \qquad\text{and}\qquad \lambda_2 = \frac{k}{m} = 3920\ \text{s}^{-2} ,\ \vek\varphi_2 \parallel \vek n ,\]

the second corresponds to the circular frequency \(\omega_2 = 62{,}610\) s\(^{-1}\) and the frequency \(9{,}9647\) Hz. Since \(\mat M = m\,\mat I\), \(\mat M\)-orthogonal is the same as perpendicular, and indeed \(\vek t\cdot\vek n = 0\). In the mode \(\vek\varphi_2\) the pin C moves along the bar and stretches and shortens it, in the mode \(\vek\varphi_1\) it moves perpendicular to it and the bar does no work.

The spectral theorem (theorem 10.13) does not exclude this example. It assumed only that \(\mat K\) is symmetric and \(\mat M\) positive definite, and the eigenvalue zero is allowed. A second question opens. The expansion in theorem 10.21 divides by \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\), because for \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) the solution of the modal equation is \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\cos\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t + \eta_{\mathrm{r}}'(0)\,\sin(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t)/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\). As \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) tends to zero, \(\cos\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t\) tends to \(1\) and \(\sin(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t)/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) tends to \(t\). So we expect a solution \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = a + bt\): a pin that we give a velocity in the mode \(\vek\varphi_1\) keeps moving on with that velocity, since no force holds it back. This is not the instability of chapter 8: the shape stays the same, the strain energy is zero at all times, and no modal coordinate grows like \(\cosh\) or \(\sinh\) (for \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} < 0\) it would grow). The following definition names such modes.

Definition 10.22 Zero-frequency mode, rigid-body mode and mechanism (način z ničelno frekvenco, togi način in mehanizem)

Let \((\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}})\) be an eigenpair of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) from definition 10.7, where \(\mat K\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite and \(\mat M\) is positive definite. If \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\), then \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is a zero-frequency mode (način z ničelno frekvenco). If in addition \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) is a rigid-body displacement of the system (definition 1.11), it is a rigid-body mode (togi način), otherwise a mechanism (mehanizem) as for the truss in definition 7.32. A mode with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) is an elastic mode (prožni način).

Source: CK §9.4 (PDF p. 285): "Rigid-body modes have a corresponding natural frequency of zero", "An eigenvalue problem that results in one or more zero eigenvalues ... is called a semidefinite eigenvalue problem" (PDF p. 286). The distinction between a rigid-body mode and a mechanism is from definition 7.32 (COOK, PDF p. 53), CK does not separate mechanisms.

The bracket without AC has one zero-frequency mode, and since B is at rest, the displacement of the pin C along the tangent is not a rigid-body displacement of the truss, so it is a mechanism. What is certain about such modes for every system is stated by a theorem. Its first part says when a frequency is zero, the second how many such modes there are, the third how their modal coordinate changes, the fourth how they lie relative to the elastic modes.

We must say what the first-order model claims. The model with the matrix \(\mat K\) says that the pin C travels along the tangent. The real motion is a rotation of bar BC about B, that is, motion along a circle of radius \(L = 5\) m. Take a displacement \(s = 10\) mm along \(\vek t\). The bar lengthens by \(\sqrt{L^2 + s^2} - L = 9{,}9999\cdot 10^{-6}\) m, which is \(s^2/(2L)\), and its energy is \(\tfrac12 k\,(10^{-5}\ \text{m})^2 = 1{,}96\cdot 10^{-4}\) J. The same displacement along the bar would cost \(\tfrac12 k\,s^2 = 196\) J, a million times more: for a displacement along the tangent the lengthening is in the ratio \(s/(2L) = 0{,}001\) to the lengthening for a displacement along the bar, and the energy is proportional to the square of the lengthening. As long as the pin moves by a small part of the bar length, the first-order mechanism is a good model. For a displacement comparable to \(L\) it is replaced by a rotation about B, which chapter 8 treats with the angle as a free coordinate.

Theorem 10.23 Zero frequencies of a positive semidefinite stiffness matrix (ničelne frekvence pri pozitivno semidefinitni togostni matriki)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric positive semidefinite and \(\mat M\) a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\). Let \(\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) and the \(\mat M\)-orthonormal (definition 10.10) \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) be the eigenvalues and modes of theorem 10.13, \(\mathcal N\) the set of columns \(\vek w\) with \(\mat K\,\vek w = \vek 0\), and \(\vek Q(t)\) a continuous column. Then:

  1. All eigenvalues satisfy \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \ge 0\), and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) exactly when \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek 0\).
  2. A column \(\vek w\) lies in \(\mathcal N\) exactly when it has zero energy, \(\vek w^\T\mat K\,\vek w = 0\). The number \(z\) of zero eigenvalues equals the largest number of linearly independent columns in \(\mathcal N\), and every column of \(\mathcal N\) is a linear combination of the modes \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  3. Every column of \(\mathcal N\) is \(\mat M\)-orthogonal to every elastic mode, \(\vek w^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = 0\) for \(\lambda_{\mathrm{s}} > 0\).
  4. For \(r \le z\) the modal coordinate (definition 10.19) of the solution of \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek Q(t)\) equals
    \[\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(t) = \eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) + \dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\,t + \int_0^t\!\!\int_0^s \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek Q(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\,\mathrm{d}s , \tag{10.28}\]
    where \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek q(0)\) and \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek q}(0)\).
Proof

We must show four points. The first follows from the energy of a mode, the second from lemma 7.16 and the expansion in modes, the third from the symmetry of the matrix \(\mat K\), the fourth from the modal equation. We always use \(\mat M\)-orthonormality, \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = 1\) for \(r = s\) and \(0\) otherwise.

  1. From \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) we get, multiplying by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\), \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). The matrix \(\mat K\) is positive semidefinite (definition 7.15), hence \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \ge 0\).
  2. If \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\), then by step 1 \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\), so by lemma 7.16 \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek 0\). If \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek 0\), then \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) by step 1. This is the first point. The first sentence of the second point is lemma 7.16.
  3. Let \(\vek w \in \mathcal N\) and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{s}} > 0\). From \(\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) and the symmetry of \(\mat K\), \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M = \lambda_{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}(\mat K\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}})^\T = \lambda_{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat K\). Hence \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\,\vek w = \lambda_{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat K\,\vek w = 0\). This is the third point.
  4. By corollary 10.14, \(\vek w = \sum_{\mathrm{r}}(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek w)\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\). By step 3 the terms with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) vanish, so \(\vek w\) is a combination of modes with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\). Since \(\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\), these are the first \(z\) modes \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  5. The modes \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{z}}\) lie in \(\mathcal N\) (step 2) and are linearly independent: from \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek 0\) we get, multiplying by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\), \(c_{\mathrm{s}} = 0\) (definition 6.22).
  6. Let \(\vek w_1, \dots, \vek w_{\mathrm{p}} \in \mathcal N\) be linearly independent. By step 4, \(\vek w_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{z} c_{\mathrm{rj}}\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\). If \(p > z\), the homogeneous system \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{rj}}x_{\mathrm{j}} = 0\) for \(r = 1, \dots, z\) would by lemma 10.9 have a nonzero solution \((x_1, \dots, x_{\mathrm{p}})\), and \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} x_{\mathrm{j}}\vek w_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}}\big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} c_{\mathrm{rj}}x_{\mathrm{j}}\big)\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek 0\) would contradict independence. So \(p \le z\), and step 5 shows that \(p = z\) is attained. This completes the second point.
  7. By theorem 10.20, \(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek Q(t)\), so for \(r \le z\) we get \(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = f(t)\) with the continuous \(f = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\vek Q\). By theorem 9.36 with characteristic polynomial \(s^2\) (the root \(0\) twice) this equation has exactly one solution of order 2 for given \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\) and \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\). The initial values are \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek q(0)\) and \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek q}(0)\) from the relation \(\eta = \mat\Phi^\T\mat M\,\vek q\) (definition 10.19).
  8. The function \(f\) is continuous, so by theorem 3.40 (point 2) the function \(g(s) = \int_0^s f(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\) is differentiable with \(g' = f\). By the same point of the theorem, applied to the continuous function \(g\), the function \(\eta(t) = \eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) + \dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\,t + \int_0^t g(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) is differentiable with \(\eta'(t) = \dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) + g(t)\), and this is differentiable with \(\eta'' = g' = f\). The function satisfies the equation and the initial values \(\eta(0) = \eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\), \(\eta'(0) = \dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\), so by step 7 it is that solution. This is equation (10.28).

Source: CK (11.54) and (11.55) (PDF p. 371): the coordinates of rigid-body modes are obtained by double integration. CK §9.4 (PDF pp. 285-286), CK Example 10.2 (PDF pp. 305-306, "Since det(K) = 0, K is a singular matrix"). The proof is not from the source.

The theorem showed that the whole theory of the previous sections accepts positive semidefiniteness, except that at zero eigenvalues straight-line motion replaces oscillation. The last point also says how many times the force must be integrated: twice, as for a freely moving particle. For \(z \ge 2\) the zero-frequency modes are not determined uniquely: any \(\mat M\)-orthonormal basis of the space \(\mathcal N\) is allowed (CK, PDF p. 311, "these two rigid-body modes are not unique"). The elastic modes, however, are by the third point all \(\mat M\)-orthogonal to the whole of \(\mathcal N\).

Let us test it on an example that has a rigid-body mode. Two railway wagons of masses \(m_1 = 20\) t and \(m_2 = 30\) t, joined by a buffer of stiffness \(k = 2\cdot 10^6\) N/m, move on a straight track without friction. The displacements of the wagons along the track from the position with the unstretched buffer are \(q_1\) and \(q_2\). The buffer is an ideal spring, the wagons are point masses. The kinetic energy is \(\tfrac12(m_1\dot q_1^2 + m_2\dot q_2^2)\), the potential energy \(\tfrac12 k\,(q_2 - q_1)^2\), so by theorem 10.2

\[\mat M = \begin{pmatrix} m_1 & 0 \\ 0 & m_2 \end{pmatrix} ,\qquad \mat K = k\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} .\]

The energy \(k\,(q_2 - q_1)^2\) is zero exactly when \(q_1 = q_2\), so \(\mathcal N\) is the line of columns \(c\,(1, 1)\), the wagons move by the same distance, and this is a rigid-body displacement (definition 1.11). By theorem 10.23, \(z = 1\), \(\lambda_1 = 0\) and \(\vek\varphi_1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt{m_1 + m_2} = 0{,}0044721\,(1, 1)\) kg\(^{-1/2}\). By the third point the second mode must be \(\mat M\)-orthogonal to it, \(m_1 q_1 + m_2 q_2 = 0\), so \(q_2/q_1 = -m_1/m_2 = -2/3\): the wagons move in opposite directions, the lighter wagon moves \(3/2\) times as far as the heavier one, because the sum \(m_1 q_1 + m_2 q_2\) must be zero. The column \(\vek q = (m_2, -m_1)\) is \(\mat M\)-orthogonal to \(\vek\varphi_1\), since \(m_2 m_1 - m_1 m_2 = 0\). By corollary 10.14, \(\vek q = c_1\vek\varphi_1 + c_2\vek\varphi_2\) with \(c_1 = \vek\varphi_1^\T\mat M\,\vek q = 0\), so \(\vek q = c_2\vek\varphi_2\), and by the first point of the theorem (in step 1 of the proof \(\vek\varphi_2^\T\mat K\,\vek\varphi_2 = \lambda_2\) with \(\vek\varphi_2^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi_2 = 1\))

\[\lambda_2 = \frac{\vek q^\T\mat K\,\vek q}{\vek q^\T\mat M\,\vek q} = \frac{k\,(m_1 + m_2)^2}{m_1 m_2^2 + m_2 m_1^2} = \frac{k\,(m_1 + m_2)}{m_1 m_2} = \frac{2\cdot 10^6\cdot 5\cdot 10^4}{6\cdot 10^8}\ \text{s}^{-2} = 166{,}67\ \text{s}^{-2} ,\]

where \(c_2^2\) cancels. Let us also check the eigenvalue equation: the first row of \(\mat K\,\vek q = \lambda_2\mat M\,\vek q\) is \(k\,(m_2 + m_1) = \lambda_2 m_1 m_2\), which is exactly the expression above, and the second row gives the same. The circular frequency is \(12{,}910\) s\(^{-1}\), the frequency \(2{,}0547\) Hz, the period \(0{,}4867\) s. The \(\mat M\)-normalized mode is \(\vek\varphi_2 = (m_2, -m_1)/\sqrt{m_1 m_2\,(m_1 + m_2)} = (0{,}0054772,\ -0{,}0036515)\) kg\(^{-1/2}\).

Figure 10.16 shows both modes. In the elastic mode a pattern appears: the centre of mass, where \(m_1 q_1 + m_2 q_2 = 0\), is at rest. This is no accident, the cause is the third point of the theorem: the condition of \(\mat M\)-orthogonality to the rigid-body mode \((1, 1)\) is exactly the condition that the sum \(m_1 q_1 + m_2 q_2\) be zero.

Two initial states show what the fourth point says. The first: wagon 1 moves at \(1\) m/s towards the resting wagon 2, the buffer is unstretched, \(\vek q(0) = \vek 0\), \(\dot{\vek q}(0) = (1, 0)\) m/s. We get \(\dot\eta_1(0) = \vek\varphi_1^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek q}(0) = m_1\cdot 1/\sqrt{m_1 + m_2} = 89{,}44\) m kg\(^{1/2}\)/s and \(\eta_1 = \dot\eta_1(0)\,t\), so the rigid part is \(\vek\varphi_1\eta_1 = 0{,}4\,t\,(1, 1)\) m: both wagons move at the speed \(m_1\cdot 1/(m_1 + m_2) = 0{,}4\) m/s. The elastic part has \(\dot\eta_2(0) = \vek\varphi_2^\T\mat M\,\dot{\vek q}(0) = 109{,}54\) m kg\(^{1/2}\)/s and \(\eta_2 = \dot\eta_2(0)\sin(\omega_2 t)/\omega_2\). The buffer shortens and stretches between \(\pm 77{,}46\) mm, which is exactly the relative speed \(1\) m/s divided by \(\omega_2 = 12{,}910\) s\(^{-1}\), and the largest force in the buffer is \(154{,}9\) kN. Of the initial kinetic energy \(\tfrac12 m_1\cdot 1^2 = 10\,000\) J, \(\tfrac12(m_1 + m_2)\,0{,}4^2 = 4000\) J is in the rigid part (a share \(m_1/(m_1 + m_2) = 40\ \%\)) and \(6000\) J in the oscillation.

The second: a locomotive pulls wagon 2 with a constant force \(F = 60\) kN, \(\vek Q = (0, F)\), from rest. The static computation \(\mat K\,\vek q = \vek Q\) has no solution, since \(\vek\varphi_1^\T\mat K\,\vek q = (\mat K\,\vek\varphi_1)^\T\vek q = 0\) for every \(\vek q\) while \(\vek\varphi_1^\T\vek Q = F/\sqrt{m_1 + m_2}\) is not zero: a force with a component in the rigid-body mode accelerates the whole system. By equation (10.28), \(\ddot\eta_1 = \vek\varphi_1^\T\vek Q\), so \(\vek\varphi_1\eta_1 = \tfrac12 a\,t^2\,(1, 1)\) with the acceleration \(a = F/(m_1 + m_2) = 1{,}2\) m/s\(^2\): in \(1\) s both wagons move by \(0{,}6\) m. The elastic part \(\ddot\eta_2 + \lambda_2\eta_2 = \vek\varphi_2^\T\vek Q = -219{,}09\) m kg\(^{1/2}\)/s\(^2\) has the constant solution \(\eta_2 = -219{,}09/166{,}67 = -1{,}3145\) m kg\(^{1/2}\), so the displacements are \(\vek\varphi_2\eta_2 = (-7{,}2,\ 4{,}8)\) mm: the buffer is stretched by \(12\) mm and pulls wagon 1 with the force \(k\cdot 0{,}012\ \text{m} = 24\) kN, which is exactly \(m_1 a = 20\,000\cdot 1{,}2\) N. The elastic part is thus the static stretch that the acceleration demands, and its shape is the elastic mode. Since the wagons start from rest, \(\eta_2 = -1{,}3145\,(1 - \cos\omega_2 t)\) m kg\(^{1/2}\) and the stretch of the buffer oscillates between \(0\) and \(24\) mm. A computation for the full system in NumPy (fourth-order Runge-Kutta) confirms the centre of mass at \(0{,}6000\) m at \(1\) s.
