The nodal model did not demand this condition, it satisfied it by itself: the last row has only half of the row of an interior node, because there is no element on the right.

We compare the frequencies with the exact ones. The table shows \(f_1\) for \(n = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\) elements, with consistent and lumped mass, the error with respect to the exact \(1253{,}20\) Hz, and \(\theta_1^2/24\) in percent, which is the leading term of the expansion computed by SymPy (below).

\(n\) \(f_1\) consist. (Hz) error \(f_1\) lumped (Hz) error \(\theta_1^2/24\) (SymPy)
1 1381,85 \(+10{,}266\) % 1128,28 \(-9{,}968\) % 10,281 %
2 1285,61 \(+2{,}586\) % 1221,24 \(-2{,}550\) % 2,570 %
4 1261,27 \(+0{,}644\) % 1245,16 \(-0{,}641\) % 0,643 %
8 1255,22 \(+0{,}161\) % 1251,19 \(-0{,}161\) % 0,161 %
16 1253,70 \(+0{,}0402\) % 1252,70 \(-0{,}0402\) % 0,0402 %
32 1253,33 \(+0{,}0100\) % 1253,08 \(-0{,}0100\) % 0,0100 %

With every halving of \(h\) the error decreases by a factor of about 4. COOK (PDF p. 397) states this for the consistent mass: when the number of elements is doubled, the frequency errors decrease four-fold for bars and sixteen-fold for beams. The reason is seen in equation (10.44). The exact value is \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2 = c^2\theta^2/h^2\) (from \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} = k_{\mathrm{r}} c\) and \(\theta = k_{\mathrm{r}} h\)). With \(u = 1 - \cos\theta\) we have \(2 + \cos\theta = 3 - u\) and the ratios of the squares of the frequencies are

\[\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{z}}}{\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2} = \frac{2u}{\theta^2} , \qquad \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{k}}}{\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2} = \frac{6u}{\theta^2\,(3 - u)} . \tag{10.45}\]

They depend only on the angle \(\theta\), which for a given shape is proportional to \(h\). To estimate the ratios we need a bound on the values of the cosine function.

Lemma 10.37 Estimate of the cosine (ocena kosinusa)

For every \(\theta \ge 0\)

\[\frac{\theta^2}{2} - \frac{\theta^4}{24} \le 1 - \cos\theta \le \frac{\theta^2}{2} . \tag{10.46}\]
Proof

We must show both sides. We start from \(\cos s \le 1\) and integrate the inequality four times over \(s \in [0, t]\) for \(t \ge 0\). All functions are continuous, so the monotonicity of the integral holds (lemma 3.39, point 4), and we compute the integrals by the fundamental theorem (theorem 3.40, point 1) with the antiderivatives from theorem 8.12.

  1. By lemma 8.10, point 1, \(\cos s \le 1\). The integral \(\int_0^t\cos s\,\mathrm{d}s = \sin t - \sin 0 = \sin t\) is therefore at most \(\int_0^t 1\,\mathrm{d}s = t\). Hence \(\sin s \le s\) for every \(s \ge 0\).
  2. By step 1, \(\int_0^t \sin s\,\mathrm{d}s = 1 - \cos t\) (antiderivative \(-\cos s\), \(\cos 0 = 1\)) is at most \(\int_0^t s\,\mathrm{d}s = t^2/2\). This is the right inequality. Hence \(1 - \cos s \le s^2/2\) for every \(s \ge 0\).
  3. By step 2, \(\int_0^t (1 - \cos s)\,\mathrm{d}s = t - \sin t\) is at most \(\int_0^t s^2/2\,\mathrm{d}s = t^3/6\). Hence \(\sin s \ge s - s^3/6\) for every \(s \ge 0\).
  4. By step 3, \(1 - \cos t = \int_0^t\sin s\,\mathrm{d}s\) is at least \(\int_0^t (s - s^3/6)\,\mathrm{d}s = t^2/2 - t^4/24\). This is the left inequality.

Source: Not from a source.

With the estimate we prove that the error of the frequencies falls with \(h^2\).

Corollary 10.38 Order of the frequency error of the bar (red napake frekvenc palice)

For the bar of theorem 10.36 let \(\theta = \theta_{\mathrm{r}}\). For the lumped mass, for every \(r\),

\[1 - \frac{\theta^2}{12} \le \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{z}}}{\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2} \le 1 , \tag{10.47}\]

and for the consistent mass, at \(\theta^2 < 6\),

\[1 \le \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{k}}}{\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2} \le \frac{6}{6 - \theta^2} . \tag{10.48}\]

Hence for the lumped mass \(1 - \theta^2/12 \le \omega_{\mathrm{h}}/\omega_{\mathrm{r}} \le 1\) and for the consistent \(1 \le \omega_{\mathrm{h}}/\omega_{\mathrm{r}} \le 1 + \theta^2/\big(2(6 - \theta^2)\big)\), where \(\omega_{\mathrm{h}} = \sqrt{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}\).

Proof

We must show the estimates of the ratios in equation (10.45) by lemma 10.37. For \(\theta_{\mathrm{r}} \in (0, \pi)\) the number \(u = 1 - \cos\theta\) lies between \(0\) and \(2\).

  1. By lemma 10.37, \(\tfrac{\theta^2}{2}\big(1 - \tfrac{\theta^2}{12}\big) \le u \le \tfrac{\theta^2}{2}\). Division by \(\theta^2/2\) gives \(1 - \theta^2/12 \le 2u/\theta^2 \le 1\), which is equation (10.47).
  2. The function \(g(u) = u/(3 - u)\) has by the quotient rule (lemma 1.81) the derivative \(3/(3 - u)^2 > 0\) on \([0, 3)\), so it increases strictly. The ratio \(6u/(\theta^2(3 - u)) = (6/\theta^2)\,g(u)\) is therefore at least its value at the smallest and at most its value at the largest \(u\) of step 1. For \(\theta^2 < 6\) both limits lie in \([0, 3)\).
  3. Upper bound: at \(u = \theta^2/2\) the ratio is \(3\big/\big(3 - \tfrac{\theta^2}{2}\big) = 6/(6 - \theta^2)\).
  4. Lower bound: at \(u = \tfrac{\theta^2}{2} - \tfrac{\theta^4}{24}\) the ratio is \(\big(1 - \tfrac{\theta^2}{12}\big)\big/\big(1 - \tfrac{\theta^2}{6} + \tfrac{\theta^4}{72}\big)\). The denominator is \(\tfrac{(\theta^2 - 6)^2}{72} + \tfrac12 > 0\) and the difference of numerator and denominator is \(\tfrac{\theta^2}{12} - \tfrac{\theta^4}{72} = \tfrac{\theta^2(6 - \theta^2)}{72} > 0\), so the ratio is greater than \(1\). This is equation (10.48).
  5. Frequencies: \(\sqrt{1 - x} \ge 1 - x\) for \(x \in [0, 1]\) (square both sides) with \(x = \theta^2/12 < 1\), and \(\sqrt{1 + y} \le 1 + y/2\) for \(y \ge 0\) (the square of the right side is \(1 + y + y^2/4\)) with \(y = \theta^2/(6 - \theta^2)\).

Source: Not from a source. COOK (PDF p. 397) gives only the result that for a bar the frequency error decreases four-fold when the number of elements is doubled.

Because \(\theta_{\mathrm{r}} = (2r - 1)\pi h/(2L)\) is proportional to \(h\), halving \(h\) reduces \(\theta^2\) four-fold, and with it the upper bounds of the error. The bounds do not give the exact coefficient, but SymPy computes it from the expansion of the ratios in powers of the angle \(\theta\) (the book does not yet have a proof of the expansion to fourth order in this part, so we state it as a computed value):

\[\begin{aligned} &\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{h}}}{\omega_{\mathrm{r}}} = 1 + \frac{\theta^2}{24} + \frac{\theta^4}{1920} + \dots \\ &\quad \text{(consistent)} , \\ &\frac{\omega_{\mathrm{h}}}{\omega_{\mathrm{r}}} = 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{24} + \frac{\theta^4}{1920} + \dots \\ &\quad \text{(lumped)} . \end{aligned} \tag{10.49}\]

The error is therefore \(\pm\theta^2/24\) with opposite signs, at least for small \(\theta\), which agrees with the bounds of the corollary (the coefficient \(1/24\) is below the bound \(1/12\) of the corollary). The table confirms this: \(\theta_1^2/24 = 0{,}643\) % at \(n = 4\) against \(0{,}644\) % and \(-0{,}641\) % (NumPy). At one element \(\theta_1 = \pi/2 = 1{,}57\) and the term \(\theta^4/1920\) is no longer negligible, so the agreement is worse there (\(10{,}28\) % against \(10{,}27\) % and \(-9{,}97\) %). Higher modes have a larger \(\theta_{\mathrm{r}}\): at \(n = 16\) we have \(\theta_3 = 5\theta_1\) and the error of the third frequency is about \(25\) times larger, \(+1{,}007\) % (\(6329{,}09\) Hz) and \(-1{,}001\) % (\(6203{,}28\) Hz) against \(0{,}0402\) % for the first. The shape of the third mode has \(12{,}8\) elements per period over the length of \(16\) elements, \(4n/(2r - 1) = 2\pi/\theta\), and this is how large the error is. The rule: the error is small when \(\theta\) is small, that is, when there are many elements per period of the shape.

Why does the consistent frequency lie above the exact one and the lumped one below? For the lumped mass we have a proof.

Corollary 10.39 Lumped masses give lower frequencies (zbrane mase dajo nižje frekvence)

For the bar of theorem 10.36, for every \(r = 1, \dots, n\),

\[\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{z}} \le \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{k}} \quad\text{and}\quad \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{z}} \le \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2 . \tag{10.50}\]
Proof

We must show the first inequality from the difference of the masses and the second from the estimate of the cosine.

  1. By equation (10.40), \(\dot{\vek d}^\T(\mat M^{\mathrm{z}} - \mat M)\dot{\vek d} \ge 0\) for every column, so the difference is positive semidefinite (definition 7.15). The same holds for the block of free nodes, because its quadratic form is the quadratic form of the full matrix at \(\dot d_0 = 0\).
  2. The matrix \(\mat K\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite, because \(\vek d^\T\mat K\,\vek d = \tfrac{EA}{h}\sum_{\mathrm{j}=1}^n (d_{\mathrm{j}} - d_{\mathrm{j}-1})^2 \ge 0\) with \(d_0 = 0\), and \(\mat M\) is symmetric and positive definite (lemma 10.34). By point 2 of corollary 10.30 of section 10.6, with \(\mat K' = \mat K\), \(\mat M' = \mat M^{\mathrm{z}}\) and the positive semidefinite difference \(\mat M' - \mat M\), increasing the mass raises no eigenvalue: \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{z}} \le \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{k}}\) for every \(r\).
  3. By lemma 10.37, \(1 - \cos\theta \le \theta^2/2\), so \(2(1 - \cos\theta) \le \theta^2\).
  4. By equation (10.44), \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{z}} = \tfrac{c^2}{h^2}\cdot 2(1 - \cos\theta_{\mathrm{r}}) \le \tfrac{c^2}{h^2}\,\theta_{\mathrm{r}}^2 = c^2k_{\mathrm{r}}^2 = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\), because \(\theta_{\mathrm{r}} = k_{\mathrm{r}} h\).

Source: Not from a source. COOK (PDF p. 397) and GR (PDF p. 389) state the same for the lumped mass as an observation ("Lumped mass matrices usually, but not always, underestimate natural frequencies").

For the consistent mass we have a reason, but no proof for every \(r\) in this chapter. By COOK (PDF pp. 396 and 397) the computed frequencies are upper bounds of the exact ones when the elements are compatible (the field is continuous at the junction of elements, as with our hat functions), the stiffness is not softened by incomplete integration and the masses are consistent. The reason is Ritz's. The quotient \(\vek d^\T\mat K\vek d/\vek d^\T\mat M\vek d\) equals, by lemma 10.34 and point 3 of theorem 7.13, the quotient of the energies of the continuous bar computed on the field \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\), and the smallest value of a quotient on a smaller set of fields is not smaller than the smallest on a larger one (for matrices this is theorem 10.26 at \(r = 1\)). The statement that for the continuous bar every eigenfrequency of such a model lies above the exact one is therefore proved in chapter 13, where the Ritz method of chapter 6 is stated for eigenfrequencies. We do not use it anywhere in this chapter. GR (PDF p. 389) says that a non-consistent mass matrix may lose the bound, and COOK (PDF p. 397) that lumped masses "usually, but not always" underestimate the frequencies. For our bar they are underestimated at every \(r\), which the corollary above guarantees, but this is a property of this example. The table and a computation with \(16\) elements (\(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}^{\mathrm{k}} \ge \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) for all \(r = 1, \dots, 16\), NumPy) confirm the upper bound for the consistent mass. For \(\theta_{\mathrm{r}}^2 < 6\) corollary 10.38 already proves it.

10.7.6 A free bar (prosta palica)

Section 10.5 showed the zero frequency of a structure that has a displacement without energy. We see the same on a bar that is not fixed anywhere. Take two elements (\(h = L/2\), nodes \(0, 1, 2\), all three unknowns):

\[\mat K = \frac{EA}{h}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat M = \frac{\rho A h}{6}\begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} . \tag{10.51}\]

The sum of each row of the matrix \(\mat K\) is zero, so \(\mat K\vek 1 = \vek 0 = 0\cdot\mat M\vek 1\) for \(\vek 1 = (1, 1, 1)\). This is an eigenpair with \(\lambda_1 = 0\) (definition 10.7), the rigid displacement of the bar without deformation (theorem 10.23). The remaining modes are \((1, 0, -1)\) and \((1, -1, 1)\) with frequencies \(2763{,}70\) and \(5527{,}41\) Hz (NumPy), and the exact ones are \(rc/(2L) = 2506{,}40\) and \(5012{,}80\) Hz, both errors \(+10{,}27\) %. The first error is the same as for one element of the fixed bar, because in the mode \((1, 0, -1)\) the middle is at rest and each half behaves as a fixed bar of length \(L/2\) with one element (\(\theta = \pi/2\)). That the second error is the same too, the computation shows without a particular reason that we would have here. The lumped mass gives \(2256{,}56\) and \(3191{,}25\) Hz. The total mass is \(\vek 1^\T\mat M\,\vek 1 = \rho A L = 0{,}78\) kg. By corollary 10.24 both modes with non-zero frequency are \(\mat M\)-orthogonal to \(\vek 1\): \(\vek 1^\T\mat M\,(1, 0, -1)^\T = \tfrac{\rho A h}{6}\,(2 - 2) = 0\), which means that the centre of mass of the bar stays in place in each of them. Why, we explain now, as section 10.5 promised for a mass matrix that is not diagonal.

For \(\vek s = \vek 1\) and the field \(u_{\mathrm{h}} = \sum_{\mathrm{I}} d_{\mathrm{I}}\psi_{\mathrm{I}}\),

\[\vek 1^\T\mat M\,\vek d = \int_0^L\rho A\,u_{\mathrm{h}}\,\mathrm{d}x . \tag{10.52}\]

On an element, namely, \(\vek 1^\T\mat m_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}} = \int\rho A\,(\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek 1)^\T\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{e}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) and \(\mat\psi_{\mathrm{e}}\,\vek 1 = \psi_1^e + \psi_2^e = 1\) (lemma 7.3), so this is \(\int\rho A\,u_{\mathrm{h}}\,\mathrm{d}x\) over the element. The selection matrix \(\mat Z_{\mathrm{e}}\) maps the vector \(\vek 1\) into the vector \(\vek 1\) of order \(2\), so the sum over the elements (lemma 10.34) gives the equation. If the nodes of the bar are displaced by \(\vek d\), each point of a cross-section is displaced by \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) and the centre of mass (definition 8.71, \(x_{\mathrm{T}} = \tfrac1m\int\rho A\,x\,\mathrm{d}x\)) is displaced by \(\tfrac1m\int\rho A\,u_{\mathrm{h}}\,\mathrm{d}x = \vek 1^\T\mat M\,\vek d/m\). For a diagonal \(\mat M\) this is the sum of the masses multiplied by the nodal displacements, divided by the mass \(m\), and for ours the sum is replaced by an integral over the field \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\). The condition \(\vek 1^\T\mat M\,\vek\phi = 0\) means that the mean displacement of the field, weighted by the mass, is zero: the centre of mass is at rest in this mode. In the mode \((1, 0, -1)\) the field \(u_{\mathrm{h}}\) is antisymmetric about the middle and the integral is indeed zero.

10.7.7 Large eigenproblems (veliki lastni problemi)

A bar of sixteen elements has \(16 \times 16\) matrices. For a uniform bar the eigenvalues are written down, but for a general bar or truss the eigenproblem \(\mat K\vek\phi = \lambda\mat M\vek\phi\) must be solved. The lecture notes of this chapter reduce it to an ordinary symmetric problem. The matrix \(\mat M\) is positive definite (lemma 10.34), so elimination has positive pivots (theorem 6.29) and writes \(\mat M = \mat L\mat D\mat L^\T\) with a positive diagonal \(\mat D\) (equation (7.45)). With \(\mat C = \mat L\sqrt{\mat D}\) we have \(\mat M = \mat C\mat C^\T\). With \(\vek y = \mat C^\T\vek\phi\) the equation \(\mat K\vek\phi = \lambda\mat C\mat C^\T\vek\phi\) becomes \(\mat C^{-1}\mat K\,\mat C^{-\T}\vek y = \lambda\vek y\) with a matrix that is symmetric, and NumPy computes all eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix. This method is ours, we did not find it in a source. For a large number of unknowns, thousands and more, it is not suitable, because the matrix is full and costs of the order of \(n^3\) operations (equation (7.43)). For such problems there are other methods: vector iteration (CK §15.2, PDF p. 489), subspace iteration and the Lanczos procedure (CK §15.3 and §15.4, PDF p. 498 onwards), and for full matrices tridiagonalisation with QR (KREYSZIG §20.9, PDF p. 914). Here we only name them, their material is in chapter 21. The next section shows a way that replaces them for frequencies: we choose only a few shapes and obtain an upper bound with them.

10.8 The Ritz method for natural frequencies (Ritzova metoda za lastne frekvence)

Bar C (palica C) of section 10.7 has 16 coordinates with 16 elements, but we are interested mainly in its lowest natural frequency. The same holds for a building with many storeys (etaže): its motion is often almost only a few simple shapes, while there are as many coordinates as storeys. Can we keep only a few shapes of the motion of a large system and still get its lowest frequencies? And on which side of the true value will we land?

The model is the system of section 10.2 without damping and without external force. The matrix \(\mat K\) of order \(n\) is symmetric, the mass matrix \(\mat M\) of order \(n\) is symmetric and positive definite (definition 6.27). The eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) are \(\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \dots \le \lambda_{\mathrm{n}}\) and its eigencolumns, the modes (nihajni načini), are \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{n}}\) with \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\,\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) equal to 1 for \(r = s\) and 0 otherwise (theorem 10.13). The Rayleigh quotient (Rayleighov količnik) \(R(\vek v) = \vek v^\T\mat K\,\vek v/\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v\) of definition 10.25 is the number we get from a column \(\vek v \ne \vek 0\) with \(n\) numbers.

The idea is the same as in section 6.4 of chapter 6. There, instead of all fields we tried only a family of fields with a few free numbers and looked for the best field in it. Now the family is the set of columns \(\vek v = c_1\vek\psi_1 + \dots + c_{\mathrm{m}}\vek\psi_{\mathrm{m}}\) with given columns \(\vek\psi_{\mathrm{j}}\), which are the numbers of the trial field in the coordinates of the system, just as the \(\psi_{\mathrm{i}}\) were functions. Instead of the lowest point of the energy we look for the points where the Rayleigh quotient is stationary, since theorem 10.27 says that the quotient is stationary exactly at the modes and that an error of order \(\varepsilon\) in the shape gives an error of order \(\varepsilon^2\) in the quotient. First a single column on frame A (okvir A) of section 10.1, with \(\mat K = k\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\), \(\mat M = \bar m\,\mat I\), \(k = 501\,760\) N/m and \(\bar m = 500\) kg.

Take the column \(\vek\psi = (1,\ 1{,}5)^\T\), the static shape of the frame under the weights of the storeys from section 10.6. Every \(\vek v = c\,\vek\psi\) with \(c \ne 0\) gives the same quotient, because \(c^2\) cancels. We compute \(\vek\psi^\T\mat K\,\vek\psi = k\,(2 \cdot 1^2 - 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 1{,}5 + 1{,}5^2) = 1{,}25\,k\) and \(\vek\psi^\T\mat M\,\vek\psi = \bar m\,(1 + 1{,}5^2) = 3{,}25\,\bar m\) (the floor mass is written \(\bar m\) here because \(m\) is the number of columns in this section). The quotient is \(\tilde\lambda = 1{,}25\,k/(3{,}25\,\bar m) = 385{,}97\ \text{1/s}^2\), the circular frequency is \(19{,}6461\) 1/s, the true one is \(\omega_1 = 19{,}5783\) 1/s. The error of the frequency is \(+0{,}346\) % and the error of \(\omega^2\) is \(+0{,}694\) %, because a relative error roughly doubles when squared.

With several columns the computation turns into a small eigenproblem. We write the columns \(\vek\psi_1, \dots, \vek\psi_{\mathrm{m}}\) as the columns of a matrix \(\mat\Psi\) with \(n\) rows and \(m\) columns, so that \(\vek v = \mat\Psi\,\vek a\) for a column \(\vek a\) with the \(m\) numbers \(c_1, \dots, c_{\mathrm{m}}\). For \(\vek v = \mat\Psi\,\vek a\) we have \(\vek v^\T\mat K\,\vek v = \vek a^\T(\mat\Psi^\T\mat K\,\mat\Psi)\,\vek a\) and similarly for \(\mat M\), so the quotient \(R(\mat\Psi\,\vek a)\) is nothing other than the Rayleigh quotient of a pair of matrices of order \(m\), which we now name.

Lemma 10.40 Reduced pair of matrices (reducirani par matrik)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be as above, \(\mat\Psi\) a matrix with \(n\) rows and \(m \le n\) columns whose columns are linearly independent (definition 6.22), and \(\tilde{\mat K} = \mat\Psi^\T\mat K\,\mat\Psi\), \(\tilde{\mat M} = \mat\Psi^\T\mat M\,\mat\Psi\) matrices of order \(m\). Then:

  1. The matrix \(\tilde{\mat K}\) is symmetric, and the matrix \(\tilde{\mat M}\) is symmetric and positive definite.
  2. There exist real numbers \(\tilde\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) and columns \(\vek a_1, \dots, \vek a_{\mathrm{m}}\) with \(m\) numbers such that \(\tilde{\mat K}\,\vek a_{\mathrm{r}} = \tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\tilde{\mat M}\,\vek a_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\vek a_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\tilde{\mat M}\,\vek a_{\mathrm{s}}\) is equal to 1 for \(r = s\) and 0 otherwise. The columns \(\mat\Psi\,\vek a_{\mathrm{r}}\) have \(n\) numbers and satisfy \((\mat\Psi\,\vek a_{\mathrm{r}})^\T\mat M\,(\mat\Psi\,\vek a_{\mathrm{s}}) = \vek a_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\tilde{\mat M}\,\vek a_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \((\mat\Psi\,\vek a_{\mathrm{r}})^\T\mat K\,(\mat\Psi\,\vek a_{\mathrm{s}}) = \tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\,\vek a_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\tilde{\mat M}\,\vek a_{\mathrm{s}}\).
  3. For \(\vek a \ne \vek 0\) we have \(R(\mat\Psi\,\vek a) = \vek a^\T\tilde{\mat K}\,\vek a/\vek a^\T\tilde{\mat M}\,\vek a\), which is the Rayleigh quotient of the pair \((\tilde{\mat K}, \tilde{\mat M})\). Its partial derivatives with respect to the components of \(\vek a\) are zero exactly at the eigencolumns of this pair, and the value of the quotient there is the corresponding eigenvalue.
Proof

We must show that the reduced pair satisfies the conditions of theorem 10.13, and then read points 2 and 3 from the theorem and from the definition of the quotient.

  1. By lemma 1.101, \(\tilde{\mat K}^\T = \mat\Psi^\T\mat K^\T\mat\Psi = \tilde{\mat K}\), because \(\mat K\) is symmetric. In the same way \(\tilde{\mat M}\) is symmetric.
  2. Let \(\vek a \ne \vek 0\). Since the columns of \(\mat\Psi\) are independent, \(\mat\Psi\,\vek a \ne \vek 0\) (definition 6.22). Hence \(\vek a^\T\tilde{\mat M}\,\vek a = (\mat\Psi\,\vek a)^\T\mat M\,(\mat\Psi\,\vek a) > 0\), because \(\mat M\) is positive definite. This is point 1.
  3. By steps 1 and 2, theorem 10.13 applied to the pair \((\tilde{\mat K}, \tilde{\mat M})\) of order \(m\) gives the numbers \(\tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) and the columns \(\vek a_{\mathrm{r}}\). The products in point 2 are only the opening of brackets: \((\mat\Psi\,\vek a_{\mathrm{r}})^\T\mat M\,(\mat\Psi\,\vek a_{\mathrm{s}}) = \vek a_{\mathrm{r}}^\T(\mat\Psi^\T\mat M\,\mat\Psi)\,\vek a_{\mathrm{s}}\), and \(\tilde{\mat K}\,\vek a_{\mathrm{s}} = \tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\tilde{\mat M}\,\vek a_{\mathrm{s}}\) gives the second.
  4. Point 3: by step 3 the numerator and denominator of the quotient \(R(\mat\Psi\,\vek a)\) are \(\vek a^\T\tilde{\mat K}\,\vek a\) and \(\vek a^\T\tilde{\mat M}\,\vek a\). The partial derivatives are zero exactly at the eigencolumns by theorem 10.27 for the pair \((\tilde{\mat K}, \tilde{\mat M})\), whose conditions are guaranteed by steps 1 and 2.

Source: CK (10.58) to (10.63) (PDF p. 318): »Ritz proposed that the coefficients ... be chosen to make R(v) stationary«. The proof is not from the source.

The lemma says that Ritz's problem is indeed an eigenproblem of the same kind as the original, only smaller. Let us name it.

Definition 10.41 Ritz approximation of eigenvalues (Ritzov približek lastnih vrednosti)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be as in definition 10.7, \(\mat\Psi\) a matrix with \(n\) rows and \(m\) linearly independent columns \(\vek\psi_1, \dots, \vek\psi_{\mathrm{m}}\), \(1 \le m \le n\), and \(\tilde{\mat K} = \mat\Psi^\T\mat K\,\mat\Psi\) and \(\tilde{\mat M} = \mat\Psi^\T\mat M\,\mat\Psi\) matrices of order \(m\). The reduced eigenproblem (reducirani lastni problem) is \(\tilde{\mat K}\,\vek a = \tilde\lambda\,\tilde{\mat M}\,\vek a\) for a column \(\vek a\) with \(m\) numbers. Its eigenvalues \(\tilde\lambda_1 \le \dots \le \tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) are the Ritz values (Ritzove vrednosti), and the columns \(\mat\Psi\,\vek a_{\mathrm{r}}\) with \(n\) numbers are the Ritz shapes (Ritzove oblike). Together they are the Ritz approximation (Ritzov približek) of the first \(m\) eigenvalues and shapes of the system. For \(m = 1\) the Ritz value is the Rayleigh quotient \(R(\vek\psi_1)\).

Source: CK (10.59) to (10.63) (PDF p. 318), which writes the matrices with a hat. The notation is ours.

Frame A with two columns shows what happens when \(m = n\). Let \(\mat\Psi\) have \(\vek\psi_1 = (1,\ 1{,}5)^\T\) and \(\vek\psi_2 = (0,\ 1)^\T\). We get \(\tilde{\mat K} = k\begin{pmatrix} 1{,}25 & 0{,}5 \\ 0{,}5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) and \(\tilde{\mat M} = \bar m\begin{pmatrix} 3{,}25 & 1{,}5 \\ 1{,}5 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\) (SymPy), and the reduced problem has \(\tilde\lambda = 383{,}31\) and \(2627{,}25\) 1/s\(^2\), exactly the eigenvalues of the frame. The reason is that two independent columns in a space with two coordinates form an invertible matrix, so we have only written the system in other coordinates (the proof is point 2 of the theorem below). The real case is \(m < n\), where we have left shapes out. The Rayleigh quotient of section 10.6 always lay above \(\lambda_1\) for frame A. Does this also hold for the other Ritz values and for every choice of \(\mat\Psi\)?

Theorem 10.42 Ritz values are upper bounds (Ritzove vrednosti so zgornje meje)

Let \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\), \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) be as at the beginning of the section, and \(\mat\Psi\) and \(\tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) as in definition 10.41 with \(m \le n\). Then:

  1. \(\tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for every \(r = 1, \dots, m\).
  2. If \(m = n\), then \(\tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for every \(r\) and \(\mat\Psi\,\vek a_{\mathrm{r}}\) is an eigencolumn of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\).
Proof

For point 1 we take the first \(r\) Ritz shapes. We must show that the set of their combinations has nowhere a quotient larger than \(\tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), but that every such set contains a column where the quotient is not smaller than \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). This is point 2 of theorem 10.28 for the columns \(\vek v_1, \dots, \vek v_{\mathrm{r}}\), written out here to the end.

  1. Let \(r \le m\) and \(\vek v_{\mathrm{j}} = \mat\Psi\,\vek a_{\mathrm{j}}\). By lemma 10.40, point 2, \(\vek v_{\mathrm{i}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v_{\mathrm{j}}\) is equal to 1 for \(i = j\) and 0 otherwise, and \(\vek v_{\mathrm{i}}^\T\mat K\,\vek v_{\mathrm{j}} = \tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{j}}\,\vek v_{\mathrm{i}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v_{\mathrm{j}}\).
  2. The columns \(\vek v_1, \dots, \vek v_{\mathrm{r}}\) are independent. If \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} t_{\mathrm{j}}\vek v_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek 0\), we multiply by \(\vek v_{\mathrm{i}}^\T\mat M\) and by step 1 we get \(t_{\mathrm{i}} = 0\).
  3. Let \(\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{j} \le \mathrm{r}} t_{\mathrm{j}}\vek v_{\mathrm{j}}\). By step 1, \(\vek v^\T\mat K\,\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} t_{\mathrm{j}}^2\) and \(\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} t_{\mathrm{j}}^2\). Since \(\tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} \le \tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for \(j \le r\), we have \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}}\tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{j}} t_{\mathrm{j}}^2 \le \tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\sum_{\mathrm{j}} t_{\mathrm{j}}^2\), so \(R(\vek v) \le \tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for every such combination.
  4. The conditions \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{i}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v = 0\) for \(i = 1, \dots, r - 1\) are \(r - 1\) homogeneous linear equations for the \(r\) numbers \(t_1, \dots, t_{\mathrm{r}}\) (for \(r = 1\) there are none). By lemma 10.9 they have a solution \((t_1, \dots, t_{\mathrm{r}}) \ne \vek 0\). The corresponding \(\vek v\) is not zero, because by step 2 the columns are independent, and it is \(\mat M\)-orthogonal to \(\vek\varphi_1, \dots, \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}-1}\).
  5. By the expansion theorem (corollary 10.14), \(\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} c_{\mathrm{s}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) with \(c_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v\), and by step 4, \(c_{\mathrm{s}} = 0\) for \(s < r\). By equation (10.31), \(R(\vek v) = \sum_{\mathrm{s} \ge \mathrm{r}}\lambda_{\mathrm{s}} c_{\mathrm{s}}^2/\sum_{\mathrm{s} \ge \mathrm{r}} c_{\mathrm{s}}^2\). Since \(\lambda_{\mathrm{s}} \ge \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for \(s \ge r\), \(R(\vek v) \ge \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\).
  6. The column from step 4 is a combination from step 3, so for the same \(\vek v\) we have \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} \le R(\vek v) \le \tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). This is point 1.
  7. For point 2, \(\mat\Psi\) is square with independent columns. From \(\mat\Psi\,\vek a = \vek 0\) it follows that \(\vek a = \vek 0\), so \(\mat\Psi\) and also \(\mat\Psi^\T\) have an inverse matrix (lemma 8.21).
  8. The pair \((\tilde\lambda, \vek a)\) solves \(\tilde{\mat K}\,\vek a = \tilde\lambda\tilde{\mat M}\,\vek a\) exactly when \(\mat\Psi^\T(\mat K - \tilde\lambda\mat M)\,\mat\Psi\,\vek a = \vek 0\), and by step 7 this holds exactly when \((\mat K - \tilde\lambda\mat M)\,\mat\Psi\,\vek a = \vek 0\). The eigenpairs of the reduced problem and of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) therefore agree through \(\vek a \mapsto \mat\Psi\,\vek a\). This map takes independent columns to independent columns (step 7), so the two eigenspaces of the same eigenvalue have the same dimension in both problems. That dimension is the number of repetitions of the eigenvalue, since by corollary 10.14 (point 2) an eigencolumn is a sum of modes with the same eigenvalue, and these are independent. The ordered lists are therefore equal.

Source: CK, text after (10.71) (PDF p. 319): »each of the \hat N < N eigenvalues produced by a Rayleigh-Ritz approximation to an N-DOF system is an upper bound to the corresponding exact eigenvalue«. CK proves it with the eigenvalue separation theorem (10.69) to (10.71), GR with a conclusion about constraints (2.239), (2.240) (PDF p. 136). The proof in steps is not from the sources.

The proof has shown two things. The Ritz value \(\tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the largest quotient on the combinations of the first \(r\) Ritz shapes, and every set of combinations of \(r\) independent columns contains a column on which the quotient is not smaller than \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). So the Ritz method does not underestimate eigenvalues. This is similar to chapter 6, where the energy of the Ritz field was above the true one (theorem 6.34): a family of fields is an additional restriction, and a restriction does not lower the eigenvalues (corollary 10.29).

Let us test the theorem on a system where \(m < n\) in the true sense, on a frame with \(n = 3\) storeys, each with mass \(\bar m = 500\) kg and stiffness \(k\) (section 10.3). The eigenvalues are \(\lambda/(k/\bar m) = 0{,}198062\), \(1{,}554958\) and \(3{,}246980\), the frequencies \(2{,}2438\), \(6{,}2870\) and \(9{,}0850\) Hz. For the columns we take two simple shapes, a displacement of all storeys by the same amount and a displacement that grows with the storey: \(\vek\psi_1 = (1,\ 1,\ 1)^\T\) and \(\vek\psi_2 = (0,\ 1,\ 2)^\T\). The storey drift (etažni zamik, section 10.2.3) is the displacement of a ceiling relative to the ceiling below it (for the first storey relative to the ground). For \(\vek\psi_1\) the first storey has drift 1 and the second and third have 0. For \(\vek\psi_2\) the first storey has drift 0 and the second and third have 1 each. The energy of a storey is \(\tfrac12\,k\) times the square of its drift, so \(\vek\psi_1^\T\mat K\,\vek\psi_1 = k\), \(\vek\psi_2^\T\mat K\,\vek\psi_2 = 2k\) and \(\vek\psi_1^\T\mat K\,\vek\psi_2 = k\,(1 \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 1) = 0\). The masses are \(\vek\psi_1^\T\mat M\,\vek\psi_1 = 3\bar m\), \(\vek\psi_1^\T\mat M\,\vek\psi_2 = (0 + 1 + 2)\,\bar m = 3\bar m\) and \(\vek\psi_2^\T\mat M\,\vek\psi_2 = (0 + 1 + 4)\,\bar m = 5\bar m\). The reduced problem with \(x = \tilde\lambda\,\bar m/k\) has the determinant

\[\det\begin{pmatrix} 1 - 3x & -3x \\ -3x & 2 - 5x \end{pmatrix} = (1 - 3x)(2 - 5x) - 9x^2 = 6x^2 - 11x + 2 = 0 ,\]

with solutions \(x = (11 \mp \sqrt{73})/12 = 0{,}204666\) and \(1{,}628667\). The Ritz values are \(\tilde\lambda_1/(k/\bar m) = 0{,}204666\) and \(\tilde\lambda_2/(k/\bar m) = 1{,}628667\), the frequencies \(2{,}2809\) and \(6{,}4343\) Hz. The error of the frequencies is \(+1{,}65\) % and \(+2{,}34\) %, and the errors of the eigenvalues are \(+3{,}33\) % and \(+4{,}74\) %. Both values are above the true ones, \(0{,}204666 \ge 0{,}198062\) and \(1{,}628667 \ge 1{,}554958\), as the theorem predicts. This approximation does not give the third value, because the reduced problem has only order \(m = 2\). The plane of two columns is a single constraint on three coordinates: the cross product \(\vek\psi_1 \times \vek\psi_2 = (1,\ -2,\ 1)^\T =: \vek b\) is perpendicular to both columns, so the plane is the set of columns with \(\vek b^\T\vek v = 0\). In the notation of corollary 10.29, \(p = 1\) and \(\mat\Psi = \mat G\,\mat T\), where \(\mat T\) is the matrix with the rows of \(\mat\Psi\) with index \(i \ne p\). The matrix \(\mat T\) is invertible, because \(\mat T\vek a = \vek 0\) implies \(\mat\Psi\,\vek a = \mat G\,\mat T\vek a = \vek 0\) and \(\vek a = \vek 0\) (lemma 8.21). The reduced pair is then \((\mat T^\T\mat K'\mat T,\ \mat T^\T\mat M'\mat T)\). By point 2 of theorem 10.42, applied to the pair \((\mat K', \mat M')\) of order \(n - 1\) with the matrix \(\mat T\) in place of \(\mat\Psi\), it has the same eigenvalues as \((\mat K', \mat M')\), so \(\tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda'_{\mathrm{r}}\). The corollary thus also gives an upper bound, \(\tilde\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2\) and \(\tilde\lambda_2 \le \lambda_3\), and indeed \(0{,}204666 \le 1{,}554958\) and \(1{,}628667 \le 3{,}246980\).

Figure 10.25 shows step 4 of the proof for \(r = 2\) and \(n = 3\). In the mode coordinates, \(\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{s}}\eta_{\mathrm{s}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) with \(\eta_{\mathrm{s}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}^\T\mat M\,\vek v\) (corollary 10.14), we have \(\vek v^\T\mat M\,\vek v = \sum\eta_{\mathrm{s}}^2\) and \(\vek v^\T\mat K\,\vek v = \sum\lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\eta_{\mathrm{s}}^2\). The plane of two columns passes through the origin and therefore meets the plane \(\eta_1 = 0\) at least in a line: the two equations \(\eta_1 = 0\) and the equation of the plane have, for three unknowns, a nontrivial solution by lemma 10.9. On this line, in the direction \((0,\ -0{,}978,\ -0{,}208)^\T\) (NumPy), \(R = 1{,}6285\,k/\bar m\), above \(\lambda_2\), because a mixture of \(\lambda_2\) and \(\lambda_3\) cannot fall below the smaller of the two. The largest quotient in the plane is therefore at least as large.

The theorem also says what it does not say. It does not say how large the error is: it can be \(+3\) %, as above, or much more if we choose bad columns. And it says nothing about the shapes: the Ritz shape \(\vek v_1\) is \(2{,}8°\) from the mode \(\vek\varphi_1\), which by theorem 10.27 gives an error of the quotient of the order of the square of the angle. The theorem also does not say how the error changes with the ordinal number \(r\). This is shown by finite element meshes.

Bar C, clamped at \(x = 0\) and free at \(x = L = 1\) m, consists of \(n_{\mathrm{e}}\) equal elements of length \(h = L/n_{\mathrm{e}}\) made of steel with wave speed \(c = 5012{,}80\) m/s (section 10.7). With the consistent mass matrix (lemma 10.31) the lowest frequencies, the true one being \(f_1 = 1253{,}20\) Hz, are:

\(n_{\mathrm{e}}\) 1 2 4 8 16 32
\(f_1\) consistent (Hz) 1381,85 1285,61 1261,27 1255,22 1253,70 1253,33
\(f_1\) lumped (Hz) 1128,28 1221,24 1245,16 1251,19 1252,70 1253,08

The consistent values fall with every doubling of \(n_{\mathrm{e}}\) and stay above the true one, the lumped ones (definition 10.32) rise and are below it (figure 10.26). Is this a rule or a coincidence? If the finer mesh arose by dividing the elements of the coarse one, the field of the coarse mesh is at the same time a field of the fine mesh, and this is exactly what the Ritz method is made for: \(\mat\Psi\) is the matrix that converts the nodal displacements of the coarse mesh into the nodal displacements of the fine one.

Corollary 10.43 Nested meshes (gnezdene mreže)

Let a bar with constant \(EA\) and \(\rho A\), clamped at \(x = 0\), be divided into a coarse mesh with \(n_{\mathrm{H}}\) elements and a fine mesh in which every element of the coarse one is divided into the same number of equal parts, with \(n_{\mathrm{h}}\) elements. Let \(\mat K_{\mathrm{H}}\), \(\mat M_{\mathrm{H}}\) and \(\mat K_{\mathrm{h}}\), \(\mat M_{\mathrm{h}}\) be the matrices of the coarse and the fine mesh with consistent masses (lemma 10.31), without the clamped node, and let \(\mat P\) be the matrix with \(n_{\mathrm{h}}\) rows and \(n_{\mathrm{H}}\) columns whose column \(I\) has in row \(j\) the value of the hat function (šotorska funkcija) of the coarse mesh of node \(I\) at the fine node \(j\) (definition 6.25). Then \(\mat P^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{h}}\,\mat P = \mat K_{\mathrm{H}}\) and \(\mat P^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{h}}\,\mat P = \mat M_{\mathrm{H}}\), and every consistent eigenvalue of the fine mesh is at most as large as that of the coarse one, \(\lambda^h_{\mathrm{r}} \le \lambda^H_{\mathrm{r}}\) for \(r = 1, \dots, n_{\mathrm{H}}\).

Proof

We must show that the fine mesh represents the field of the coarse mesh exactly, that the quadratic forms of the two meshes are then equal, and apply theorem 10.42 with \(\mat\Psi = \mat P\).

  1. Let \(\vek d_{\mathrm{H}}\) be the column of free nodal displacements of the coarse mesh and \(u_{\mathrm{H}}\) the field (theorem 7.13). On every element of the fine mesh that lies inside one element of the coarse one, \(u_{\mathrm{H}}\) is a straight line. A straight line is determined by the values at the end points (definition 7.1), so \(u_{\mathrm{H}}\) is a field of the fine mesh with nodal displacements \(\vek d_{\mathrm{h}} = \mat P\,\vek d_{\mathrm{H}}\): the value of \(u_{\mathrm{H}}\) at the fine node \(j\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{I}} \psi^H_{\mathrm{I}}(x_{\mathrm{j}})\,d_{\mathrm{I}}\).
  2. By point 3 of theorem 7.13, \(\tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{h}}^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{h}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{h}} = \tfrac12\int_0^L EA\,(u_{\mathrm{H}}')^2\,\mathrm{d}x\), and the same field written in the coarse mesh gives \(\tfrac12\,\vek d_{\mathrm{H}}^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{H}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{H}}\). Hence \(\vek d_{\mathrm{H}}^\T\mat P^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{h}}\,\mat P\,\vek d_{\mathrm{H}} = \vek d_{\mathrm{H}}^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{H}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{H}}\) for every \(\vek d_{\mathrm{H}}\).
  3. By lemma 10.34 (without time, so with \(\vek d\) in place of \(\dot{\vek d}\)) \(\vek d_{\mathrm{h}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{h}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{h}} = \int_0^L\rho A\,u_{\mathrm{H}}^2\,\mathrm{d}x = \vek d_{\mathrm{H}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{H}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{H}}\), that is \(\vek d_{\mathrm{H}}^\T\mat P^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{h}}\,\mat P\,\vek d_{\mathrm{H}} = \vek d_{\mathrm{H}}^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{H}}\,\vek d_{\mathrm{H}}\).
  4. A symmetric matrix \(\mat S\) with \(\vek d^\T\mat S\,\vek d = 0\) for every \(\vek d\) is zero: for \(\vek d = \vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) we get \(S_{\mathrm{ii}} = 0\), and for \(\vek d = \vek e_{\mathrm{i}} + \vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) we get \(2S_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\). The matrices \(\mat P^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{h}}\,\mat P - \mat K_{\mathrm{H}}\) and \(\mat P^\T\mat M_{\mathrm{h}}\,\mat P - \mat M_{\mathrm{H}}\) are symmetric, so by steps 2 and 3 both equalities hold.
  5. The columns of \(\mat P\) are independent: the node \(I\) of the coarse mesh is also a node of the fine one, and there the hat function \(I\) has the value 1 and all the others 0. The submatrix of the rows of the coarse nodes is therefore the identity matrix, and \(\mat P\,\vek a = \vek 0\) gives \(\vek a = \vek 0\).
  6. Theorem 10.42 with \(\mat\Psi = \mat P\) and \(m = n_{\mathrm{H}}\): by step 4 the Ritz problem is exactly \(\mat K_{\mathrm{H}}\,\vek a = \tilde\lambda\,\mat M_{\mathrm{H}}\,\vek a\), so \(\tilde\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \lambda^H_{\mathrm{r}} \ge \lambda^h_{\mathrm{r}}\).

Source: COOK (PDF p. 396): »if ... elements are compatible ... and mass matrices are consistent, then computed natural frequencies are upper bounds to exact frequencies«. GR (PDF p. 389): finite elements of displacement type are upper bounds in the Rayleigh-Ritz sense. The proof in steps is not from the sources.

The proof has shown that nesting by itself applies the Ritz method, because the coarse mesh is a subspace of the fine one. A test on bar C: the fine mesh has 16 elements, the coarse one 4, so \(\mat P\) is a matrix with 16 rows and 4 columns, each column has the hat function of a coarse node at the fine nodes, for example the first one \((\tfrac14,\ \tfrac12,\ \tfrac34,\ 1,\ \tfrac34,\ \tfrac12,\ \tfrac14,\ 0, \dots, 0)^\T\). NumPy gives zero matrices for the differences \(\mat P^\T\mat K_{16}\,\mat P - \mat K_4\) and \(\mat P^\T\mat M_{16}\,\mat P - \mat M_4\). The Ritz approximation with 4 columns is therefore exactly the four-element model, and we compare its frequencies with the first four frequencies of the sixteen-element model and with the true ones, all in Hz:

\(r\) 1 2 3 4
4 elements (Ritz) 1261,27 3978,85 7227,70 10 451,89
16 elements 1253,70 3773,21 6329,09 8945,89
true 1253,20 3759,60 6266,01 8772,41

Every value of the four-element model is above the sixteen-element one, and that is above the true one, as corollary 10.43 and theorem 10.42 require. The errors of the coarse model are \(0{,}64\) %, \(5{,}83\) %, \(15{,}35\) % and \(19{,}15\) %, those of the fine one \(0{,}04\) %, \(0{,}36\) %, \(1{,}01\) % and \(1{,}98\) %. The highest Ritz value is the worst. By theorem 10.36 the error depends on \(\theta_{\mathrm{r}} = (2r - 1)\pi h/(2L)\), where \(\theta = \pi\) is one whole half-wave of the sine per element, the shortest one that an element can still show. With four elements \(\theta_1 = \pi/8 = 0{,}39\) and \(\theta_4 = 7\pi/8 = 2{,}75\), almost \(\pi\), so the fourth mode is shown with barely one element per half-wave. This is why we use the Ritz method for a few of the lowest frequencies and not for all \(m\).

For lumped masses the theorem does not hold, and the numbers show this. The lumped matrix of the fine mesh, mapped by \(\mat P\), is not the lumped matrix of the coarse one: \(\mat P^\T\mat M_{16,\mathrm{z}}\,\mat P = \tfrac{\rho A L}{16}\,\mathrm{tridiag}(0{,}625,\ 2{,}75,\ 0{,}625)\) with the last diagonal entry \(1{,}375\), while \(\mat M_{4,\mathrm{z}} = \tfrac{\rho A L}{16}\,\mathrm{diag}(4,\ 4,\ 4,\ 2)\). The first diagonal entry is, for example, the sum of the squares of the values of the hat function at the fine nodes, \(2\,(\tfrac1{16} + \tfrac4{16} + \tfrac9{16}) + 1 = 2{,}75\), and not \(4\), as in the coarse lumped matrix, which assigns the whole mass of an element to its two nodes. Corollary 10.43 therefore does not hold for lumped masses: the coarse mesh has \(f_1 = 1245{,}16\) Hz, the fine one \(1252{,}70\) Hz, so the coarse one is below the fine one, and both are below the true one. Theorem 10.42 of course holds for the pair \((\mat K_{16}, \mat M_{16,\mathrm{z}})\) and \(\mat\Psi = \mat P\), but this is a different reduced pair: its lowest frequency is \(1260{,}24\) Hz, above the fine \(1252{,}70\) Hz, and not the \(1245{,}16\) Hz of the coarse lumped mesh. That the lumped values here lie below the true one is a property of this bar (GR, PDF p. 389, »in general mass lumping induces an overestimation of the inertia of the system«) and not a theorem: the theorem is proved only for consistent masses.

What has this section given us? A small eigenproblem of order \(m\) that uses only \(m\) chosen shapes out of \(n\) coordinates, and the guarantee that each of the \(m\) values obtained is above the true one with the same ordinal number. The guarantee is no more than that: it does not say how far above, and not which shapes to choose. A good choice is shapes that are already close to the modes, such as static shapes under weight (section 10.6) or low modes of parts of a structure. Such a selection in a large structure is treated in chapter 21. The same idea, with the energy scalar product \(B(u, w)\) of chapter 6 in place of the matrix \(\mat K\) and with mass in place of \(\mat M\), we use for the natural frequencies of bars and beams with trial functions. Chapter 6 promised this to us, and chapter 13 carries it out.

10.9 Damping and modal superposition (dušenje in modalna superpozicija)

So far we let frame A (the two-storey frame of section 10.1) vibrate without damping. A real frame comes to rest, because in the joints, in the floors and in the material mechanical energy turns into heat. Let us therefore add dampers to the frame. The question is what remains of the modal picture. Does every mode still behave as a single oscillator of chapter 9, or do the modes become entangled again? And if they do, how large is the error when we separate them?

The equation of motion with damping is \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C\dot{\vek q} + \mat K \vek q = \vek Q(t)\) (theorem 10.2). The damping matrix (matrika dušenja) \(\mat C\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite (definition 7.15). For \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) we have already done the decoupling. Insert \(\vek q = \mat\Phi\boldsymbol\eta\) (definition 10.19) and multiply the equation from the left by \(\mat\Phi^{\T}\). Because of \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\mat\Phi = \mat I\) and \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat K\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{n}})\) (lemma 10.16) we get

\[\ddot{\boldsymbol\eta} + \mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi\,\dot{\boldsymbol\eta} + \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{n}})\,\boldsymbol\eta = \mat\Phi^{\T} \vek Q(t) . \tag{10.53}\]

Masses and stiffnesses are decoupled. The damping is decoupled only if the matrix \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi\) is diagonal. Otherwise row \(r\) still contains terms \((\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi)_{\mathrm{rs}}\,\dot\eta_{\mathrm{s}}\) of other modes, and the modal coordinates influence each other.

10.9.1 Classical damping (klasično dušenje)

Diagonality gets a name.

Definition 10.44 Classical damping (klasično dušenje)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric positive definite matrix, \(\mat M\) a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\), \(\mat\Phi\) the modal matrix of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) (definition 10.15) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} = \sqrt{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}} > 0\). A symmetric positive semidefinite matrix \(\mat C\) of order \(n\) is classical damping (klasično dušenje) if \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi\) is a diagonal matrix. We write its diagonal elements as \(2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\), that is,

\[\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac{\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T} \mat C\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}}{2\omega_{\mathrm{r}}} \ge 0 , \qquad r = 1, \dots, n , \tag{10.54}\]

and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the damping ratio of the \(r\)-th mode (razmernik dušenja \(r\)-tega načina). For a repeated eigenvalue we require diagonality for at least one choice of the columns \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) of theorem 10.13.

Source: CK (10.79)-(10.80) (PDF p. 322), where the same is called "modal damping", "proportional damping" or "classical damping". Nonnegativity from definition 7.15: \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T} \mat C\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} \ge 0\).

The symbol \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\) has the same meaning as in definition 9.5. Row \(r\) of equation (10.53) is the equation of an oscillator with mass \(1\), stiffness \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) and damping constant \(2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\), and its damping ratio is \(2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}/(2\sqrt{1\cdot\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2}) = \zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\).

Where does such a matrix \(\mat C\) occur at all? We usually do not know the dampers of a structure one by one, since damping arises in joints and in nonstructural parts. It is measured as the damping ratio of individual modes, which for structures according to Craig and Kurdila lies between \(0{,}01\) and \(0{,}1\) (CK PDF 322). We therefore need matrices \(\mat C\) for which the \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\) are chosen or computed without difficulty. The simplest is the sum of the mass matrix and the stiffness matrix, because both are already diagonal in modal coordinates.

Definition 10.45 Rayleigh damping (Rayleighovo dušenje)

Let \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) be symmetric positive definite matrices of order \(n\). Rayleigh damping (Rayleighovo dušenje) is the matrix

\[\mat C = a_0 \mat M + a_1 \mat K , \qquad a_0 \ge 0 , \quad a_1 \ge 0 , \tag{10.55}\]

where \(a_0\) (unit 1/s) and \(a_1\) (unit s) are real constants.

Source: CK (10.76) (PDF p. 321), where it is also called "proportional damping".

This is classical damping, and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\) is obtained without computing the matrix \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi\).

Lemma 10.46 Damping ratios of Rayleigh damping (razmerniki Rayleighovega dušenja)

Let \(\mat C = a_0 \mat M + a_1 \mat K\) be Rayleigh damping and \(\mat K\) positive definite. Then \(\mat C\) is classical damping with

\[\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac{a_0}{2\omega_{\mathrm{r}}} + \frac{a_1\omega_{\mathrm{r}}}{2} , \qquad r = 1, \dots, n . \tag{10.56}\]

Let \(i < j\) be two modes with \(0 < \omega_{\mathrm{i}} < \omega_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(\zeta_{\mathrm{j}}\) the desired damping ratios. The constants for which Rayleigh damping gives exactly these ratios are

\[a_0 = \frac{2\omega_{\mathrm{i}}\omega_{\mathrm{j}}(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\omega_{\mathrm{j}} - \zeta_{\mathrm{j}}\omega_{\mathrm{i}})}{\omega_{\mathrm{j}}^2 - \omega_{\mathrm{i}}^2} , \qquad a_1 = \frac{2(\zeta_{\mathrm{j}}\omega_{\mathrm{j}} - \zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\omega_{\mathrm{i}})}{\omega_{\mathrm{j}}^2 - \omega_{\mathrm{i}}^2} , \tag{10.57}\]

and we can use them if both are nonnegative. The damping ratio of the other modes is then given by equation (10.56).

Proof

We must show that \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi\) is diagonal with elements \(2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) and that the constants solve the two equations for \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{j}}\).

  1. By lemma 10.16, \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\mat\Phi = \mat I\) and \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat K\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(\omega_1^2, \dots, \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2)\). Hence \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi = a_0 \mat I + a_1\,\mathrm{diag}(\omega_1^2, \dots, \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2)\), a diagonal matrix with elements \(a_0 + a_1\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\).
  2. The matrix \(\mat C\) is symmetric as a sum of symmetric matrices and positive semidefinite, because \(a_0, a_1 \ge 0\) and \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) are positive definite (definition 6.27). So it is classical damping, and by equation (10.54), \(2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}} = a_0 + a_1\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\). Division by \(2\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) gives equation (10.56).
  3. The requirement on \(\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{j}}\) gives two linear equations for \(a_0\) and \(a_1\): \(a_0 + a_1\omega_{\mathrm{i}}^2 = 2\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\omega_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(a_0 + a_1\omega_{\mathrm{j}}^2 = 2\zeta_{\mathrm{j}}\omega_{\mathrm{j}}\). Subtract them: \(a_1(\omega_{\mathrm{j}}^2 - \omega_{\mathrm{i}}^2) = 2(\zeta_{\mathrm{j}}\omega_{\mathrm{j}} - \zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\omega_{\mathrm{i}})\), from which \(a_1\) is the one in equation (10.57), because \(\omega_{\mathrm{j}}^2 - \omega_{\mathrm{i}}^2 > 0\). From the first equation \(a_0 = 2\zeta_{\mathrm{i}}\omega_{\mathrm{i}} - a_1\omega_{\mathrm{i}}^2\), which after bringing to a common denominator gives \(a_0\) of equation (10.57).

Source: CK (10.77)-(10.78) (PDF p. 321). The expressions for \(a_0\) and \(a_1\) are the solution of a system of two equations (checked with SymPy), they are not written in the source.

Expression (10.56) has two parts. The term \(a_0/(2\omega_{\mathrm{r}})\) falls with frequency, the term \(a_1\omega_{\mathrm{r}}/2\) rises. The first belongs to \(a_0 \mat M\), which acts on every mass \(m_{\mathrm{i}}\) with the force \(-a_0 m_{\mathrm{i}}\dot q_{\mathrm{i}}\), as if every mass were connected to the resting surroundings by a damper. The second belongs to \(a_1 \mat K\), which is like a damper in parallel with every spring. Such dampers do not exist in reality, but the matrix is simple and the computation with it is transparent.

Frame A has \(\omega_1 = 19{,}578\) 1/s and \(\omega_2 = 51{,}257\) 1/s, and its modal matrix (in kg\(^{-1/2}\)) is \(\mat\Phi = \begin{pmatrix} 0{,}023511 & 0{,}038042 \\ 0{,}038042 & -0{,}023511 \end{pmatrix}\). We want \(\zeta_1 = \zeta_2 = 0{,}02\), a value inside the range from \(0{,}01\) to \(0{,}1\) given by CK. Equation (10.57) gives \(a_0 = 0{,}56668\) 1/s and \(a_1 = 5{,}6469\cdot 10^{-4}\) s. The damping matrix is

\[\mat C = a_0 \mat M + a_1 \mat K = \begin{pmatrix} 850{,}02 & -283{,}34 \\ -283{,}34 & 566{,}68 \end{pmatrix} \text{N s/m} ,\]

and the computation confirms that \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(0{,}7831,\ 2{,}0503)\) 1/s, the off-diagonal elements are below \(10^{-15}\). Check: \(2\cdot 0{,}02\cdot 19{,}578 = 0{,}7831\) and \(2\cdot 0{,}02\cdot 51{,}257 = 2{,}0503\). Between the two modes the damping ratio is smaller than \(0{,}02\). It is smallest at \(\omega = \sqrt{a_0/a_1} = \sqrt{\omega_1\omega_2} = 31{,}678\) 1/s (that is \(5{,}042\) Hz), where it equals \(\sqrt{a_0 a_1} = 0{,}01789\), and outside the interval between \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) it grows (figure 10.27). A mode at \(\omega = 300\) 1/s would already have \(\zeta = 0{,}0856\). Rayleigh damping therefore damps higher modes more strongly. This is not a property of the structure but a consequence of the formula, and we must check it by measuring the damping ratios.

With two constants we can prescribe two damping ratios. For \(n = 3\) this is not enough. Take a frame with three equal storeys (mass \(500\) kg, storey stiffness \(k = 501\,760\) N/m, section 10.3), which has \(\omega = 14{,}098\), \(39{,}502\) and \(57{,}082\) 1/s. If we fit Rayleigh damping to \(\zeta_1 = \zeta_3 = 0{,}02\), we get \(a_0 = 0{,}45224\) 1/s, \(a_1 = 5{,}6195\cdot 10^{-4}\) s and \(\zeta_2 = 0{,}01682\) by equation (10.56). The second mode is not free. For all three modes at once we need another form of the matrix.

Definition 10.47 Modal damping (modalno dušenje)

Let \(\mat\Phi\) be the modal matrix of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) with positive \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) and let \(\zeta_1, \dots, \zeta_{\mathrm{n}} \ge 0\) be arbitrary numbers. Modal damping (modalno dušenje) with damping ratios \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\) is the matrix

\[\mat C = \mat M\mat\Phi\,\mathrm{diag}(2\zeta_1\omega_1, \dots, 2\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\omega_{\mathrm{n}})\,\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M . \tag{10.58}\]

Source: CK (10.79)-(10.84) (PDF pp. 322-323), where the same formula is derived from \(\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat\Phi^{\T}\mat M\).

Lemma 10.48 Modal damping is classical damping (modalno dušenje je klasično dušenje)

The matrix (10.58) is classical damping with damping ratios \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\). Every classical damping with these damping ratios has the form (10.58).

Proof

We must show both directions, each in one step.

  1. If \(\mat C\) is given by equation (10.58), then \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi = (\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\mat\Phi)\,\mathrm{diag}(2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}})\,(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\mat\Phi) = \mathrm{diag}(2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}})\), because \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\mat\Phi = \mat I\) (lemma 10.16). The matrix \(\mat C\) is symmetric, because \(\mat M\) and the diagonal matrix are symmetric, and positive semidefinite: \(\vek v^{\T} \mat C\vek v = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} 2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T} \mat M\vek v)^2 \ge 0\) for every column \(\vek v\) (we write \(\mat C = \mat M\mat\Phi\,\mathrm{diag}(2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}})\,(\mat M\mat\Phi)^{\T}\) and the sum is a quadratic form in the column \(\mat\Phi^{\T}\mat M\vek v\)). By definition 10.44 it is classical damping.
  2. If \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi = \mat D\) is diagonal, we use \(\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\) (lemma 10.16) and its transpose \(\mat\Phi^{-\T} = \mat M\mat\Phi\). From \(\mat C = \mat\Phi^{-\T} \mat D\,\mat\Phi^{-1}\) it follows that \(\mat C = \mat M\mat\Phi\,\mat D\,\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. CK (10.81)-(10.84) (PDF pp. 322-323) derives the formula in direction 2.

Classical and modal damping are therefore the same set of matrices, with different starting points: for classical damping we have the matrix \(\mat C\) and read \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\) from it, for modal damping we choose \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\) and build \(\mat C\) from them. For three storeys with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0{,}02\) in all three modes we get

\[\mat C = \begin{pmatrix} 858{,}20 & -251{,}63 & -54{,}66 \\ -251{,}63 & 803{,}55 & -306{,}29 \\ -54{,}66 & -306{,}29 & 551{,}91 \end{pmatrix} \text{N s/m} .\]

The element \(C_{13} = -54{,}66\) N s/m says that we would have to connect the first and the third floor with a damper that the frame does not have: the force on floor \(1\) from the dampers between the ground and floor \(1\) and between floors \(1\) and \(2\) is determined only by the velocities of floors \(1\) and \(2\). Modal damping is mathematically convenient, but physically we cannot always build it from dampers. It is a computation with prescribed damping ratios, not a prediction of dampers.

10.9.2 Modal superposition (modalna superpozicija)

With classical damping every mode behaves as an oscillator of chapter 9. Let us write this as a theorem that combines existence and uniqueness of the solution, the decoupling and the formula.

Theorem 10.49 Modal superposition (modalna superpozicija)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric positive definite matrix, \(\mat M\) a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\), \(\mat\Phi\) their modal matrix and \(\mat C\) classical damping with damping ratios \(0 \le \zeta_{\mathrm{r}} < 1\). Let \(\vek Q\) be a column of piecewise continuous functions on \([0, T]\). Denote \(\omega_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{r}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}\sqrt{1 - \zeta_{\mathrm{r}}^2}\) and \(\boldsymbol\eta = \mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M \vek q\). Solutions are understood as in section 9.4.4, for each component.

  1. The function \(\vek q\) solves the equation \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C\dot{\vek q} + \mat K \vek q = \vek Q(t)\) if and only if for every \(r = 1, \dots, n\)
    \[\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + 2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T} \vek Q(t) . \tag{10.59}\]
  2. For given columns \(\vek q(0)\) and \(\dot{\vek q}(0)\) a solution exists and is unique, \(\vek q(t) = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^n\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(t)\), with \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T} \mat M \vek q(0)\) and \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T} \mat M\dot{\vek q}(0)\).
  3. For \(t \in [0, T]\)
    \[\begin{aligned} &\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(t) = \mathrm{e}^{-\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t}\Big(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\cos\omega_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{r}}t \\ &\quad + \frac{\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0) + \zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)}{\omega_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{r}}}\sin\omega_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{r}}t\Big) \\ &\quad + \int_0^t h_{\mathrm{r}}(t - s)\,\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T} \vek Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s . \end{aligned} \tag{10.60}\]
    where \(h_{\mathrm{r}}(u) = \mathrm{e}^{-\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}} u}\sin(\omega_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{r}}u)/\omega_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{r}}\).
Proof

We must show that the substitution \(\vek q = \mat\Phi\boldsymbol\eta\) is invertible, that it decouples the equations, and that every row falls under the theorems of chapter 9.

  1. By lemma 10.16, \(\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\), so \(\boldsymbol\eta = \mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M \vek q\) is uniquely determined by the column \(\vek q = \mat\Phi\boldsymbol\eta\). The components of \(\boldsymbol\eta\) are linear combinations of the components of \(\vek q\) and conversely, so \(\vek q\) is a solution in the sense of section 9.4.4 if and only if \(\boldsymbol\eta\) is.
  2. Insert \(\vek q = \mat\Phi\boldsymbol\eta\) into the equation and multiply it from the left by \(\mat\Phi^{\T}\). The matrix \(\mat\Phi^{\T}\) is invertible, so the new equation is equivalent to the original. We get equation (10.53).
  3. Because of \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\mat\Phi = \mat I\), \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat K\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2)\) (lemma 10.16) and \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}})\) (definition 10.44), row \(r\) of equation (10.53) is exactly equation (10.59). This proves item 1.
  4. The initial values \(\vek q(0)\) and \(\dot{\vek q}(0)\) determine \(\boldsymbol\eta(0) = \mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M \vek q(0)\) and \(\dot{\boldsymbol\eta}(0) = \mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\dot{\vek q}(0)\) and conversely. Row \(r\) is a second-order equation with constant coefficients, the characteristic polynomial \(s^2 + 2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}} s + \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) has leading coefficient \(1 \ne 0\), and the right-hand side \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T} \vek Q\) is piecewise continuous. By theorem 9.36 it has exactly one solution for given \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\) and \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\). The function \(\vek q = \mat\Phi\boldsymbol\eta\) built from these solutions is, by step 3, a solution of the original equation. If \(\tilde{\vek q}\) is another solution with the same initial values, the rows for \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\eta} = \mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\tilde{\vek q}\) solve the same equations with the same initial values, so \(\tilde{\boldsymbol\eta} = \boldsymbol\eta\) and \(\tilde{\vek q} = \mat\Phi\tilde{\boldsymbol\eta} = \vek q\). This proves item 2.
  5. Row \(r\) is the equation of chapter 9 with \(m = 1\), \(k = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\), \(c = 2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\), so with natural frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) and damping ratio \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} < 1\) (definition 9.5). Theorem 9.79 for \(t_0 = 0\) and \(m = 1\) gives \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \eta_{\mathrm{pr}} + \int_0^t h_{\mathrm{r}}(t - s)\,\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), where \(\eta_{\mathrm{pr}}\) is the free motion with the given initial values. By theorem 9.43 (the underdamped case) this is the first term of equation (10.60). This proves item 3.

Source: CK (11.8)-(11.18) (PDF pp. 344-346), (11.34) (PDF p. 360), GR section 2.7 (PDF pp. 109-113, undamped: normal equations (2.105), initial conditions (2.107), Duhamel integral (2.113)). The damped form with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\) is from CK. The proof of existence and uniqueness from theorem 9.36 for each row separately is not in the source.

The theorem showed that classical damping splits a problem of order \(n\) into \(n\) oscillators, each of which obeys everything we learned in chapter 9. Free damped vibration, the step response, beating and the harmonic response hold mode by mode. The force \(\vek Q\) enters mode \(r\) as the modal force \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T} \vek Q(t)\) (modalna sila): with weights that are the components of the mode.

Let us test the theorem on frame A with Rayleigh damping at \(\zeta_1 = \zeta_2 = 0{,}02\). On the upper floor a constant force of \(100\) N starts to act at \(t = 0\), and the frame was at rest until then. The static displacement is \(\vek q_{\mathrm{st}} = \mat K^{-1}\vek Q = (0{,}19930,\ 0{,}39860)\) mm (this is \(100\) N times the second column of the flexibility matrix \(\mat D\) of lemma 10.3: a force on floor \(2\) moves floor \(1\) by \(F/k\) and floor \(2\) by \(2F/k\)). The modal forces are \(f_1 = \varphi_{21}\cdot 100 = 3{,}8042\) and \(f_2 = \varphi_{22}\cdot 100 = -2{,}3511\) in units of N kg\(^{-1/2}\) (with \(\mat\Phi\) from the example above). By theorem 9.69 every mode has the response \(f_{\mathrm{r}}/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) multiplied by

\[g_{\mathrm{r}}(t) = 1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t}\Big(\cos\omega_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{r}}t + \frac{\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}}{\omega_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{r}}}\sin\omega_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{r}}t\Big) ,\]

which reaches at most \(1 + \mathrm{e}^{-\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\pi/\sqrt{1 - \zeta_{\mathrm{r}}^2}} = 1{,}9391\). The static displacement splits into the modal shares \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} f_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), that is, on floor \(1\) and on floor \(2\):

  • mode 1: \(0{,}23334\) mm on floor \(1\) and \(0{,}37756\) mm on floor \(2\), that is \(1{,}1708\) and \(0{,}9472\) of the static displacement,
  • mode 2: \(-0{,}03404\) mm on floor \(1\) and \(0{,}02104\) mm on floor \(2\), that is \(-0{,}1708\) and \(0{,}0528\) of the static displacement.

The sum is the static displacement. The largest displacement of floor \(2\) is \(0{,}76160\) mm, that is \(1{,}9107\) times the static displacement. Here the shares are positive and add up to \(1\), so \(q_2(t)/q_{2,\mathrm{st}} = 0{,}9472\,g_1(t) + 0{,}0528\,g_2(t)\) is an average of the two \(g_{\mathrm{r}}\) and cannot exceed \(1{,}9391\). Floor \(1\), however, is surprising: its maximum is \(0{,}42100\) mm, that is \(2{,}1124\) times the static displacement, at \(t = 0{,}1443\) s (figure 10.28). The maximum of twice the static displacement from theorem 9.69 holds for one oscillator, here it is exceeded, because floor \(1\) has shares with opposite signs. Mode 1 alone would give floor \(1\) the factor \(1{,}1708\cdot 1{,}9391 = 2{,}2703\) of the static displacement, because its share \(1{,}1708\) is larger than \(1\), the sum of both shares. Mode 2 has the share \(-0{,}1708\) and it reduces the sum. At the moment of the maximum of the sum \(g_1 = 1{,}892\) and \(g_2 = 0{,}601\), so the sum is \(1{,}1708\cdot 1{,}892 - 0{,}1708\cdot 0{,}601 = 2{,}1124\). The reduction is only \(0{,}1027\), not \(1{,}9391\cdot 0{,}1708 = 0{,}33\), because mode 2 is not at its maximum at this time: its period is \(0{,}1226\) s, so by \(0{,}1443\) s it has already fallen once to \(g_2 = 0{,}118\) and is rising again. For a sum with shares of opposite signs, twice the static displacement is therefore not an upper bound. The upper bound is the sum of the absolute values of the shares multiplied by \(1{,}9391\), here \((1{,}1708 + 0{,}1708)\cdot 1{,}9391 = 2{,}60\).

10.9.3 Damping that is not classical (dušenje, ki ni klasično)

What happens if the dampers are such that the matrix \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi\) is not diagonal? Take a single damper between the ground and floor \(1\), in parallel with the columns of the lower storey. The force on floor \(1\) is \(-c_{\mathrm{d}}\dot q_1\) and floor \(2\) does not feel it directly, so

\[\mat C = c_{\mathrm{d}}\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix} , \qquad \mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi = c_{\mathrm{d}}\begin{pmatrix} \varphi_{11}^2 & \varphi_{11}\varphi_{12} \\ \varphi_{11}\varphi_{12} & \varphi_{12}^2 \end{pmatrix} . \tag{10.61}\]

By \(\varphi_{\mathrm{ij}}\) we denote the element of \(\mat\Phi\) in row \(i\) and column \(j\), so \(\varphi_{11} = 0{,}023511\) and \(\varphi_{12} = 0{,}038042\) kg\(^{-1/2}\). Choose \(c_{\mathrm{d}}\) so that the diagonal element of the first mode is \(2\cdot 0{,}02\cdot\omega_1\), that is, \(c_{\mathrm{d}} = 2\cdot 0{,}02\,\omega_1/\varphi_{11}^2 = 1416{,}70\) N s/m. Then

\[\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi = \begin{pmatrix} 0{,}7831 & 1{,}2671 \\ 1{,}2671 & 2{,}0503 \end{pmatrix} \text{1/s} .\]

The diagonal is the same as for Rayleigh damping, since \(\varphi_{12}^2/\varphi_{11}^2 = 2{,}618 = \omega_2/\omega_1\) (the same golden number as in the ratio of frequencies in section 10.2), so \(\zeta_2 = 0{,}02\) as well. The off-diagonal element \(1{,}2671\) 1/s, however, is not small. It equals \(\sqrt{0{,}7831\cdot 2{,}0503}\), because the matrix has the form \(c_{\mathrm{d}}\,\vek b\vek b^{\T}\) with the column \(\vek b = (\varphi_{11}, \varphi_{12})^{\T}\), where the product of the diagonal elements \(c_{\mathrm{d}}\varphi_{11}^2\cdot c_{\mathrm{d}}\varphi_{12}^2\) equals the square of the off-diagonal one \((c_{\mathrm{d}}\varphi_{11}\varphi_{12})^2\). The modes are therefore coupled and theorem 10.49 cannot be used for this case, since it requires a diagonal matrix.

What remains of the modes? Let us try in the free equation \(\vek q = \mathrm{Re}(\vek u\,\mathrm{e}^{st})\) with a complex number \(s\) and a complex column \(\vek u \ne 0\) (theorem 9.28, lemma 9.32). The equation \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C\dot{\vek q} + \mat K \vek q = 0\) becomes

\[(s^2 \mat M + s \mat C + \mat K)\,\vek u = 0 . \tag{10.62}\]

With classical damping the solutions are \(\vek u = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(s = -\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}} \pm \mathrm{i}\,\omega_{\mathrm{d},\mathrm{r}}\). Here the columns \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) no longer solve the equation. The numbers \(s\) are the zeros of the determinant of the matrix \(s^2 \mat M + s\mat C + \mat K\) (definition 2.50), a polynomial of fourth degree in \(s\). We compute them with NumPy from the first-order form (zapis prvega reda), in which \(\vek q\) and \(\dot{\vek q}\) are collected into a column of \(2n = 4\) numbers. The matrix of this form is not symmetric, so the spectral theorem of section 10.3 does not apply to it. The roots are \(-0{,}39177 \pm 19{,}58141\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(-1{,}02493 \pm 51{,}2281\,\mathrm{i}\) 1/s, and the damping ratios \(-\mathrm{Re}\,s/|s|\) are both \(0{,}0200\). With classical damping and the same damping ratios they would be \(-0{,}39157 \pm 19{,}5744\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(-1{,}02513 \pm 51{,}2464\,\mathrm{i}\), which differs in the fourth digit. Frequencies and decay hardly change. The shape of the motion changes.

The columns \(\vek u\) for the two roots with positive imaginary part have a complex ratio between the floors: \(u_2/u_1 = 1{,}61696 + 0{,}04000\,\mathrm{i}\) for the first and \(-0{,}61696 + 0{,}04000\,\mathrm{i}\) for the second. With classical damping the ratios are real, \(1{,}61803\) and \(-0{,}61803\). The ratio \(1{,}61696 + 0{,}04000\,\mathrm{i}\) has modulus \(1{,}61745\) and argument \(1{,}417^\circ\). The real solution \(\vek q = \mathrm{Re}(\vek u\,\mathrm{e}^{st})\) then has the floors with a phase shift of \(1{,}417^\circ\): floor \(2\) leads floor \(1\) by \(1{,}417/360 = 0{,}39\,\%\) of the period, that is \(1{,}26\) ms at \(T = 0{,}3209\) s, so the floors do not pass through zero together (figure 10.29). Such a solution is called a complex mode (kompleksni način). With classical damping the floors are always in phase or in antiphase, as in section 10.2.

How large is the error if we nevertheless neglect the coupling, that is, use classical damping with the same diagonal of \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi\)? This is the matrix \(\mat C\) of the Rayleigh damping from the example above. We compare the response to the force \(100\) N \(\cos\Omega t\) on floor \(2\). Try \(\vek q = \mathrm{Re}(\vek x\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t})\) as in theorem 9.52: differentiation becomes multiplication by \(\mathrm{i}\Omega\) and we get two complex linear equations

\[(\mat K - \Omega^2 \mat M + \mathrm{i}\Omega \mat C)\,\vek x = \vek Q_0 , \tag{10.63}\]

which we solve with NumPy for every \(\Omega\) (the general relation between force and response is treated in the next section). The largest amplitude of the upper floor near \(\omega_1\) is \(9{,}4445\) mm with the coupling and \(9{,}4418\) mm without it, that is, \(-0{,}029\,\%\). Near \(\omega_2\) it is \(0{,}5418\) mm with the coupling and \(0{,}5337\) mm without it, \(-1{,}50\,\%\).

Why is the error at \(\omega_1\) so small and at \(\omega_2\) fifty times larger? At \(\Omega = \omega_1\) the modal coordinate \(\eta_2\) is small and in phase with the force, so the coupling term \(\tilde c_{12}\Omega\eta_2\) in the equation for \(\eta_1\) is only \(2{,}5\,\%\) of the term \(\tilde c_{11}\Omega\eta_1\) (the notation \(\tilde c_{\mathrm{rs}}\) means the element \((\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi)_{\mathrm{rs}}\)). In addition, the coupling term lies in the complex plane perpendicular to the force, so it changes the modulus of the sum only in second order: \(\tfrac12\cdot 0{,}025^2 = 0{,}03\,\%\). At \(\Omega = \omega_2\) it is just the opposite: at resonance mode \(2\) is excited and its velocity drives mode \(1\) with \(38\,\%\) of the modal force \(f_1\). Mode \(1\) is off resonance at this frequency, but it contributes \(0{,}089\) mm of the \(0{,}540\) mm of the upper floor (\(16{,}5\,\%\)), and the coupling changes its amplitude by \(38\,\%\). The computed effect on the floor is nevertheless only \(1{,}5\,\%\): at \(\omega_2\) the contribution of mode \(1\) on floor \(2\) is in quadrature (a phase difference of \(90^\circ\)) with the contribution of mode \(2\), so the modulus changes only in second order, \(\tfrac12\cdot 0{,}165^2 = 1{,}4\,\%\). The coupling is therefore not small in the matrix (\(1{,}2671\) against \(0{,}78\) and \(2{,}05\)), but it is small in its effect, because the modes at different frequencies (\(2{,}6\) times apart) do not meet in resonance. We must be careful where the response itself is small: at \(7{,}130\) Hz the upper floor has \(0{,}0250\) mm with the coupling and \(0{,}0150\) mm without it, a relatively large difference at a small amplitude.

For systems whose damping is not classical and where such errors are not acceptable, we need the first-order form and complex modes in full. This theory requires the eigenproblem of a nonsymmetric matrix of order \(2n\), which the spectral theorem of section 10.3 does not cover, and it is in chapter 20. The other way out is numerical solution in time, which does not need modes and which one of the following sections treats.

10.9.4 Truncation of modes (odrez načinov)

For large systems we do not use all \(n\) modes. Bar C of section 10.7 has \(16\) modes with \(16\) finite elements, and a model of a structure can have more than a million (CK PDF 344). If we keep the \(N\) lowest modes, the sum \(\vek q = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^N\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\) is no longer exact. How large is the error? Higher modes respond statically to a slow force: the harmonic response of a mode at \(\Omega \ll \omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) is close to \(f_{\mathrm{r}}/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) (theorem 9.52). We therefore need to know how much of the static displacement falls on each mode.

Lemma 10.50 Flexibility matrix by modes (podajnostna matrika po načinih)

Let \(\mat K\) be a symmetric positive definite matrix, \(\mat M\) a symmetric positive definite matrix of order \(n\) and \(\mat\Phi\) their modal matrix. Then

\[\mat K^{-1} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^n\frac{\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}} . \tag{10.64}\]
Proof

We must show that the right-hand side is a matrix that gives \(\mat I\) when multiplied by \(\mat K\).

  1. From \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\mat\Phi = \mat I\) it follows that \(\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat\Phi^{\T}\mat M\), so \(\mat\Phi\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M = \mat I\) and \(\mat\Phi\mat\Phi^{\T} = \mat M^{-1}\).
  2. From \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat K\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}) =: \Lambda_{\mathrm{d}}\) (the matrix with \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) on the diagonal) it follows that \(\mat K = \mat\Phi^{-\T}\Lambda_{\mathrm{d}}\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat M\mat\Phi\Lambda_{\mathrm{d}}\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\), where we used \(\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\) and \(\mat\Phi^{-\T} = \mat M\mat\Phi\).
  3. Let \(\mat B = \mat\Phi\Lambda_{\mathrm{d}}^{-1}\mat\Phi^{\T}\), the matrix with the sum on the right-hand side of equation (10.64) (it exists, because \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\mat K\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) by definition 6.27, since \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} \ne \vek 0\)). Then \(\mat K\mat B = \mat M\mat\Phi\Lambda_{\mathrm{d}}(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat M\mat\Phi)\Lambda_{\mathrm{d}}^{-1}\mat\Phi^{\T} = \mat M\mat\Phi\mat\Phi^{\T} = \mat M \mat M^{-1} = \mat I\) by step 1. By definition 1.107, \(\mat B = \mat K^{-1}\).

Source: The proof is not from a source.

For a static force \(\vek F\) the displacement is therefore \(\mat K^{-1}\vek F = \sum_{\mathrm{r}}\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F)/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). Mode \(r\) contributes \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\T}\vek F)/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). This is the static share that we computed above for frame A, and it falls as \(1/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\).

Bar C: steel, \(L = 1\) m, \(A = 100\) mm\(^2\), clamped at \(x = 0\), free at \(x = L\), \(16\) equal elements with the mass matrix of lemma 10.31. A force of \(1\) kN acts on the free end. The static displacement of the end is \(FL/(EA) = 51{,}0204\) µm. The share of mode \(r\) in the displacement of the end is \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)^2F/\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), where \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)\) is the last component of the column \(\boldsymbol\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\), and with one, two, three, five and all sixteen modes it is

\[81{,}12\,\%,\quad 90{,}19\,\%,\quad 93{,}50\,\%,\quad 96{,}29\,\%,\quad 100\,\%\]

of the static displacement (figure 10.30). The first mode thus gives \(81{,}12\,\%\), the other fifteen modes together the remaining \(18{,}88\,\%\). Why does the sum approach so slowly? With the normalization \(\mat\Phi^{\T}\mat M\mat\Phi = \mat I\) we have \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}(L)^2\rho A L = 2{,}003,\ 2{,}029,\ 2{,}082\) for \(r = 1, 2, 3\), so almost constant: all modes have about the same value at the free end. The eigenvalues, however, grow like \((2r-1)^2\), since \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}/\lambda_1\) divided by \((2r-1)^2\) equals \(1{,}000\), \(1{,}006\) and \(1{,}019\) (the frequencies of the bar are close to \((2r-1)\,c/(4L)\), section 10.7). So the shares fall like \(1/(2r-1)^2\): \(81{,}12\,\%\), \(9{,}07\,\%\), \(3{,}31\,\%\), \(1{,}72\,\%\) and \(1{,}07\,\%\). The sum of the remaining shares for \(r > N\) is approximately proportional to \(1/N\), which can be seen from \(18{,}88\,\%\) at \(N = 1\) and \(3{,}71\,\%\) at \(N = 5\) (ratio \(5{,}1\), prediction \(5\)). With ten modes the error is still \(1{,}33\,\%\).

The error does not come from damping or from fast motions, but from the fact that higher modes respond statically to every slow force, and truncation loses these shares. Craig and Kurdila call the solution with the kept modes the mode-displacement solution (rešitev z odmiki načinov) and write that it can give an inaccurate result even under static loading, because the series converges slowly (CK §11.4, PDF 367). The improved mode-acceleration solution (rešitev s pospeški načinov) adds to the truncated modes their static part, computed directly (pseudostatic response, CK (11.40), PDF 361). This improvement, the effective modal mass and the additional mass method are only named, they are treated in chapter 21. For bar C the displacement of the end under a static force is known directly (\(FL/(EA)\)), so truncation here is only an example of slow convergence.

The section showed three things. With classical damping (a diagonal matrix \(\mat\Phi^{\T} \mat C\mat\Phi\), obtained by Rayleigh's choice or by chosen \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\)) every mode remains an oscillator of chapter 9 (theorem 10.49), which we proved by the substitution \(\vek q = \mat\Phi\boldsymbol\eta\). With damping that is not classical the modes couple and become complex, but for frame A the error of the resonance peaks is \(0{,}03\,\%\) and \(1{,}5\,\%\), because modes with a frequency ratio of \(2{,}6\) do not meet in resonance.
