With truncation of modes the error decreases only as \(1/N\), because higher modes contribute a static part. Section 10.10 computes the response to harmonic excitation from the modal sum.

10.10 Harmonic excitation and the frequency response matrix (harmonično vzbujanje in matrika frekvenčnega odziva)

We attach a shaker (stresalnik) to the upper floor of frame A from section 10.1, a machine that pushes it with the force \(100\ \text{N}\cdot\cos\Omega t\). The frame has two rigid floors of mass \(m = 500\) kg, each storey has stiffness \(k = 501\,760\) N/m, so \(\mat M = m\mat I\) and \(\mat K = k\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), the coordinate \(q_1\) is the displacement of the lower floor and \(q_2\) that of the upper floor. The damping is Rayleigh damping (definition 10.45) with damping ratio \(\zeta = 0{,}02\) in both modes, \(a_0 = 0{,}56668\) 1/s and \(a_1 = 5{,}6469\cdot 10^{-4}\) s (section 10.9). The natural frequencies of the frame are \(3{,}116\) and \(8{,}158\) Hz. We ask two questions. How far does each floor move at each shaker frequency? And why does one of the floors stand still at some frequency although we push it with \(100\) N?

For a single oscillator in section 9.6 we obtained the response with the complex notation. The cosine is the real part of a complex exponential function, and the derivative of that function is only a product with \(\mathrm{i}\Omega\) (theorem 9.28), so the differential equation for \(q = Z\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) turns into an ordinary equation for the number \(Z\). We do the same with a column. A complex column (kompleksen stolpec) is a column with complex elements, a complex matrix is a matrix with complex elements, and we compute the product as for real ones (definition 1.98), with addition and multiplication of complex numbers. The real part of a column \(\vek z\) is the column of the real parts of its elements, \(\mathrm{Re}\,\vek z\), and the derivative of a column is the column of derivatives. For a real matrix \(\mat A\) we have \(\mathrm{Re}(\mat A\vek z) = \mat A\,\mathrm{Re}\,\vek z\), because the element \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}}z_{\mathrm{j}}\) is a sum of products of real and complex numbers and its real part is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\mathrm{Re}\,z_{\mathrm{j}}\). We try \(\vek q = \vek z\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) with a constant complex column \(\vek z\). Each derivative multiplies by \(\mathrm{i}\Omega\), and the equation \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek Q_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\) becomes \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M + \mathrm{i}\Omega\mat C)\,\vek z = \vek Q_0\). For \(n = 1\) the matrix in brackets has the form \(k - m\Omega^2 + \mathrm{i}\,c\,\Omega\), which is the characteristic polynomial from section 9.6 at \(s = \mathrm{i}\Omega\). Its inverse gets a name.

Definition 10.51 Frequency response matrix (matrika frekvenčnega odziva)

Let \(\mat M\), \(\mat K\) and \(\mat C\) be real matrices of order \(n\) as in theorem 10.2 and \(\Omega > 0\) a circular frequency. The complex matrix of order \(n\)

\[\mat S(\Omega) = \mat K - \Omega^2\mat M + \mathrm{i}\,\Omega\,\mat C \tag{10.65}\]

is the dynamic stiffness matrix (dinamična togostna matrika). If it has an inverse matrix (definition 1.107), the frequency response matrix is

\[\mat H(\Omega) = \mat S(\Omega)^{-1} = \big(\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M + \mathrm{i}\,\Omega\,\mat C\big)^{-1} . \tag{10.66}\]

It is a complex matrix of order \(n\), its element \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}(\Omega)\) has the unit of the coordinate \(q_{\mathrm{i}}\) divided by the unit of the force \(Q_{\mathrm{j}}\), for displacements m/N. For \(n = 1\) it is the frequency response of definition 9.51.

Source: GR, equations (2.80) to (2.83) (PDF p. 102): GR writes the matrix \(\mat K - \omega^2\mat M\) without damping and calls it the impedance matrix or dynamic stiffness matrix, and its inverse the admittance matrix or dynamic flexibility. The term with \(\mat C\) is not from the source. CK, equation (11.31) (PDF p. 350) gives the element \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) as a sum over the modes, as in theorem 10.53.

When does the inverse matrix exist? We wrote the proof of lemma 8.21 on a matrix with a full set of pivots for real matrices, but it uses only addition, multiplication and division by a number that is not zero (in step 2 we divide by \(U_{\mathrm{kk}}\)), and these operations obey the same rules for complex numbers (lemma 9.20). So the lemma holds word for word also for complex matrices and columns, including the last claim about the transposed matrix. We use it for \(\mat S(\Omega)\).

Lemma 10.52 Existence of the frequency response matrix (obstoj matrike frekvenčnega odziva)

Let \(\mat M\) be a symmetric positive definite, \(\mat K\) a symmetric and \(\mat C\) a symmetric positive semidefinite real matrix of order \(n\) and \(\Omega > 0\). The matrix \(\mat S(\Omega)\) has no inverse matrix exactly when there is a real column \(\vek\varphi \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat K\vek\varphi = \Omega^2\mat M\vek\varphi\) and \(\mat C\vek\varphi = \vek 0\).

Proof

We must show both directions. For the inverse we use lemma 8.21 for complex matrices, and for the other direction the real and imaginary parts of the equation \(\mat S\vek w = \vek 0\).

  1. If \(\vek\varphi\) is real, \(\vek\varphi \neq \vek 0\), \(\mat K\vek\varphi = \Omega^2\mat M\vek\varphi\) and \(\mat C\vek\varphi = \vek 0\), then \(\mat S\vek\varphi = \mat K\vek\varphi - \Omega^2\mat M\vek\varphi + \mathrm{i}\Omega\mat C\vek\varphi = \vek 0\). If \(\mat S\) had an inverse matrix, we would have \(\vek\varphi = \mat S^{-1}\mat S\vek\varphi = \vek 0\), which is false, so it has none.
  2. Conversely let \(\mat S\) have no inverse matrix. By lemma 8.21 there is a complex column \(\vek w \neq \vek 0\) with \(\mat S\vek w = \vek 0\). Write \(\vek w = \vek x + \mathrm{i}\vek y\) with real columns \(\vek x\), \(\vek y\), not both zero.
  3. Multiply \(\mat S\vek w = \vek 0\) from the left by the row \(\bar{\vek w}^\T = \vek x^\T - \mathrm{i}\vek y^\T\). For a real symmetric matrix \(\mat A\) we have \(\bar{\vek w}^\T\mat A\vek w = \vek x^\T\mat A\vek x + \vek y^\T\mat A\vek y + \mathrm{i}\,(\vek x^\T\mat A\vek y - \vek y^\T\mat A\vek x)\) and the last bracket is zero, because \(\vek y^\T\mat A\vek x = (\vek x^\T\mat A^\T\vek y)^\T = \vek x^\T\mat A\vek y\) is a number. Hence
    \[0 = \big(\vek x^\T\mat K\vek x + \vek y^\T\mat K\vek y\big) - \Omega^2\big(\vek x^\T\mat M\vek x + \vek y^\T\mat M\vek y\big) + \mathrm{i}\,\Omega\big(\vek x^\T\mat C\vek x + \vek y^\T\mat C\vek y\big) .\]
  4. The imaginary part is zero: \(\Omega\,(\vek x^\T\mat C\vek x + \vek y^\T\mat C\vek y) = 0\). Since \(\Omega > 0\) and both terms are nonnegative (\(\mat C\) is positive semidefinite), \(\vek x^\T\mat C\vek x = 0 = \vek y^\T\mat C\vek y\), so by lemma 7.16 \(\mat C\vek x = \vek 0\) and \(\mat C\vek y = \vek 0\).
  5. Therefore \(\mat S\vek w = (\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M)\vek w = \vek 0\). The matrix \(\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M\) is real, so its product with \(\vek w\) splits into the real part \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M)\vek x\) and the imaginary part \((\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M)\vek y\), both zero. One of \(\vek x\), \(\vek y\) is not zero, and it is the wanted \(\vek\varphi\).

Source: The lemma is not from a source.

The lemma says when the frequency response matrix is missing. Without damping (\(\mat C = \mat 0\)) it is missing at \(\Omega^2 = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\), that is at every natural frequency, which is resonance. With a damper it is missing only if the damper has no force on a natural mode, \(\mat C\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek 0\). For system A with Rayleigh damping \(\mat C\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = (a_0 + a_1\lambda_{\mathrm{r}})\mat M\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} \neq \vek 0\), so \(\mat H(\Omega)\) exists at every frequency.

What does the matrix tell us about the motion? The answer is a theorem. It states that the response to a harmonic force is the complex product \(\mat H\vek Q_0\), that every initial condition in addition dies out, and that the element \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) equals \(H_{\mathrm{ji}}\).

Theorem 10.53 Response to a harmonic force with several degrees of freedom (odziv na harmonično silo pri več prostostnih stopnjah)

Let \(\mat M\), \(\mat K\) and \(\mat C\) be as in lemma 10.52, \(\vek Q_0\) a complex column with \(n\) elements, \(\Omega > 0\), and let \(\mat S(\Omega)\) have an inverse matrix. For the equation

\[\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \mathrm{Re}\big(\vek Q_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big) \tag{10.67}\]

the following holds:

  1. The column \(\vek q_{\mathrm{p}}(t) = \mathrm{Re}\big(\mat H(\Omega)\,\vek Q_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\big)\) is a solution.
  2. Every solution of equation (10.67) is \(\vek q_{\mathrm{p}}\) plus a solution of the free equation \(\mat M\ddot{\vek x} + \mat C\dot{\vek x} + \mat K\vek x = \vek 0\), and every such sum is a solution.
  3. The matrix \(\mat H(\Omega)\) is symmetric, \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} = H_{\mathrm{ji}}\).
  4. Let \(\mat K\) be positive definite as well, \(\mat C\) classical damping (definition 10.44) with all ratios \(0 < \zeta_{\mathrm{r}} < 1\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} = \sqrt{\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}}\). Then \(\mat H(\Omega)\) exists at every \(\Omega > 0\),
    \[\mat H(\Omega) = \sum_{\mathrm{r}=1}^{n} \frac{\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T}{\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2 - \Omega^2 + 2\mathrm{i}\,\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Omega} , \tag{10.68}\]
    and for every solution \(\vek q\) of equation (10.67) we have \(\vek q(t) - \vek q_{\mathrm{p}}(t) \to \vek 0\) as \(t \to \infty\).
Proof

We must show that the complex column solves the complex equation, that its real part solves the real one, that the difference of two solutions is a free motion, and that the matrix is symmetric. Then the modal matrix \(\mat\Phi\) diagonalizes \(\mat S\), and the free motion dies out in modal coordinates.

  1. Let \(\vek z(t) = \mat H(\Omega)\,\vek Q_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\). By theorem 9.28 \(\dot{\vek z} = \mathrm{i}\Omega\,\vek z\) and \(\ddot{\vek z} = -\Omega^2\vek z\), since the derivative of a column is the column of derivatives and the constant complex factor stays.
  2. Substitute: \(\mat M\ddot{\vek z} + \mat C\dot{\vek z} + \mat K\vek z = (\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M + \mathrm{i}\Omega\mat C)\,\vek z = \mat S\,\mat H\,\vek Q_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t} = \vek Q_0\,\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\Omega t}\), because \(\mat S\mat H = \mat I\).
  3. The matrices \(\mat M\), \(\mat C\), \(\mat K\) are real, so the real part of the left side equals \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{p}} + \mat C\dot{\vek q}_{\mathrm{p}} + \mat K\vek q_{\mathrm{p}}\) with \(\vek q_{\mathrm{p}} = \mathrm{Re}\,\vek z\) (the real part of a product with a real matrix is the matrix times the real part, as we said before the definition, and the real part of a derivative is the derivative of the real part, definition 9.29). The real part of the right side is the force. This proves point 1.
  4. If \(\vek q\) and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{p}}\) are solutions, the difference \(\vek x = \vek q - \vek q_{\mathrm{p}}\) is a solution of the free equation, because the left side is linear in \(\vek q\). Conversely the sum \(\vek q_{\mathrm{p}} + \vek x\) is a solution if \(\vek x\) is a solution of the free equation. This is point 2.
  5. The matrices \(\mat K\), \(\mat M\), \(\mat C\) are symmetric, so \(\mat S^\T = \mat S\). By the last claim of lemma 8.21 (for complex matrices) \(\mat H = \mat S^{-1} = (\mat S^\T)^{-1} = (\mat S^{-1})^\T = \mat H^\T\). This is point 3.
  6. For point 4 we use the modal matrix of definition 10.15, \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat M\mat\Phi = \mat I\) and \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat K\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_{\mathrm{n}})\) (lemma 10.16), and the classical damping \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat C\mat\Phi = \mathrm{diag}(2\zeta_1\omega_1, \dots, 2\zeta_{\mathrm{n}}\omega_{\mathrm{n}})\). Then \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat S\mat\Phi = \mat B\) with diagonal elements \(B_{\mathrm{rr}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2 - \Omega^2 + 2\mathrm{i}\,\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Omega\). The imaginary part \(2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Omega\) is positive, so \(B_{\mathrm{rr}} \neq 0\) and \(\mat B\) has the inverse matrix \(\mat B^{-1} = \mathrm{diag}(1/B_{\mathrm{rr}})\).
  7. From \(\mat\Phi^{-1} = \mat\Phi^\T\mat M\) (lemma 10.16) we get \(\mat\Phi\mat\Phi^\T\mat M = \mat I\), so \(\mat\Phi\mat\Phi^\T = \mat M^{-1}\) and \(\mat M\mat\Phi\mat\Phi^\T = \mat I\). Multiply \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat S\mat\Phi = \mat B\) from the left by \(\mat M\mat\Phi\). We get \(\mat S\mat\Phi = \mat M\mat\Phi\mat B\).
  8. Let \(\mat X = \mat\Phi\mat B^{-1}\mat\Phi^\T\). By step 7, \(\mat S\mat X = \mat M\mat\Phi\,\mat B\mat B^{-1}\mat\Phi^\T = \mat M\mat\Phi\mat\Phi^\T = \mat I\). The matrix \(\mat X\) is symmetric, because \(\mat B^{-1}\) is diagonal, so by lemma 1.101 \(\mat X\mat S = (\mat S^\T\mat X^\T)^\T = (\mat S\mat X)^\T = \mat I\). So \(\mat S\) is invertible with inverse matrix \(\mat X\) at every \(\Omega > 0\). The element \((i, j)\) of \(\mat X\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}} \varphi_{\mathrm{ir}}\varphi_{\mathrm{jr}}/B_{\mathrm{rr}}\), which is (10.68).
  9. Let \(\vek q\) be a solution, \(\vek x = \vek q - \vek q_{\mathrm{p}}\) the free motion by point 2 and \(\vek\eta = \mat\Phi^\T\mat M\vek x\) its modal coordinates. By theorem 10.49 (at zero force) every solution \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\) solves \(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + 2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}}\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\), which is the free motion of an oscillator with \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\). By theorem 9.52, point 3, \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}}(t) \to 0\). Hence \(\vek x = \mat\Phi\vek\eta = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}} \to \vek 0\).

Source: GR, equations (2.80) to (2.85) (PDF pp. 102-103): the frequency response matrix and its expansion in the undamped modes. CK, equations (11.30) and (11.31) (PDF pp. 349-350): \(\overline{H}_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{r}} \phi_{\mathrm{ir}}\phi_{\mathrm{jr}}/K_{\mathrm{r}} \cdot 1/((1 - r_{\mathrm{r}}^2) + \mathrm{i}\,2\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} r_{\mathrm{r}})\), in our case with modes normalized by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = 1\), where \(K_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) is the modal stiffness. The symmetry in step 5 and the convergence in step 9 are not from the source.

The proof showed three things. The steady response is a single cosine in each coordinate with amplitude \(|(\mat H\vek Q_0)_{\mathrm{i}}|\) and phase \(\arg(\mat H\vek Q_0)_{\mathrm{i}}\), so the phasor of the displacement in coordinate \(i\) is the complex number \((\mat H\vek Q_0)_{\mathrm{i}}\) (phasors from section 9.6). The free motion that joins the steady response because of the initial values dies out, because each mode is an oscillator from chapter 9 with its own damping ratio. And the matrix \(\mat H\) is a sum of \(n\) simple terms, one for each mode. For a force \(F\) on coordinate \(j\) the amplitude of coordinate \(i\) is \(|H_{\mathrm{ij}}|\,F\), so we call \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) the response of coordinate \(i\) to a unit force in coordinate \(j\) at frequency \(\Omega\).

The symmetry \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} = H_{\mathrm{ji}}\) says that the response of coordinate \(i\) to a force in \(j\) equals the response of coordinate \(j\) to the same force in \(i\), in amplitude and in phase. This is dynamic reciprocity (dinamična vzajemnost), the vibration form of Maxwell's theorem (theorem 4.140), which Rayleigh extended, as the history box in chapter 4 says. At \(\Omega = 0\) we indeed have \(\mat H(0) = \mat K^{-1}\), the flexibility matrix \(\mat D\) of lemma 10.3, and the symmetry is the symmetry of the flexibility matrix. For system A, \(\mat H(0) = \frac{1}{k}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1{,}9930 & 1{,}9930 \\ 1{,}9930 & 3{,}9860 \end{bmatrix}\cdot 10^{-6}\) m/N. At \(\Omega = \omega_1 = 19{,}578\) 1/s we have \(|H_{12}| = |H_{21}| = 58{,}330\cdot 10^{-6}\) m/N and the difference \(|H_{12} - H_{21}|\) is \(7\cdot 10^{-21}\) m/N, which is the rounding error of the computer (numerical computation).

Example 10.54 Frame A under a shaker on the upper floor (okvir A pri stresalniku na zgornji plošči)

The force \(100\ \text{N}\cdot\cos\Omega t\) acts on the upper floor, so \(\vek Q_0 = (0, 100)^\T\) N. By theorem 10.53 the amplitudes of the floors are \(|H_{12}|\cdot 100\ \text{N}\) and \(|H_{22}|\cdot 100\ \text{N}\), and the lag of the upper floor is \(-\arg H_{22}\). The computation with \(\mat H = (\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M + \mathrm{i}\Omega\mat C)^{-1}\) (numerical computation) gives:

\(f = \Omega/(2\pi)\) (Hz) \(\vert q_1\vert\) (mm) \(\vert q_2\vert\) (mm) lag of \(q_2\)
\(0\) \(0{,}19930\) \(0{,}39860\) \(0^\circ\)
\(1{,}558\) \(0{,}27569\) \(0{,}52506\) \(1{,}48^\circ\)
\(3{,}116 = \omega_1/(2\pi)\) \(5{,}8330\) \(9{,}4394\) \(89{,}85^\circ\)
\(5{,}042\) \(0{,}19901\) \(0{,}19927\) \(176{,}93^\circ\)
\(7{,}130\) \(0{,}19717\) \(0{,}01496\) \(97{,}19^\circ\)
\(8{,}158 = \omega_2/(2\pi)\) \(0{,}85133\) \(0{,}53109\) \(96{,}97^\circ\)
\(12{,}237\) \(0{,}01105\) \(0{,}04298\) \(178{,}55^\circ\)
  1. At \(f = 0\) the force is slow, \(\mat H(0) = \mat K^{-1}\) and the floors move by the static displacements \(0{,}19930\) and \(0{,}39860\) mm, because each storey carries \(100\) N, so the lower one moves \(100/k = 0{,}19930\) mm and the upper one by as much again (matrix \(\mat D\) from section 10.1).
  2. At \(f = 3{,}116\) Hz, that is at \(\omega_1\), the upper floor swings by \(9{,}4394\) mm, which is \(23{,}7\) times the static displacement \(0{,}39860\) mm. The ratio \(|q_1|/|q_2| = 0{,}6179\) is almost exactly the ratio of the components of the first mode \(1/1{,}618034 = 0{,}6180\): near resonance the sum in equation (10.68) is dominated by the term \(r = 1\), which is \(\vek\varphi_1\,(\vek\varphi_1^\T\vek Q_0)\) times a scalar, so it has the shape of the mode, no matter where the shaker stands.
  3. At \(f = 8{,}158\) Hz the same holds for the second mode. The ratio of magnitudes \(|q_1|/|q_2| = 1{,}603\) is close to the ratio of the components of the second mode \(1{,}618\) and the floors move almost in opposite directions (the phases differ by \(189{,}7^\circ\)). The peak is lower, \(0{,}531\) mm, because the term \(r = 2\) equals \(\varphi_{22}^2/(2\zeta\lambda_2)\cdot 100\ \text{N} = 0{,}526\) mm, with \(\varphi_{22}^2 = 5{,}53\cdot 10^{-4}\) 1/kg instead of \(\varphi_{21}^2 = 1{,}447\cdot 10^{-3}\) 1/kg and \(\lambda_2 = 2627{,}25\) 1/s\(^2\) instead of \(383{,}31\) 1/s\(^2\). The rest up to \(0{,}531\) mm is added by the term of the first mode, which at \(\omega_2\) is real and adds at a right angle to the purely imaginary term \(r = 2\).
  4. At \(f = 12{,}237\) Hz, \(1{,}5\,\omega_2\), the excitation is above both frequencies, and the upper floor lags by almost \(180^\circ\) and moves only \(0{,}043\) mm. The inertia of the floors dominates the springs, as for the oscillator at \(r = 2\) in section 9.6.

At each resonance, then, one mode determines the motion. How exactly? We estimate the peak of the upper floor at \(\omega_1\) with a single term of the sum (10.68). The term \(r = 1\) at \(\Omega = \omega_1\) is purely imaginary, \(\varphi_{21}^2/(2\mathrm{i}\,\zeta\omega_1^2)\), with \(\varphi_{21} = 0{,}038042\) kg\(^{-1/2}\) its magnitude is \(\varphi_{21}^2/(2\zeta\lambda_1) = 0{,}0014472/(2\cdot 0{,}02\cdot 383{,}31) = 9{,}4389\cdot 10^{-5}\) m/N, which is \(9{,}4389\) mm at \(100\) N. The term of the second mode at \(\Omega = \omega_1\) is almost real, \(2{,}46\cdot 10^{-7}\) m/N, and adds to the first at a right angle in the complex plane, so it adds only \(5\cdot 10^{-5}\) relatively to the magnitude. The full value \(|H_{22}(\omega_1)|\cdot 100\ \text{N}\) is \(9{,}4394\) mm, and the largest value over all frequencies is \(9{,}4418\) mm, because the peak is at \(3{,}1146\) Hz, a little below \(\omega_1\): there the real part of the term of the first mode is positive like the term of the second mode, and the two add. The estimate with one term is smaller than the largest value by \(0{,}03\ \%\).

Let us look at the second question. In the table at \(7{,}130\) Hz the upper floor is almost at rest (\(0{,}01496\) mm), and the lower one moves \(0{,}19717\) mm, although the shaker pushes the upper one with \(100\) N. At \(5{,}042\) Hz the lower floor would stand still if we put the shaker on it. The frequency at which the principal element \(H_{\mathrm{kk}}\) is zero is called the antiresonance (antiresonanca) of coordinate \(k\). For two degrees of freedom we find it directly from the inverse of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix (lemma 4.49).

Theorem 10.55 Antiresonance of a system with two degrees of freedom (antiresonanca sistema z dvema prostostnima stopnjama)

Let \(n = 2\), \(\mat M = \mathrm{diag}(m_1, m_2)\) with \(m_1, m_2 > 0\), \(\mat K = \begin{bmatrix} k_{11} & k_{12} \\ k_{12} & k_{22} \end{bmatrix}\) positive definite with \(k_{12} \neq 0\) and \(\mat C = \mat 0\). Let \(\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2\) be the eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) (theorem 8.123) and \(\Omega > 0\) with \(\Omega^2 \neq \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\). With \(x = \Omega^2\) and \(\Delta(x) = (k_{11} - m_1x)(k_{22} - m_2x) - k_{12}^2\) the following holds:

  1. \(\mat H(\Omega) = \dfrac{1}{\Delta(x)}\begin{bmatrix} k_{22} - m_2x & -k_{12} \\ -k_{12} & k_{11} - m_1x \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\Delta(x) = m_1m_2\,(x - \lambda_1)(x - \lambda_2)\).
  2. The element \(H_{12}\) has no zero. The element \(H_{11}\) is zero exactly at \(x = k_{22}/m_2\) and \(H_{22}\) exactly at \(x = k_{11}/m_1\).
  3. \(\lambda_1 < k_{22}/m_2 < \lambda_2\) and \(\lambda_1 < k_{11}/m_1 < \lambda_2\).
  4. On \(\lambda_1 < x < \lambda_2\) we have \(\Delta < 0\), and \(H_{11}\) is negative at \(x < k_{22}/m_2\), positive at \(x > k_{22}/m_2\) and tends to \(-\infty\) as \(x \to \lambda_1\) and to \(+\infty\) as \(x \to \lambda_2\). The same holds for \(H_{22}\) with \(k_{11}/m_1\).
Proof

We must show the form of the matrix, the places of the zeros and their position between the eigenvalues.

  1. The dynamic stiffness matrix is \(\mat S = \begin{bmatrix} k_{11} - m_1x & k_{12} \\ k_{12} & k_{22} - m_2x \end{bmatrix}\) and its determinant (definition 2.50) is \(\Delta(x)\). The coefficient at \(x^2\) is \(m_1m_2\). The eigenvalues solve \(\det(\mat K - \lambda\mat M) = 0\) (theorem 8.123), that is \(\Delta(\lambda) = 0\). For \(\lambda_1 = \lambda_2\) there would not be two different roots, but \(\Delta(k_{22}/m_2) = -k_{12}^2 < 0\) for \(k_{12} \neq 0\) and \(m_1m_2 > 0\) means that \(\Delta\) has two different real roots, so \(\lambda_1 < \lambda_2\) and \(\Delta = m_1m_2(x - \lambda_1)(x - \lambda_2)\). Because \(\Omega^2 \neq \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) we have \(\Delta \neq 0\).
  2. By lemma 4.49 \(\mat H = \mat S^{-1}\) is the matrix of point 1.
  3. The numerators in \(H_{11}\) and \(H_{22}\) are \(k_{22} - m_2x\) and \(k_{11} - m_1x\), and the numerator in \(H_{12}\) is \(-k_{12} \neq 0\) and constant. So \(H_{12}\) has no zero, \(H_{11}\) is zero exactly at \(x = k_{22}/m_2\) and \(H_{22}\) at \(x = k_{11}/m_1\). This is point 2.
  4. The parabola \(\Delta\) has a positive leading coefficient, so it is negative exactly between the roots. Since \(\Delta(k_{22}/m_2) = -k_{12}^2 < 0\) by step 1 and \(\Delta(k_{11}/m_1) = -k_{12}^2 < 0\), the numbers \(k_{22}/m_2\) and \(k_{11}/m_1\) lie between \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\), strictly, where point 3 of theorem 8.123 states only inequalities. This is point 3.
  5. On \(\lambda_1 < x < \lambda_2\) we have \(\Delta < 0\), so \(H_{11}\) has the sign of the numerator with the opposite sign. The numerator \(k_{22} - m_2x\) is positive at \(x < k_{22}/m_2\) and negative at \(x > k_{22}/m_2\), so \(H_{11}\) is first negative and then positive, with the zero at \(x = k_{22}/m_2\). As \(x \to \lambda_1\), \(\Delta \to 0\) from the negative side and the numerator is positive by point 3, so \(H_{11} \to -\infty\), as \(x \to \lambda_2\) the numerator is negative, so \(H_{11} \to +\infty\). For \(H_{22}\) the computation is the same. This is point 4.

Source: GR, §2.6.2 and example 2.7 (PDF pp. 103-105): for any order GR states that the principal element \(h_{\mathrm{kk}}\) increases throughout with \(\omega^2\) and that an antiresonance lies between two resonances, and that the antiresonances are the natural frequencies of the system with the coordinate \(k\) held. The proof for \(n = 2\) is not from the source.

The proof showed that between two resonances the element \(H_{11}\) changes sign, at a frequency that the system itself determines. Which frequency is it? The quantity \(k_{22}/m_2\) is the eigenvalue of the system in which we hold coordinate \(1\), since the mass \(m_2\) remains on a spring of stiffness \(k_{22}\) (the stiffness \(k_{22}\) is the force in coordinate \(2\) that holds \(q_2 = 1\) at \(q_1 = 0\), as in section 10.1). Similarly \(k_{11}/m_1\) is the eigenvalue of the system with coordinate \(2\) held. At the antiresonance of coordinate \(1\) the mass \(m_2\) therefore oscillates as if free and its spring force on the mass \(m_1\) exactly balances the shaker, so the mass \(m_1\) stands still. For general order the same picture is given by the sum (10.68) at \(\zeta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\): the derivative of the principal element with respect to \(x = \Omega^2\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{r}} \varphi_{\mathrm{kr}}^2/(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} - x)^2 > 0\), so between neighbouring resonances at which \(\varphi_{\mathrm{kr}}\) and \(\varphi_{\mathrm{k},\mathrm{r}+1}\) are not zero the element goes from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\) and crosses zero exactly once. We do not prove this for \(n > 2\), but GR states it and calls it the antiresonance of coordinate \(k\).

Example 10.56 Antiresonances of frame A (antiresonanci okvira A)

For A we have \(m_1 = m_2 = m\), \(k_{11} = 2k\), \(k_{12} = -k\), \(k_{22} = k\), so the antiresonance of coordinate \(1\) lies at \(x = k/m\) and that of coordinate \(2\) at \(x = 2k/m\), that is at \(\Omega = 31{,}678\) 1/s (\(5{,}042\) Hz) and \(\Omega = 44{,}800\) 1/s (\(7{,}130\) Hz). The eigenvalues are \((3 \mp \sqrt5)/2\cdot k/m = 0{,}382\,k/m\) and \(2{,}618\,k/m\) (section 10.2) and both antiresonances lie between them, as point 3 of the theorem claims.

  1. At \(x = k/m\) we have \(\Delta = (2k - k)(k - k) - k^2 = -k^2\) and \(\mat H = \frac{1}{-k^2}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & k \\ k & k \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{k}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\). The force \(100\) N on the lower floor gives \(\vek q = \mat H\,(100, 0)^\T\,\text{N} = (0, -100\ \text{N}/k)^\T = (0, -0{,}19930)^\T\) mm: the lower floor stands still, the upper one moves by \(-0{,}19930\) mm. The spring between the floors is then shortened by \(0{,}19930\) mm and pushes the lower floor with the force \(k\,(q_2 - q_1) = -100\) N, exactly against the shaker. The upper storey acts as a tuned damper of the lower one, because the free upper mass on the spring \(k\) has exactly the frequency \(\sqrt{k/m}\). We shall use the same idea in the next section.
  2. At \(x = 2k/m\) we again have \(\Delta = 0\cdot(-k) - k^2 = -k^2\) and \(\mat H = \frac{1}{k}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). The force on the upper floor gives \(\vek q = (-100/k, 0)^\T\): the upper floor stands still, the lower one moves by \(-0{,}19930\) mm. The lower storey, held by both springs with the total stiffness \(2k\), has as a free system the frequency \(\sqrt{2k/m}\) and we excite it exactly at it. The same value \(2007{,}04\) 1/s\(^2\) is the eigenvalue of the frame with the upper floor held, which we met in corollary 10.29 on constraints.
  3. At \(x = k/m\) and a force on the upper floor, however, by step 1 \(\vek q = (-1, -1)^\T\cdot 100\ \text{N}/k\): both floors move equally and the upper spring is not stretched. The antiresonance is not a property of the frequency alone, but of the coordinate on which the force acts.
  4. With damping (\(\zeta = 0{,}02\)) the antiresonance does not reach zero. For a force on the lower floor \(|H_{11}(5{,}042\ \text{Hz})| = 0{,}0712\cdot 10^{-6}\) m/N, which is \(3{,}6\ \%\) of the static value \(1{,}9930\cdot 10^{-6}\) m/N, and the lower floor moves \(0{,}00712\) mm. For a force on the upper floor \(|H_{22}(7{,}130\ \text{Hz})| = 0{,}1496\cdot 10^{-6}\) m/N, which is \(3{,}8\ \%\) of the static value \(3{,}9860\cdot 10^{-6}\) m/N (table, \(0{,}01496\) mm).

The figures show the same as a function of frequency. Figure 10.31 shows \(|H_{12}|\) and \(|H_{22}|\) on logarithmic axes, figure 10.32 the phases, and figure 10.33 the shapes that the floors take at five frequencies from the table.

Figure 10.33 tells what the shaker does to the frame. At \(3{,}12\) and \(8{,}16\) Hz the frame sways in the shape of a mode, at \(5{,}04\) Hz the floors move as one mass, because the upper spring remains unstretched (step 3 of example 10.56), and at \(7{,}13\) Hz only the lower floor moves. The frequency response is therefore a map of the system: the peaks are its modes, the valleys its subsystems with one coordinate held, and the low frequencies its static flexibility \(\mat K^{-1}\).

10.11 The dynamic vibration absorber (dinamični dušilnik nihanja)

System A, the cantilever with a weight from section 9.1 (mass \(m = 50\) kg, stiffness \(k = 62\,720\) N/m, natural circular frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 35{,}4175\) 1/s, damping ratio \(\zeta = 0{,}01\)), swings by \(15{,}944\) mm under a force \(Q_0 = 20\) N at the frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), while the static displacement is only \(0{,}3189\) mm (section 9.6). Let the force come from a machine that runs at one constant frequency near \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), and let the cantilever be unchangeable. Can a small extra mass on a spring stop the swing?

The answer is yes, and we already know the idea from frame A (example 10.56 in section 10.10). For a force on the lower floor at the frequency \(\sqrt{k/m}\) the lower floor stood still, while the upper one moved and with its spring pulled the lower one back with a force exactly opposite to the external one. The upper floor was an extra mass on a spring by accident. Here we do it on purpose: we attach a mass \(m_{\mathrm{a}}\) on a spring \(k_{\mathrm{a}}\) to the main system (primary system, glavni sistem, figure 10.34) and choose them so that at the frequency of the excitation the spring returns exactly the opposite force. Such a device is called a dynamic vibration absorber (dinamični dušilnik nihanja). The word absorber does not mean the viscous damper of section 9.1.2: the device does not dissipate energy, it takes it over and gives it back.

The model is this. The main mass \(m\) has a spring \(k\) and a viscous damper \(c \ge 0\) to the ground and the force \(Q_0\cos\Omega t\) in the direction of the coordinate \(q_1\). The absorber is a mass \(m_{\mathrm{a}}\) connected to the main mass by a spring \(k_{\mathrm{a}}\), with no damping of its own, its displacement is \(q_2\). The ratio \(\mu = m_{\mathrm{a}}/m\) is called the mass ratio (razmerje mas). We measure both coordinates upwards from the equilibrium position. The weight of both masses shifts the equilibrium, as in section 9.1, and does not change the equations. The kinetic energy is \(T = \tfrac12 m\dot q_1^2 + \tfrac12 m_{\mathrm{a}}\dot q_2^2\), the potential energy \(V = \tfrac12 k q_1^2 + \tfrac12 k_{\mathrm{a}} (q_2 - q_1)^2\) and the dissipation function \(\mathcal D = \tfrac12 c\,\dot q_1^2\). All three functions are quadratic, so theorem 10.2 is exact and we obtain

\[\begin{aligned} m\,\ddot q_1 + c\,\dot q_1 + k\,q_1 + k_{\mathrm{a}}\,(q_1 - q_2) &= Q_0\cos\Omega t , \\ m_{\mathrm{a}}\,\ddot q_2 + k_{\mathrm{a}}\,(q_2 - q_1) &= 0 , \end{aligned} \tag{10.69}\]

that is \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek Q\) with \(\mat M = \mathrm{diag}(m, m_{\mathrm{a}})\), \(\mat C = \mathrm{diag}(c, 0)\) and \(\mat K = \begin{bmatrix} k + k_{\mathrm{a}} & -k_{\mathrm{a}} \\ -k_{\mathrm{a}} & k_{\mathrm{a}} \end{bmatrix}\). We can also read the matrix \(\mat K\) by the column rule (definition 7.4): at \(q_1 = 1\), \(q_2 = 0\) the springs \(k\) and \(k_{\mathrm{a}}\) are stretched and hold the main mass with a force \(k + k_{\mathrm{a}}\), while the spring \(k_{\mathrm{a}}\) pulls the other mass with a force \(-k_{\mathrm{a}}\). We obtain the same equations from Newton's law for each mass separately: the force of the spring \(k_{\mathrm{a}}\) on the main mass is \(k_{\mathrm{a}}(q_2 - q_1)\), and on the absorber the equal and opposite one.

What must the absorber satisfy? If the main mass stood still, \(q_1 = 0\), the spring would act on it with a force \(k_{\mathrm{a}} q_2\), and this would balance the external force at \(q_2 = -(Q_0/k_{\mathrm{a}})\cos\Omega t\). The second row of equations (10.69) with \(q_1 = 0\) is \(m_{\mathrm{a}}\ddot q_2 + k_{\mathrm{a}} q_2 = 0\): the absorber must move like a free oscillator and at the same time with the frequency of the excitation \(\Omega\). This is possible exactly when its natural frequency \(\sqrt{k_{\mathrm{a}}/m_{\mathrm{a}}}\) equals \(\Omega\). The theorem says this precisely.

Theorem 10.57 Dynamic vibration absorber (dinamični dušilnik nihanja)

Let \(m > 0\), \(k > 0\), \(c \ge 0\), \(m_{\mathrm{a}} > 0\), \(k_{\mathrm{a}} > 0\), \(Q_0\) a real number and \(\Omega > 0\). For the system (10.69) with the tuning (uglasitev) \(k_{\mathrm{a}} = m_{\mathrm{a}}\Omega^2\):

  1. The functions \(q_1 = 0\) and \(q_2 = -\dfrac{Q_0}{k_{\mathrm{a}}}\cos\Omega t\) are a solution. In it the main mass stands still and the force of the spring \(k_{\mathrm{a}}\) on the main mass is \(k_{\mathrm{a}}(q_2 - q_1) = -Q_0\cos\Omega t\), exactly opposite to the external force. This holds for every \(c\) and for every pair \(m_{\mathrm{a}}\), \(k_{\mathrm{a}}\) with the ratio \(k_{\mathrm{a}}/m_{\mathrm{a}} = \Omega^2\).
  2. If \(c > 0\), every solution approaches this one: for every start \(q_1(t) \to 0\) and \(q_2(t) + \dfrac{Q_0}{k_{\mathrm{a}}}\cos\Omega t \to 0\) as \(t\) tends to infinity.
Proof

We must show that the given functions solve both rows, and then that the free motion of the system with damping dies out. The first is a calculation with the cosine, the second goes through the roots of the characteristic polynomial.

  1. By theorem 8.12 the function \(q_2\) has the second derivative \(\ddot q_2 = -\Omega^2 q_2\). Since \(q_1 = 0\), all terms with \(q_1\) in the first row of equations (10.69) vanish and \(-k_{\mathrm{a}} q_2 = Q_0\cos\Omega t\) remains. This holds by the choice of \(q_2\).
  2. In the second row, \(m_{\mathrm{a}}\ddot q_2 + k_{\mathrm{a}} q_2 = (k_{\mathrm{a}} - m_{\mathrm{a}}\Omega^2)\,q_2 = 0\) by the tuning \(k_{\mathrm{a}} = m_{\mathrm{a}}\Omega^2\). This proves item 1, the spring force is \(k_{\mathrm{a}} q_2 = -Q_0\cos\Omega t\).
  3. Let \((q_1, q_2)\) be any solution of equations (10.69). The equations are linear, so the difference \((e_1, e_2)\) between it and the solution of item 1 solves the homogeneous system, that is the same system with \(Q_0 = 0\). We must show that \(e_1 \to 0\) and \(e_2 \to 0\).
  4. From the first row of the homogeneous system, \(k_{\mathrm{a}} e_2 = m\ddot e_1 + c\,\dot e_1 + (k + k_{\mathrm{a}})\,e_1\), so \(e_2\) is a linear combination of \(e_1\) and its derivatives. The second row is \(m_{\mathrm{a}}\ddot e_2 + k_{\mathrm{a}} e_2 = k_{\mathrm{a}} e_1\). The solutions are differentiable as many times as we like, because from these two rows a derivative of higher order is expressed by derivatives of lower order. So we apply the operator \(m_{\mathrm{a}}\,\mathrm{d}^2/\mathrm{d}t^2 + k_{\mathrm{a}}\) to both sides of the first relation. On the left, by the second row, it is \(k_{\mathrm{a}}\,(m_{\mathrm{a}}\ddot e_2 + k_{\mathrm{a}} e_2) = k_{\mathrm{a}}^2 e_1\), hence \(\big(m_{\mathrm{a}}\,\mathrm{d}^2/\mathrm{d}t^2 + k_{\mathrm{a}}\big)\big(m\,\mathrm{d}^2/\mathrm{d}t^2 + c\,\mathrm{d}/\mathrm{d}t + k + k_{\mathrm{a}}\big)e_1 - k_{\mathrm{a}}^2 e_1 = 0\). The function \(e_1\) is therefore a solution of a linear equation of fourth order with constant coefficients and the characteristic polynomial \(P(s) = (m_{\mathrm{a}} s^2 + k_{\mathrm{a}})\,(m s^2 + c\,s + k + k_{\mathrm{a}}) - k_{\mathrm{a}}^2\) (definition 9.33).
  5. By theorem 9.39, on every interval \([0, T]\) the function is \(e_1 = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} p_{\mathrm{j}}(t)\,\mathrm{e}^{\sigma_{\mathrm{j}} t}\) with polynomials \(p_{\mathrm{j}}\) and roots \(\sigma_{\mathrm{j}}\) of the polynomial \(P\). The coefficients of the polynomials are determined by the initial values \(e_1(0), \dots, e_1^{(3)}(0)\) and not by \(T\), so they are the same for every \(T\) and the formula holds for every \(t \ge 0\). The derivative of such a sum is again such a sum (product rule and theorem 9.28, item 3), so \(e_2\) is one too. Since \(|\mathrm{e}^{\sigma t}| = \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{Re}(\sigma)\,t}\) (theorem 9.28, item 2, for \(\sigma t = \mathrm{Re}(\sigma)\,t + \mathrm{i}\,\mathrm{Im}(\sigma)\,t\)), by lemma 9.15 (item 2) every term \(t^l\,\mathrm{e}^{\sigma t}\) tends to zero if \(\mathrm{Re}\,\sigma < 0\). So we must prove that every root \(s\) of the polynomial \(P\) has a negative real part.
  6. Let \(P(s) = 0\) and \(\vek x = (m_{\mathrm{a}} s^2 + k_{\mathrm{a}},\ k_{\mathrm{a}})^\T\). The matrix \(\mat S = s^2\mat M + s\,\mat C + \mat K\) has the rows \(\big(m s^2 + c\,s + k + k_{\mathrm{a}},\ -k_{\mathrm{a}}\big)\) and \(\big(-k_{\mathrm{a}},\ m_{\mathrm{a}} s^2 + k_{\mathrm{a}}\big)\). The first row, multiplied by \(\vek x\), gives \((m s^2 + c\,s + k + k_{\mathrm{a}})(m_{\mathrm{a}} s^2 + k_{\mathrm{a}}) - k_{\mathrm{a}}^2 = P(s) = 0\), and the second \(-k_{\mathrm{a}}(m_{\mathrm{a}} s^2 + k_{\mathrm{a}}) + (m_{\mathrm{a}} s^2 + k_{\mathrm{a}})\,k_{\mathrm{a}} = 0\). So \(\mat S\vek x = \vek 0\). The column \(\vek x\) is not zero, because \(k_{\mathrm{a}} \ne 0\). Its first element \(x_1 = m_{\mathrm{a}} s^2 + k_{\mathrm{a}}\) is different from zero: if \(x_1 = 0\), then \(P(s) = -k_{\mathrm{a}}^2 \ne 0\).
  7. Multiply \(\mat S\vek x = \vek 0\) from the left by the conjugate transposed column \(\overline{\vek x}^\T\). We get \(a\,s^2 + b\,s + d = 0\) with \(a = \overline{\vek x}^\T\mat M\vek x = m|x_1|^2 + m_{\mathrm{a}}|x_2|^2\), \(b = \overline{\vek x}^\T\mat C\vek x = c\,|x_1|^2\) and \(d = \overline{\vek x}^\T\mat K\vek x = k\,|x_1|^2 + k_{\mathrm{a}}\,|x_1 - x_2|^2\), because \((k + k_{\mathrm{a}})|x_1|^2 - k_{\mathrm{a}}(\overline{x_1} x_2 + \overline{x_2} x_1) + k_{\mathrm{a}}|x_2|^2 = k|x_1|^2 + k_{\mathrm{a}}|x_1 - x_2|^2\). All three numbers are real, since they are sums of squares of moduli (section 9.3). Since \(x_1 \ne 0\), \(m, m_{\mathrm{a}}, k > 0\) and \(c > 0\), we have \(a > 0\), \(b > 0\) and \(d > 0\).
  8. The roots of the equation \(a s^2 + b s + d = 0\) with real coefficients are \(s = \big(-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ad}\big)/(2a)\). If \(b^2 < 4ad\), the root is complex with real part \(-b/(2a) < 0\) (section 9.3). If \(b^2 \ge 4ad\), the root is real, and since \(ad > 0\), we have \(\sqrt{b^2 - 4ad} < b\), so \(s < 0\). In both cases \(\mathrm{Re}\,s < 0\). This proves item 2.

Source: CK, equations (9.14) to (9.16) (PDF p. 291-292): CK reads the same from them for the undamped main system, »the absorber will exert a force on the main mass that is exactly equal and opposite to the original disturbing force, regardless of the separate values k2 and m2«. Our steps 1 and 2 are the same calculation with a damper \(c\) on the main mass. The proof of item 2 is not from the source.

The theorem says two things. First, the spring of the absorber does not balance the swing but the force: the main mass no longer feels the external force, because at the tuning the spring force cancels it at all times. The damping of the main system does not change item 1, because the damping force \(c\,\dot q_1\) vanishes at \(q_1 = 0\). Second, the solution of item 1 makes sense only if the system also reaches it. Item 2 says that it does, whenever the main system has some damping, even though the absorber itself is not damped. The reason is step 6: in no free motion can the main mass stand still (\(x_1 \ne 0\)), because the moving absorber would drive it through its spring (the first row of the system \(\mat S\vek x = \vek 0\) gives \(x_2 = 0\) as well at \(x_1 = 0\)). So every free motion moves the main mass and its damper takes energy.

Example 10.58 An absorber on system A (dušilnik nihanja na sistemu A)

Take \(\mu = 0{,}05\), so \(m_{\mathrm{a}} = 2{,}5\) kg, and the tuning to \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 35{,}4175\) 1/s: \(k_{\mathrm{a}} = m_{\mathrm{a}}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2 = 3136{,}0\) N/m. Let \(Q_0 = 20\) N and \(\zeta = 0{,}01\) as in section 9.6.

By theorem 10.57 the main mass stands still at \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), while the absorber oscillates with the amplitude \(Q_0/k_{\mathrm{a}} = 20/3136 = 6{,}378\) mm and its spring acts on the main mass with a force of amplitude \(20\) N. Before the absorber the swing of the main mass was \(15{,}944\) mm. A calculation with the matrix \(\big(\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M + \mathrm{i}\,\Omega\,\mat C\big)^{-1}\) (NumPy, at \(\zeta = 0{,}01\)) gives at \(\Omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) the amplitude \(0{,}000000\) mm for the main mass and \(6{,}3776\) mm for the absorber.

The roots of the polynomial \(P\) from step 4 of the proof are by NumPy \(-0{,}15743 \pm 31{,}68147\,\mathrm{i}\) and \(-0{,}19675 \pm 39{,}59314\,\mathrm{i}\) 1/s. They have negative real parts, as item 2 requires, and the damping ratios of both modes are equal, \(0{,}00497\). The free motion dies out to one hundredth after \(\ln 100/0{,}15743 = 29{,}3\) s, while for system A alone (\(\zeta = 0{,}01\)) it takes \(13{,}00\) s (section 9.6). So the decay is slower with the absorber. The reason is that the damper \(c\) acts only on the main mass, and the main mass carries only a part of the motion of each mode. In step 8 the real part of the root is \(-b/(2a) = -\tfrac{c}{2m}\cdot m|x_1|^2/(m|x_1|^2 + m_{\mathrm{a}}|x_2|^2)\). The first factor is \(c/(2m) = \zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 0{,}35418\) 1/s, the second, the share of the main mass, is \(0{,}4445\) in the first and \(0{,}5555\) in the second mode. The products are \(0{,}15743\) and \(0{,}19675\) 1/s, as for the roots.

The ratios are equal because of two coefficients of the polynomial \(P\). Let the roots be \(-\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} \pm \mathrm{i}\beta_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(\rho_{\mathrm{j}} = \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}^2 + \beta_{\mathrm{j}}^2\) and \(\zeta_{\mathrm{j}} = \alpha_{\mathrm{j}}/\sqrt{\rho_{\mathrm{j}}}\) (\(j = 1, 2\)). The polynomial \(P/(m\,m_{\mathrm{a}})\) is the product \((s^2 + 2\alpha_1 s + \rho_1)(s^2 + 2\alpha_2 s + \rho_2)\). Comparing the coefficients at \(s^3\) gives \(2(\alpha_1 + \alpha_2) = c/m\), at \(s\) gives \(2(\alpha_1\rho_2 + \alpha_2\rho_1) = (c/m)\,k_{\mathrm{a}}/m_{\mathrm{a}}\), and the constant term is \(\rho_1\rho_2 = k k_{\mathrm{a}}/(m\,m_{\mathrm{a}}) = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^4\). The first two relations together give \(\alpha_1\rho_2 + \alpha_2\rho_1 = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2(\alpha_1 + \alpha_2)\), and with \(\alpha_{\mathrm{j}} = \zeta_{\mathrm{j}}\sqrt{\rho_{\mathrm{j}}}\) and \(\sqrt{\rho_1\rho_2} = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) this becomes \((\zeta_1 - \zeta_2)(\sqrt{\rho_2} - \sqrt{\rho_1}) = 0\). Since \(\sqrt{\rho_1} = 31{,}68147 \ne 39{,}59314 = \sqrt{\rho_2}\), we have \(\zeta_1 = \zeta_2\). The coefficient at \(s^3\) gives their value: \(\zeta_1 = \zeta_2 = \zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}}/(\sqrt{\rho_1} + \sqrt{\rho_2}) = 0{,}35418/71{,}2755 = 0{,}00497\).

The tuning holds at one frequency only, so the system with the absorber no longer has one natural frequency like A, but two (as in section 10.2), and between them lies the frequency \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) where the main mass stands still. Where are the two natural frequencies?

Corollary 10.59 Frequencies of the system with a tuned absorber (frekvenci sistema z uglašenim dušilnikom nihanja)

Let \(c = 0\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = \sqrt{k/m}\), \(k_{\mathrm{a}} = m_{\mathrm{a}}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) and \(\mu = m_{\mathrm{a}}/m\). The natural circular frequencies of the system (10.69) are \(\omega_1 = r_1\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(\omega_2 = r_2\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) with

\[r_{1,2}^2 = 1 + \frac{\mu}{2} \mp \sqrt{\mu + \frac{\mu^2}{4}} , \qquad r_1 < 1 < r_2 , \qquad r_1 r_2 = 1 . \tag{10.70}\]

Hence \(\omega_1\omega_2 = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\): the tuned frequency is the geometric mean of the two natural frequencies.

Proof

We must show that \(\lambda = r^2\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\) is an eigenvalue exactly when \(r^2\) solves a quadratic equation, and read off its solutions.

  1. The eigenvalues of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\) of order \(2\) solve \(\det(\mat K - \lambda\mat M) = 0\) (theorem 8.123). Here \(\det(\mat K - \lambda\mat M) = (k + k_{\mathrm{a}} - \lambda m)(k_{\mathrm{a}} - \lambda m_{\mathrm{a}}) - k_{\mathrm{a}}^2\).
  2. Insert \(k = m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\), \(k_{\mathrm{a}} = \mu m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\), \(m_{\mathrm{a}} = \mu m\) and \(\lambda = r^2\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\): the factors are \(m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2(1 + \mu - r^2)\) and \(\mu m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2(1 - r^2)\), \(k_{\mathrm{a}}^2 = \mu^2 m^2\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^4\). The determinant is \(\mu\,m^2\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^4\,\big[(1 + \mu - r^2)(1 - r^2) - \mu\big]\).
  3. The square bracket is \((1 - r^2)^2 + \mu(1 - r^2) - \mu = 1 - 2r^2 + r^4 - \mu r^2\), so the equation is \(r^4 - (2 + \mu)\,r^2 + 1 = 0\), quadratic in \(u = r^2\).
  4. Its solutions are \(u = \tfrac12(2 + \mu) \pm \sqrt{\tfrac14(2 + \mu)^2 - 1}\), where \(\tfrac14(2 + \mu)^2 - 1 = \mu + \mu^2/4 > 0\). This is equation (10.70).
  5. The constant term of the quadratic equation is the product of its solutions, so \(r_1^2 r_2^2 = 1\), and since \(r_1^2, r_2^2\) are positive (the sum \(2 + \mu\) and the product \(1\) are positive), \(r_1 r_2 = 1\). Since \(\mu/2 < \sqrt{\mu + \mu^2/4}\) (squares: \(\mu^2/4 < \mu + \mu^2/4\)), \(r_1^2 < 1 < r_2^2\).

Source: CK, figure 9.4 (PDF p. 292): for \(\mu = 0{,}20\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{p}} = \omega_{\mathrm{a}}\) it gives \(\omega_1/\omega_{\mathrm{a}} = 0{,}8011\) and \(\omega_2/\omega_{\mathrm{a}} = 1{,}2483\). The formula (10.70) gives \(0{,}80109\) and \(1{,}24830\). The formula and the proof are not from the source.

The product \(r_1 r_2 = 1\) has its cause in the determinants: the product of the two eigenvalues is \(\det\mat K/\det\mat M = k\,k_{\mathrm{a}}/(m\,m_{\mathrm{a}}) = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}^4\), because \(\det\mat K = (k + k_{\mathrm{a}})\,k_{\mathrm{a}} - k_{\mathrm{a}}^2 = k\,k_{\mathrm{a}}\).

For \(\mu = 0{,}05\) we have \(\sqrt{\mu + \mu^2/4} = \sqrt{0{,}050625} = 0{,}225\) exactly, so \(r_1^2 = 0{,}8\) and \(r_2^2 = 1{,}25\), \(r_1 = 0{,}89443\) and \(r_2 = 1{,}11803\). The natural frequencies are \(5{,}0418\) and \(6{,}3022\) Hz, system A alone has \(5{,}637\) Hz. For \(\mu = 0{,}1\) we have \(r_1 = 0{,}85431\) and \(r_2 = 1{,}17054\), that is \(4{,}8156\) and \(6{,}5982\) Hz. A heavier absorber moves the natural frequencies further apart.

What does the absorber do at frequencies other than \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\)? The answer comes from the frequency response matrix \(\mat H(\Omega) = (\mat K - \Omega^2\mat M + \mathrm{i}\,\Omega\,\mat C)^{-1}\) of definition 10.51, which holds for every \(\mat C\) for which it is invertible. By the formula for the inverse of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix (lemma 4.49) its element in the first row and first column is

\[H_{11}(\Omega) = \frac{k_{\mathrm{a}} - m_{\mathrm{a}}\Omega^2}{\big(k + k_{\mathrm{a}} - m\Omega^2 + \mathrm{i}\,c\,\Omega\big)\big(k_{\mathrm{a}} - m_{\mathrm{a}}\Omega^2\big) - k_{\mathrm{a}}^2} ,\]

as for the antiresonance in theorem 10.55, only with damping. The amplitude of the main mass is \(X = Q_0\,|H_{11}|\). The numerator \(k_{\mathrm{a}} - m_{\mathrm{a}}\Omega^2\) is zero exactly at the tuning, whatever \(c\) is: this is item 1 of theorem 10.57 in another form. With \(k = m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\), \(k_{\mathrm{a}} = \mu m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\), \(r = \Omega/\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) and \(c\,\Omega/k = 2\zeta r\) the ratio of the amplitude to the static displacement \(Q_0/k\) is

\[\frac{X}{Q_0/k} = \frac{|1 - r^2|}{\big|(1 + \mu - r^2 + 2\mathrm{i}\,\zeta r)(1 - r^2) - \mu\big|} . \tag{10.71}\]

At \(\zeta = 0\) this is the first of formulas (9.14) in CK (PDF p. 291) with \(\omega_{\mathrm{a}} = \omega_{\mathrm{p}}\), and for \(\mu \to 0\) it is \(1/|1 - r^2 + 2\mathrm{i}\zeta r|\), the dynamic factor \(D\) of definition 9.53. Figure 10.35 shows the formula for system A and \(\mu = 0\), \(0{,}05\), \(0{,}1\).

Example 10.60 The band in which the absorber works (pas, v katerem dušilnik nihanja deluje)

System A, \(\zeta = 0{,}01\), \(Q_0 = 20\) N, static displacement \(0{,}3189\) mm. Without an absorber the peak of the response is \(15{,}944\) mm at \(r = 1\). An absorber with \(\mu = 0{,}05\) has by equation (10.71) a zero at \(r = 1\) and two peaks, \(17{,}826\) mm at \(r = 0{,}89441\) and \(14{,}261\) mm at \(r = 1{,}11801\). At these frequencies the response is higher than without an absorber: at \(r = 0{,}8944\) system A alone was at \(1{,}588\) mm, at \(r = 1{,}118\) at \(1{,}270\) mm. So the absorber does not reduce the response at all frequencies. The peak that was at \(r = 1\) it splits into two new peaks on both sides and makes a zero in between.

The response is below the static displacement \(0{,}3189\) mm for \(r\) from \(0{,}97692\) to \(1{,}02469\), that is for frequencies around \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) in a band of width \(\pm 2{,}4\ \%\). For \(\mu = 0{,}1\) the peaks are \(18{,}663\) mm (\(r = 0{,}85429\)) and \(13{,}621\) mm (\(r = 1{,}17051\)), the band is from \(0{,}95685\) to \(1{,}04881\), that is \(\pm 4{,}6\ \%\). The band is wider for the heavier absorber, because near \(r = 1\) the numerator of equation (10.71) equals \(|\varepsilon|\) with \(\varepsilon = 1 - r^2\), while for small \(\varepsilon\) and \(\zeta r\) the denominator is approximately \(|(\mu + \varepsilon + 2\mathrm{i}\zeta r)\,\varepsilon - \mu| \approx \mu\). The ratio is then approximately \(|\varepsilon|/\mu\) and is below \(1\) for \(|1 - r^2| < \mu\), that is, with \(1 - r^2 \approx 2(1 - r)\), for \(|r - 1| < \mu/2\), so \(\pm 2{,}5\ \%\) at \(\mu = 0{,}05\) and \(\pm 5\ \%\) at \(\mu = 0{,}1\). The exact values are a little smaller (\(2{,}4\ \%\) and \(4{,}6\ \%\)), because we neglected \(\varepsilon^2\) and \(\mu\varepsilon\).

What does it mean that the absorber works only in a band? Let the frequency of the machine move away from the tuned one by \(3\ \%\) (\(r = 1{,}03\)). The response at \(\mu = 0{,}05\) is still \(0{,}393\) mm, while without an absorber it would be \(4{,}960\) mm. At \(5\ \%\) it is \(0{,}732\) mm against \(3{,}048\) mm. At \(10\ \%\) it is \(3{,}930\) mm against \(1{,}510\) mm: there the absorber has increased the response, because the frequency is already near its peak at \(r = 1{,}118\). If the machine stands at \(r = 0{,}8944\) at start-up, the response is \(17{,}826\) mm. CK (PDF p. 293) writes that on start-up through the first new resonance the amplitudes of both masses do not become large if the excitation frequency does not dwell there.

The absorber must also survive its own swing. The amplitude \(Q_0/k_{\mathrm{a}} = Q_0/(m_{\mathrm{a}}\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2)\) is \(6{,}378\) mm for \(m_{\mathrm{a}} = 2{,}5\) kg and \(3{,}189\) mm for \(5\) kg, so it is inversely proportional to the mass. The spring \(k_{\mathrm{a}}\) and its fastening must therefore withstand a force of amplitude \(Q_0 = 20\) N and a swing of \(6{,}4\) mm for arbitrarily many oscillations. CK (PDF p. 293) points out that the amplitude of the absorber mass and the largest force in its spring must be limited, and leaves the question whether the absorber should have damping too to its source [9.1]. Damped absorbers with optimal tuning are not treated here.

The absorber has one more consequence, which we see in the motion without an external force.

Example 10.61 Release of the main mass: the absorber and beats (sprostitev glavne mase: dušilnik nihanja in utripanje)

Take an absorber with \(\mu = 0{,}05\) without damping, \(c = 0\). We displace the main mass by \(1\) mm and release it, the absorber being at equilibrium: \(q_1(0) = 1\) mm, \(q_2(0) = 0\), velocities zero. The natural frequencies are \(\omega_1 = 31{,}6784\) and \(\omega_2 = 39{,}5980\) 1/s (equation (10.70)). The second row of the equation \((\mat K - \lambda\mat M)\vek\varphi = \vek 0\) is \(-k_{\mathrm{a}}\varphi_1 + (k_{\mathrm{a}} - \lambda m_{\mathrm{a}})\varphi_2 = 0\), so the ratio of the displacements is \(\varphi_2/\varphi_1 = k_{\mathrm{a}}/(k_{\mathrm{a}} - \lambda m_{\mathrm{a}}) = 1/(1 - r^2)\), that is \(5\) at \(r_1^2 = 0{,}8\) and \(-4\) at \(r_2^2 = 1{,}25\). The modes are \(\vek\varphi_1 = (1,\ 5)^\T\) and \(\vek\varphi_2 = (1,\ -4)^\T\): at the lower frequency both masses move in the same direction, the absorber five times as much, at the higher one in opposite directions. The start \((1,\ 0)^\T\) mm is \(a_1\vek\varphi_1 + a_2\vek\varphi_2\) with \(a_1 + a_2 = 1\) and \(5a_1 - 4a_2 = 0\), so \(a_1 = 4/9\) and \(a_2 = 5/9\). By the expansion in modes (section 10.4),

\[q_1 = \tfrac49\cos\omega_1 t + \tfrac59\cos\omega_2 t , \qquad q_2 = \tfrac{20}{9}\big(\cos\omega_1 t - \cos\omega_2 t\big) = \tfrac{40}{9}\,\sin\tfrac12(\omega_1 + \omega_2)t\,\sin\tfrac12(\omega_2 - \omega_1)t\]

in mm. The last equality is the same identity as in step 3 of the proof of theorem 9.56, applied to the difference of two cosines. So these are beats, but here they are caused by two natural frequencies of the same system and not by a force and a natural frequency. The fast oscillation has the circular frequency \(\tfrac12(\omega_1 + \omega_2) = 35{,}6382\) 1/s (period \(0{,}1763\) s), while the amplitude of the absorber, \(\tfrac{40}{9}\,|\sin\tfrac12(\omega_2 - \omega_1)t|\), repeats with the period \(2\pi/(\omega_2 - \omega_1) = 0{,}7934\) s and reaches \(40/9 = 4{,}444\) mm. The amplitude of the main mass varies between \(a_1 + a_2 = 1\) mm and \(a_2 - a_1 = 1/9\) mm, it does not fall to zero, because \(a_1\) and \(a_2\) differ. The total energy \(\tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek q} + \tfrac12\vek q^\T\mat K\vek q = 32{,}928\) mJ is constant (theorem 10.20, equation (10.24): the energies are sums over the modes, and since \(c = 0\), every mode solves \(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\) by equation (10.23), so \(\tfrac12\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}^2 + \tfrac12\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}^2\) is constant, because its derivative is \(\dot\eta_{\mathrm{r}}\,(\ddot\eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\eta_{\mathrm{r}}) = 0\)). The share of the main mass, \(\tfrac12 m\dot q_1^2 + \tfrac12 k q_1^2\), averaged over one fast oscillation around the time \(0\) is \(92{,}7\ \%\) and around the time \(0{,}397\) s it is \(6{,}1\ \%\), so at half the period of the envelope (figure 10.36). So the energy travels from the main mass into the absorber and back, and every \(0{,}793\) s it is at the main mass again.

Example 10.62 The upper floor of frame A as an absorber (zgornja plošča okvirja A kot dušilnik nihanja)

In frame A (section 10.2.1) every floor has the mass \(m = 500\) kg and every storey the stiffness \(k = 501\,760\) N/m. Let a force \(Q_0 = 100\) N act on the lower floor with the frequency \(\Omega = \sqrt{k/m} = 31{,}678\) 1/s (\(5{,}042\) Hz). The main system is the lower floor with the mass \(m\) and the spring \(k\) to the ground, and the absorber is the upper floor with \(m_{\mathrm{a}} = m\) and \(k_{\mathrm{a}} = k\), so \(k_{\mathrm{a}} = m_{\mathrm{a}}\Omega^2\). By theorem 10.57 the lower floor stands still, the upper one oscillates with the amplitude \(Q_0/k_{\mathrm{a}} = 100/501\,760 = 0{,}1993\) mm, and its spring pulls the lower floor with a force \(-100\) N. This is the same as shown by step 1 of example 10.56. With Rayleigh damping with \(\zeta = 0{,}02\) (step 4 of example 10.56) the amplitude of the lower floor there is \(0{,}00712\) mm and not zero: the damping also acts on the motion of the upper floor, so the absorber is then not undamped, as the theorem assumes.

Here \(\mu = 1\) and equation (10.70) gives \(r_{1,2}^2 = \tfrac32 \mp \sqrt{\tfrac54}\), that is \(r_1 = 0{,}61803\) and \(r_2 = 1{,}61803\) (the golden ratio). The natural frequencies are \(19{,}578\) and \(51{,}257\) 1/s (\(3{,}116\) and \(8{,}158\) Hz), exactly the natural frequencies of frame A, since this is the same system. An absorber with the mass of the main mass is no longer a small addition, but half of the system.

The absorber uses the same zero as the antiresonance of frame A and moves it to a frequency we choose. We obtain it with a small mass (\(\mu = 0{,}05\) means \(5\ \%\) of the mass of the main mass), at the price of two new resonances on both sides of the tuned frequency. The band in which the absorber works is the narrower, the lighter it is, and its swing the larger. For a machine that runs at the same frequency this is a good price. For a frequency that varies, an absorber with one spring and one mass is not enough.

10.12 Numerical integration in time (numerično reševanje v času)

So far we have written the motion of a system with several degrees of freedom with natural modes. With classical damping (section 10.9) every mode solves the equation of chapter 9, and the motion is the sum of these solutions. This route has two limits. The first is damping that couples the modes. For frame A with one damper in the first storey the matrix \(\mat\Phi^\T\mat C\,\mat\Phi\) has the off-diagonal entries \(1{,}267\) 1/s, so the equations by modes do not separate (section 10.9). The second limit is a force that is known only as a sequence of measured numbers, for example one every thousandth of a second. The Duhamel integral (theorem 9.79) cannot be evaluated with a formula, because there is no formula for the force. In both cases we solve the equation of motion step by step: from the state at one time we compute the state at a slightly later time. The question of the section is how a computer makes such a step, how it makes it so that the error does not grow beyond all bounds, and when this fails.

The starting point is the equation of motion of theorem 10.2,

\[\mat M\,\ddot{\vek q} + \mat C\,\dot{\vek q} + \mat K\,\vek q = \vek Q(t) , \tag{10.72}\]

with a positive definite mass matrix \(\mat M\), symmetric matrices \(\mat C\) and \(\mat K\) of order \(n\), the force \(\vek Q(t)\) and the initial columns \(\vek q(0) = \vek q_0\), \(\dot{\vek q}(0) = \vek v_0\). We choose a time step (časovni korak) \(\Delta t > 0\) and the times \(t_{\mathrm{k}} = k\,\Delta t\) for \(k = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) Instead of functions of time we look for sequences of columns \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\) that are meant to approximate \(\vek q(t_{\mathrm{k}})\), \(\dot{\vek q}(t_{\mathrm{k}})\) and \(\ddot{\vek q}(t_{\mathrm{k}})\). We require equation (10.72) at the times \(t_{\mathrm{k}}\),

\[\mat M\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \mat C\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \mat K\,\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek Q_{\mathrm{k}} , \qquad \vek Q_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek Q(t_{\mathrm{k}}) . \tag{10.73}\]

This is one equation for three unknown columns. A rule is still missing that tells how the displacement, velocity and acceleration change in one step. The rule we choose is called a scheme (shema). Different rules give different schemes, and the question is which one is good.

We shall first test each scheme on a single natural mode, the equation \(\ddot q + \omega^2 q = 0\) with \(q(0) = 1\) and \(\dot q(0) = 0\). Its exact solution is \(q = \cos\omega t\) with the period \(T = 2\pi/\omega\) (chapter 9). For \(\mat C = \mat 0\) and \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) the system splits in the scheme into such equations by modes, which we shall show in the proofs of theorems 10.67 and 10.70. A test on one mode is therefore a test on every mode.

10.12.1 The trapezoidal rule (trapezno pravilo)

Velocity is the integral of acceleration, displacement the integral of velocity. On one step we know the acceleration only at its end points, \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\). If we replace the acceleration on the step by their mean value, the velocity changes by \(\Delta t\) times this mean acceleration. We do the same with the displacement: we replace the velocity by the mean of its values at the end points, and the displacement changes by the area of the trapezoid under the straight line between \(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}\). Hence the name. We cannot compute the velocity and the displacement until we know the acceleration at the end of the step, and that is determined by the equation of motion at the end of the step. The unknowns are therefore obtained together from a system of equations.

Definition 10.63 Trapezoidal rule (trapezno pravilo)

Let \(\mat M\) be positive definite, \(\mat C\) and \(\mat K\) symmetric matrices of order \(n\), \(\vek Q(t)\) a column of forces, \(\Delta t > 0\) a time step and \(\vek q_0\), \(\vek v_0\) initial columns. The trapezoidal rule (or the average acceleration scheme, shema s povprečnim pospeškom) is the sequence of columns \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\) with \(k = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) that is determined by the initial values \(\vek q_0\), \(\vek v_0\), by equation (10.73) at \(k = 0\), which gives \(\vek a_0\), and for every \(k \ge 0\) by the equations

  1. \[\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \frac{\Delta t}{2}\,(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}) , \tag{10.74}\]
  2. \[\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \frac{\Delta t}{2}\,(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}) , \tag{10.75}\]
  3. equation (10.73) at \(k + 1\), that is \(\mat M\,\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \mat C\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \mat K\,\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek Q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\).

Source: COOK §11.13 (PDF p. 430 to 432): "average acceleration" is Newmark's scheme, "often called the trapezoidal rule", because \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac12\Delta t(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}})\) is the area of a trapezoid (PDF pp. 431 to 432). BATHE §9.2.3 (9.18) and (9.19), PDF p. 794: Newmark's scheme with the parameters \(\delta = 1/2\) and \(\alpha = 1/4\) is the "constant-average-acceleration method (also called trapezoidal rule)". The notation with equations (10.74) and (10.75) is ours, from both equations in the source follows COOK's (11.13-3) with \(\gamma = 1/2\), \(\beta = 1/4\) (see lemma 10.64).

Let us determine how a computer actually makes one step. We express the unknowns \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\), \(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) and \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) from equations (10.74), (10.75) and the third equation of the definition by \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\), and one system of linear equations with the unknown \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) remains. Its matrix does not depend on \(k\), so for the given \(\Delta t\) we factorize it once (solving large systems is in chapter 17) and at every step only apply the factorization (COOK PDF p. 432).

Lemma 10.64 One step of the trapezoidal rule (en korak trapeznega pravila)

In definition 10.63 let \(\mat C\) and \(\mat K\) be positive semidefinite. The matrix

\[\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}} = \mat K + \frac{2}{\Delta t}\,\mat C + \frac{4}{\Delta t^2}\,\mat M \tag{10.76}\]

is positive definite, hence invertible. The columns \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\), \(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}\), \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) satisfy equations (10.74), (10.75) and the third equation of the definition exactly when

\[\begin{aligned} &\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \vek Q_{\mathrm{k}+1} \\ &\quad + \mat M\Big(\frac{4}{\Delta t^2}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \frac{4}{\Delta t}\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} \\ &\qquad + \vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\Big) + \mat C\Big(\frac{2}{\Delta t}\,\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}}\Big) \end{aligned} \tag{10.77}\]

and

\[\begin{aligned} &\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \frac{2}{\Delta t}\,(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek q_{\mathrm{k}}) - \vek v_{\mathrm{k}} , \\ &\qquad \vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \frac{4}{\Delta t^2}\,(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} \\ &\quad - \Delta t\,\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}) - \vek a_{\mathrm{k}} . \end{aligned} \tag{10.78}\]

The trapezoidal rule therefore has exactly one sequence for every start \(\vek q_0\), \(\vek v_0\) and every force.

Proof

We show that the equations of the definition can be expressed by equations (10.78) and that equation (10.77) remains after substitution.

  1. We solve equation (10.74) for \(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}\). With \(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \frac{2}{\Delta t}(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek q_{\mathrm{k}}) - \vek v_{\mathrm{k}}\) we get the first equation (10.78).
  2. We solve equation (10.75) for \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\): \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \frac{2}{\Delta t}(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek v_{\mathrm{k}}) - \vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\). We insert step 1 into it: \(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} = \frac{2}{\Delta t}\big(\frac{2}{\Delta t}(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek q_{\mathrm{k}}) - 2\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}\big) - \vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\), which is the second equation (10.78).
  3. We insert steps 1 and 2 into the third equation of the definition. The term \(\mat M\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) is \(\frac{4}{\Delta t^2}\mat M\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \mat M\big(\frac{4}{\Delta t^2}\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \frac{4}{\Delta t}\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek a_{\mathrm{k}}\big)\), the term \(\mat C\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) is \(\frac{2}{\Delta t}\mat C\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \mat C\big(\frac{2}{\Delta t}\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}}\big)\). We collect the terms with the unknown \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) on the left, the rest on the right, and obtain equation (10.77) with the matrix (10.76).
  4. Steps 1 to 3 are reversible, since each solves one equation for one unknown. The equations of the definition therefore hold exactly when (10.77) and (10.78) hold.
  5. For \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\) we have \(\vek x^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}\vek x = \vek x^\T\mat K\vek x + \frac{2}{\Delta t}\vek x^\T\mat C\vek x + \frac{4}{\Delta t^2}\vek x^\T\mat M\vek x \ge \frac{4}{\Delta t^2}\vek x^\T\mat M\vek x > 0\), because \(\mat K\) and \(\mat C\) are positive semidefinite and \(\mat M\) is positive definite. If \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}\vek x = \vek 0\) held with \(\vek x \ne \vek 0\), then also \(\vek x^\T\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}\vek x = 0\), a contradiction. A square matrix whose equation \(\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}\vek x = \vek 0\) has only the zero solution is invertible (lemma 8.21). Hence equation (10.77) has exactly one solution.

Source: COOK (11.13-3) to (11.13-5), PDF p. 432: the same system with \(\gamma = 1/2\) and \(\beta = 1/4\). It says there that \([\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}]\) is nonsingular if \([\mat M]\) is positive definite, even for an unsupported structure, and that a diagonal mass matrix is of no use, because \([\mat K_{\mathrm{ef}}]\) contains \([\mat K]\) (PDF p. 432). The proof is not from the source.

A test on one mode. For \(\ddot q + \omega^2 q = 0\), \(\omega = 1\) 1/s, \(q_0 = 1\), \(v_0 = 0\) and the step \(\Delta t = T/10 = 0{,}62832\) s we have \(a_0 = -\omega^2 q_0 = -1\) 1/s\(^2\) and \(K_{\mathrm{ef}} = 1 + 4/\Delta t^2 = 11{,}1321\) 1/s\(^2\). The right-hand side of equation (10.77) is \(4/\Delta t^2 + a_0 = 9{,}1321\) 1/s\(^2\), so \(q_1 = 0{,}82034\). The exact value is \(\cos 0{,}62832 = 0{,}80902\), the error of the first step is \(1{,}4\) %.

A question follows that the first step does not open: what happens after a thousand steps? The error may accumulate slowly, and then the scheme is merely inaccurate. But the sequence \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\) may also grow beyond all bounds, although the exact motion of the undamped system is bounded, since the energy is conserved (section 10.4). Such a failure is a different kind of error than inaccuracy, and we call it instability.

Definition 10.65 Stability of a scheme (stabilnost sheme)

Let \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) be positive definite matrices of order \(n\) and let a scheme (the trapezoidal rule or central differences) for the equation \(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q = \vek 0\) with the step \(\Delta t\) determine a sequence \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\) from the initial values. The scheme is stable (stabilna) at this step if for every choice of initial values the sequence \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\) is bounded, that is, if there is a number \(B\) with \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\,\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} \le B\) for every \(k\). The scheme is unconditionally stable (brezpogojno stabilna) if it is stable at every \(\Delta t > 0\). The scheme is conditionally stable (pogojno stabilna) with the critical time step (kritični korak) \(\Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\) if it is stable exactly for \(\Delta t < \Delta t_{\mathrm{kr}}\). The initial values are \(\vek q_0\) and \(\vek v_0\) for the trapezoidal rule and \(\vek q_0\) and \(\vek q_1\) for central differences (section 10.12.2).

Source: COOK §11.13, PDF p. 430: "those in common use are unconditionally stable: even very large values of Δt do not make calculations blow up (but may destroy accuracy)". BATHE §9.2.1, PDF p. 790: "conditionally stable". Boundedness in the norm \(\sqrt{\vek q^\T\mat M\vek q}\) is our choice: since \(\mat M\) is positive definite, by theorem 8.26 we have \(\vek q^\T\mat M\vek q \ge \mu\,|\vek q|^2\) with \(\mu > 0\), so a bounded norm is the same as bounded components.

The trapezoidal rule has a property that is rare among schemes: it conserves energy exactly. The energy for \(\mat C = \mat 0\) and \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) is \(\mathcal{E} = \tfrac12\dot{\vek q}^\T\mat M\dot{\vek q} + \tfrac12\vek q^\T\mat K\vek q\) and is constant for the exact solution (section 10.4). We write its discrete version with the values of the scheme, \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac12\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat K\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\).

Theorem 10.66 Energy of the trapezoidal rule (energija pri trapeznem pravilu)

Let \(\mat M\) be positive definite and \(\mat K\), \(\mat C\) symmetric matrices of order \(n\), let \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) and let the trapezoidal rule (definition 10.63) exist. With \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac12\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat K\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\) we have for every \(k \ge 0\) and every \(\Delta t > 0\)

\[\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} = -\frac{\Delta t}{4}\,(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1})^\T\mat C\,(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}) . \tag{10.79}\]

Therefore:

  1. For \(\mat C = \mat 0\) we have \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} = \mathcal{E}_0\) for every \(k\).
  2. If \(\mat C\) is positive semidefinite, \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}}\) does not increase with the step.
  3. If \(\mat K\) is positive definite, \(\mat C\) positive semidefinite and \(\lambda_1\) the smallest eigenvalue of the pair \((\mat K, \mat M)\), then \(\tfrac12\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} \le \mathcal{E}_0\) and \(\tfrac12\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} \le \mathcal{E}_0/\lambda_1\) for every \(k\) and every \(\Delta t\). For \(\mat C = \mat 0\) the trapezoidal rule is unconditionally stable.
Proof

We transform the energy difference into products of sums and differences, replace the differences by the rules of the scheme and use the equation of motion.

  1. Since \(\mat M\) and \(\mat K\) are symmetric, \(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}^\T\mat M\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek v_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} = (\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}})^\T\mat M(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek v_{\mathrm{k}})\), because on expanding the product the mixed terms \(-\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}^\T\mat M\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(+\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) cancel (they are equal numbers, since \(\mat M\) is symmetric). The same holds for \(\mat K\) and \(\vek q\). Hence \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac12(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}})^\T\mat M(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek v_{\mathrm{k}}) + \tfrac12(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek q_{\mathrm{k}})^\T\mat K(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek q_{\mathrm{k}})\).
  2. We replace the differences by equations (10.75) and (10.74): \(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek v_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1})\) and \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \vek q_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1})\). We get \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}+1} - \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} = \tfrac{\Delta t}{4}\big[(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}})^\T\mat M(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek a_{\mathrm{k}}) + (\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek q_{\mathrm{k}})^\T\mat K(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}})\big]\).
  3. We add the equation of motion (10.73) with \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) at \(k\) and \(k + 1\): \(\mat M(\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1}) = -\mat C(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}) - \mat K(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1})\).
  4. We insert this into the first term of step 2. The first term is then \(-\tfrac{\Delta t}{4}(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}})^\T\mat C(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}) - \tfrac{\Delta t}{4}(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}})^\T\mat K(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1})\). The second term of step 2 is \(+\tfrac{\Delta t}{4}(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek q_{\mathrm{k}})^\T\mat K(\vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}})\), and it equals the term with \(\mat K\) just obtained with the opposite sign, because \(\mat K\) is symmetric (a number equals its transpose). The terms with \(\mat K\) cancel and equation (10.79) remains.
  5. Points 1 and 2 are special cases of equation (10.79): for \(\mat C = \mat 0\) the right-hand side is zero, for a positive semidefinite \(\mat C\) we have \(\vek w^\T\mat C\vek w \ge 0\) for \(\vek w = \vek v_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek v_{\mathrm{k}+1}\) and the right-hand side is at most zero.
  6. Point 3. By point 2 we have \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}} \le \mathcal{E}_0\). Both terms of the energy are nonnegative (\(\mat M\) positive definite, \(\mat K\) positive definite), so each of them is at most \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{k}}\), hence \(\tfrac12\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\vek v_{\mathrm{k}} \le \mathcal{E}_0\). By theorem 10.26 we have \(\lambda_1\,\vek q^\T\mat M\vek q \le \vek q^\T\mat K\vek q\) for every \(\vek q\), so \(\tfrac12\lambda_1\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat M\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} \le \tfrac12\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}^\T\mat K\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} \le \mathcal{E}_0\). The bounds do not contain \(\Delta t\). The sequence \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\) is therefore bounded at every step, which by definition 10.65 means unconditional stability for \(\mat C = \mat 0\).

Source: COOK §11.14 (PDF pp. 435 to 437) proves stability by analysing one mode, \(Z = \lambda^n\), and also mentions "energy stability analysis", which it does not carry out (PDF p. 435). The energy computation above is not from the source.

The proof has shown why the energy stays constant. In exact time the derivative of the energy is \(\dot{\mathcal{E}} = \dot{\vek q}^\T(\mat M\ddot{\vek q} + \mat K\vek q) = 0\), because the equation of motion cancels the bracket. The trapezoidal rule repeats this computation with values averaged over the step, and therefore the terms with \(\mat K\) and with \(\mat M\) cancel exactly, not only approximately. The theorem, however, does not say whether the state is at the right place on the path of constant energy. The next theorem says that.

For \(\mat C = \mat 0\) and \(\vek Q = \vek 0\) the scheme also splits by modes. Let \(\mat K\) be positive definite and let \(\lambda_{\mathrm{r}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\), \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) be the eigenpairs of \((\mat K, \mat M)\) from theorem 10.13. The modal coordinate is \(\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\) and its velocity \(\xi_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}\). For the exact solution \(\eta_{\mathrm{r}} = \eta_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\cos\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t + \xi_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\,\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^{-1}\sin\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t\) (theorem 10.21). We write the pair \((\eta_{\mathrm{r}}, \xi_{\mathrm{r}}/\omega_{\mathrm{r}})\) as the complex number \(z_{\mathrm{r}} = \eta_{\mathrm{r}} + \mathrm{i}\,\xi_{\mathrm{r}}/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) (section 9.3). The exact solution is then \(z_{\mathrm{r}}(t) = z_{\mathrm{r}}(0)\,(\cos\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t - \mathrm{i}\sin\omega_{\mathrm{r}} t)\): the number rotates in the complex plane with constant size and with the turn \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t\) per step (lemma 9.25).

Theorem 10.67 Turn per step of the trapezoidal rule (zasuk na korak pri trapeznem pravilu)

Let \(\mat K\) and \(\mat M\) be positive definite, \(\mat C = \mat 0\), \(\vek Q = \vek 0\), \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}} > 0\) as in theorem 10.13, \(\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\), \(\xi_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} = \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek v_{\mathrm{k}}\) and \(z_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} = \eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} + \mathrm{i}\,\xi_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}/\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\) for \(r = 1, \dots, n\). For the trapezoidal rule with the step \(\Delta t\) and \(x_{\mathrm{r}} = \omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t/2\) we have

\[\begin{aligned} z_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}+1} &= \frac{1 - \mathrm{i}\,x_{\mathrm{r}}}{1 + \mathrm{i}\,x_{\mathrm{r}}}\,z_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} \\ &= \big(\cos 2\alpha_{\mathrm{r}} - \mathrm{i}\sin 2\alpha_{\mathrm{r}}\big)\,z_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} , \\ &\qquad \tan\alpha_{\mathrm{r}} = x_{\mathrm{r}} , \ \ \alpha_{\mathrm{r}} \in (0, \tfrac{\pi}{2}) . \end{aligned} \tag{10.80}\]

The size \(|z_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}|\) is therefore constant, and the turn per step is \(2\alpha_{\mathrm{r}} = 2\arctan(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t/2)\) instead of the exact \(\omega_{\mathrm{r}}\Delta t\).

Proof

We show that at every step the complex number \(z_{\mathrm{r}}\) is multiplied by the same number of size \(1\).

  1. Splitting by modes. We multiply equations (10.74) and (10.75) by \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\). We get \(\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}+1} = \eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(\xi_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} + \xi_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}+1})\) and \(\xi_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}+1} = \xi_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}} + \tfrac{\Delta t}{2}(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} + \vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek a_{\mathrm{k}+1})\). The equation of motion is \(\mat M\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} = -\mat K\vek q_{\mathrm{k}}\). By corollary 10.14 we have \(\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} = \sum_{\mathrm{s}} \eta_{\mathrm{s},\mathrm{k}}\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\), and by theorem 10.13 \(\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{s}}\mat M\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = 1\) for \(s = r\), \(0\) otherwise, so \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{s}} = \lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\) for \(s = r\) and \(0\) otherwise. Hence \(\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat M\vek a_{\mathrm{k}} = -\vek\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}^\T\mat K\vek q_{\mathrm{k}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{r}}^2\,\eta_{\mathrm{r},\mathrm{k}}\).
